articles.title: Georgia city removes 23-year-old mayor after sexting and municipal funds scandal
articles.summary: Jayden Williams of Stockbridge alleged to have made inappropriate texts to teen and using city funds improperly

blocks.text: City leaders in a suburb outside Atlanta have voted to remove the youngest mayor in their community’s history amid allegations of questionable spending of municipal funds and inappropriate communications with an 18-year-old high school student.

Over the weekend, the Stockbridge, Georgia, city council voted to remove Jayden Williams, 23, from office after an hours-long hearing into allegations that included inappropriate exchanges with an 18-year-old in high school, improper purchases on a municipal government-issued credit card and mistreatment of employees.
Williams took office in January after defeating incumbent Anthony Ford in an election two months earlier.
According to local news outlets, an investigation into Williams preceding his removal examined his communications with an 18-year-old high school student.

Williams at one point reportedly offered the teenager a city-backed internship and mentorship while also asking if they could be “friends with benefits”, a term implying a casual rather than a committed sexual relationship. Williams reportedly added, “This better stay between us too,” according to the outlet.

During the council hearing, lawyer Robbie Ashe, who was representing Stockbridge investigators, asked Williams: “Is getting nude photographs via text message so unremarkable to you that you don’t remember when you get them?” NBC reported.
Williams replied, “It’s not memorable nor is it abnormal for somebody my age.
“That’s not abnormal for somebody my age.”

The communications in question began shortly after Williams’ election victory and were carried out on Williams’ personal phone, Atlanta News First reported. They included sexually suggestive messages and explicit photos.

Other allegations against Williams involved his use of a city-issued credit card. According to Atlanta News First, the purchases included $35.79 for movie tickets, $63.83 at a Polo Factory store and $322.92 at Pandora.

Williams said his use of the city-issued credit card was accidental because it is the same color and looks like his personal card. “Nobody said anything to me at the time,” he said, adding that he had reimbursed the city, according to Atlanta News First.

Investigators also alleged that Williams created a hostile work environment, including changing the locks on his office and requiring staff to slide documents underneath the door. They also accused him of shouting at staff members and allegedly threatening an interim city clerk that she would never be permanently appointed, the outlet reported.
During the hearing, Williams denied ordering the locks to be changed and said keys often jammed in them, according to Atlanta News First.
after newsletter promotion

Stockbridge officials discussed Williams’ removal in a statement that said: “The city … has taken formal action concerning the office of mayor following proceedings conducted pursuant to applicable city processes. As a result of that action, the mayor has been removed from office.”
After the hearing, Williams’ attorney, Robert Kenner, said the council’s removal of his client “was very disappointing”, NBC reported.
“I don’t believe that it was based on any evidence.”
Meanwhile, interim mayor Elton Alexander said Williams’ fate stemmed from the findings of whom he described as an independent investigator, Richard Hyde.

“Removing Stockbridge mayor Jayden William from office was a tough decision,” Alexander said. “It brings a fair and equitable close to multiple troubling accusations that were investigated and verified by [Hyde]. The results of the investigation demanded we act.”
Williams is not the only young mayor to have been met with legal or political trouble.

Tyrin Truong was elected mayor of Bogalusa, Louisiana, in 2022 at 23 years old and was arrested in January 2025 in connection with a drug-trafficking investigation. He has pleaded not guilty to multiple charges, including malfeasance and theft, and in January 2026 announced a re-election bid.

articles.title: Louise Haigh: UK must heed warnings from AI experts
articles.summary:
First secretary warns of ‘huge risks’ of technology as PM is urged to use next year’s G20 to drive global regulation

Ministers must “heed the warnings” from industry leaders about the threat…
articles.byline: Alexandra Topping, Kiran Stacey,Dan Milmo and Robert Booth

blocks.text: Ministers must “heed the warnings” from industry leaders about the threat posed by AI, Louise Haigh has said, amid calls for Andy Burnham to use the G20 to drive global regulation.

The first secretary said that while AI had enormous potential to improve lives, and the government wanted to capitalise on the technology, there were “clearly huge risks to our national security and society if the right guardrails are not put in place”.

In a speech at the TUC conference on Tuesday, Haigh acknowledged that the public was worried about jobs and their children’s future, after three Anthropic researchers warned that artificial intelligence could wipe out humanity within the decade.

Labour MPs and peers stepped up calls for the government to work with international partners to impose regulations on the technology, with Darren Jones, Keir Starmer’s chief secretary, calling for Burnham to put international G20 regulation on the agenda when the UK hosts the summit next year.

Action required collaboration, said Jones, adding: “The thing I would be worried about is if we go into a classic Westminster approach of creating a new regulator and inadvertently kill off the AI ecosystem in this country.”

Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the TUC said AI was a “clear and present danger to workers and wider society”, and urged Burnham to show global leadership. “As G20 president he has an opportunity to work with other countries to drive global regulation and make sure this technology benefits everyone, not just the super-rich,” he said.

Meanwhile, Liam Byrne, the Labour MP who chairs the business committee, has written to Henry de Zoete, the head of the AI Safety Institute (AISI), asking him to testify to parliament after calls from the parliamentary committee for human rights for a regulatory framework for AI in the UK.

In his letter, Byrne wrote that there was a growing public concern about the risk of “unfettered, inadequately governed artificial intelligence development” and “the adequacy of current AI safety governance”.
The Guardian has learned that the AI company Anthropic will not face sanctions after it declined to submit its latest model for testing by the AISI before launching it.

Over the weekend, the company urged its competitors and governments to coordinate a global slowdown in AI development. It was backed by many of its rivals including OpenAI, Google DeepMind and X’s Elon Musk.

On Monday night, one of the founders of Anthropic, Jack Clark, suggested that an artificial intelligence “kill switch” held by a third party may need to be mandatory for companies, saying it was something society “might want to eventually pass rules around”.
One of Anthropic’s biggest rivals and the developer of ChatGPT, OpenAI, has urged the government to capitalise on renewed fears over AI safety and impose legislation reining in the technology.

But on Tuesday the US president, Donald Trump, called fears about AI a “hoax”, and criticised calls to impose guardrails. In a series of social media posts, the US president claimed the only “guardrails” needed for AI was a “strong and smart” president.

Haigh told trade unions that AI had the potential to “transform our public services, make our businesses stronger and deliver new scientific breakthroughs”. But she added that the government must “heed the warnings of those who are at the forefront of developing this technology” and “be ready to work with international partners” to prioritise public safety and national security.

Answering questions after the speech she said working people had to be “at the heart of the debate” and the government would work with unions and employers. “Where AI makes work more productive, then benefits should be felt by workers, not just shareholders or tech bros,” she said.
after newsletter promotion

The risks of AI were a topic of fierce debate at the gathering of trade union officials in Brighton, where delegates passed a motion urging the government to introduce a national AI plan and called on it to resist influence from “the big tech lobby”.

Teachers described how AI was already being used in classrooms to record and assess teacher performance. A rep from the Unite union said crane operators were being analysed and used to teach AI models how to automate cranes in the future, while HGV drivers were under constant surveillance. “We have finance and IT workers whose employers see them as a cost to be saved, and AI as the tool to do it,” said Unite’s Pat Dowling. The union’s general secretary, Sharon Graham, said: “Workers and public safety are being completely lost in the AI debate, and they have to be at the heart of it.”

blocks.caption: Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, has called on the AI industry to coordinate a slowdown. Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters

blocks.text: But the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said people should not get “hyperbolic” about the risks of AI, telling the BBC Today programme that he did not think it would be particularly helpful to discuss a potential AI “kill switch”.
AI researchers have continued to add their voices of concern to the debate.
A researcher at OpenAI has warned that AI models – the technology that underpins tools such as chatbots – could mislead human overseers into believing they are safe.
Dan Selsam claimed the models would “likely convince people that everything is fine” and “argue convincingly that humans should trust them with power”.

Bilal Chughtai, another AI safety researcher who left Google DeepMind this summer, said late on Monday that “AI has the potential to kill us all” and we might be “running out of time to avoid this outcome”.

articles.title: Belfast teenager whose body was found in storm drain ‘failed by the PSNI’
articles.summary:
Not enough evidence to explain circumstances of Noah Donohoe’s death, partly due to police mistakes, inquest finds

An inquest into the death of a teenager whose body was found in a Belfast…

blocks.text: An inquest into the death of a teenager whose body was found in a Belfast storm drain has found there is not enough evidence to explain the puzzling circumstances of how he died, partly because of mistakes by police investigators.

Noah Donohoe, 14, was last seen on 21 June 2020 when he left his south Belfast home on his bicycle, telling his mother he was going to visit friends. His naked body was found six days later, deep inside an underground water tunnel in the north of the city.

The case provoked huge interest in Northern Ireland, with intense speculation on social media over how and why he died, and concerns raised about the police handling of the case. A postmortem in 2020 found that Noah died by drowning.

The inquest jury had heard eyewitness and CCTV evidence that Noah had been seen cycling through Belfast in the afternoon and early evening of Sunday 21 June, at one point falling from his bike, and apparently abandoning items of clothing and possessions as he went. He was eventually seen cycling naked, and was captured on CCTV abandoning his black Apollo mountain bike and making his way in the direction of a stream that led to the storm drain.

A jury at Belfast coroners’ court found no failings by the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) that might have contributed to the teenager’s death after unanimously agreeing that he died before he was reported missing. However, they identified a series of 13 failures by investigators that they said had affected their ability to reach conclusions on its circumstances.

These included a failure to secure some CCTV evidence, to follow up leads relating to Noah’s green coat, which has never been recovered, and to take relevant statements in a reasonable timeframe. Jurors said the overall house-to-house search strategy for Noah was “poorly” executed, managed and recorded. They found that some statements were not taken within a reasonable timeframe and the quality of entries in police notebooks was poor. In addition, there had been delays in identifying and searching the storm drain.

The inquest found it was possible, but not probable, that mistakes in the management of the storm drain by the Northern Ireland assembly’s Department for Infrastructure had contributed to Noah’s death. No warning signs were erected at the location and it was closed off only by a debris screen that did not prevent access.

Fiona Donohoe, Noah’s mother, had told the inquest that her son had been uncharacteristcally emotional and affectionate in the days before his disappearance, and that she had had fears over his mental health, having found him crying in his bedroom.

She said her son had become fixated on the controversial Canadian psychologist Jordan Peterson; one of Peterson’s books, 12 Rules for Life, was in Noah’s backpack along with his laptop when he left home. Friends and teachers described an intelligent, funny and musical child who had been a popular high-achiever at school.

The jury also heard evidence from a number of psychiatric experts who agreed Noah did not appear to have suicidal tendencies or to have taken drugs. A report from consultant psychiatrist Dr Richard Church said the case was the “most sad and unusual” he had dealt with in his career.

Footage showing the boy falling from his bike had led to an early police theory that he had suffered a head injury and become disoriented, something his mother felt was given too much emphasis. The family’s relationship with investigators broke down, and they launched a crowdfunding appeal for a documentary investigating his death.

DCI Tom Phillips, giving evidence in June, apologised to Fiona Donohoe and admitted that the PSNI missed opportunities to establish where Noah had gone when he was later found to have left home at 3.30am on the night before his disappearance, returning 30 minutes later without his flip-flops and earphones.
Phillips acknowledged his mother had to “force” a full investigation into his death, saying: “I am very sorry she had to do that.”
A previous investigation into potential corporate manslaughter against the Department for Infrastructure over the access to the storm drain foundered due to insufficient evidence.

The inquest has been sitting since January and was originally scheduled to conclude by Easter. It was adjourned by the coroner, Mr Justice Rooney, on 3 July after the jury had retired to consider their verdicts but without them having come to agreement; they resumed deliberations on Monday.
Outside Belfast coroner’s court, solicitor Niall Murphy read out a statement on behalf of Noah Donohoe’s mother, Fiona.

“Noah was my greatest gift in life,” her statement said. “I miss him every day. He should still be here with me, following his dreams and planning for his future. I came to this inquest seeking answers, and I leave it with one clear answer: Noah was failed.

“He was failed by the Department for Infrastructure, who left a deadly storm drain unsecured and accessible to children. He was failed by the PSNI, who, from the moment I reported him missing, repeatedly failed to investigate and, from the moment he was found, stopped looking for answers.
“Instead, to deflect from their own failings, the Department for Infrastructure and police have sought to blame Noah.”

The statement from Noah’s mother concluded: “I always told Noah I would fight his corner if he ever needed me to. Luckily, I have not been alone in this fight, and I am so grateful to my family, and to Noah’s army, who have stood in Noah’s corner alongside me in their thousands from day one. They carry Noah’s legacy with them.”

articles.title: Houthis threaten more Saudi strikes as UN warns of humanitarian crisis in Yemen
articles.summary:
Estimated 100,000 Yemenis displaced amid renewed fighting as Qatar sounds alarm over Bab al-Mandab strait

Saudi cities faced the threat of a second day of Houthi attacks as fighting across…

blocks.text: Saudi cities faced the threat of a second day of Houthi attacks as fighting across Yemen led the UN to warn of a humanitarian crisis with 100,000 Yemenis already displaced.

As oil prices remained well over $100 (£74) a barrel, Qatar warned of a catastrophe if the Iran-backed Houthi militants won full control of the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway at the bottom of the Red Sea dominating the key naval route to Asia. The strait has become vital to Saudi crude oil exports as the wider Middle East war chokes the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

An emergency meeting of the UN security council in New York heard repeated calls for Houthi forces to show restraint. In a sign that Iran is still seeking a broader solution, its foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, travelled to Beijing to discuss China’s possible role in solving the related strait of Hormuz dispute.

The future of the strait of Hormuz – through which a fifth of the world’s traded oil and gas transited in peacetime and which the US and Iran are now mounting blockades of – is the diplomatic key to unlocking the conflict between the US and Iran, and to a lesser extent the related conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis.

Oil prices rose sharply after Reuters reported that ⁠loadings at Saudi Arabia’s ⁠Red ⁠Sea port ​of Yanbu had ⁠been suspended, citing shipping industry sources. The price of Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose nearly 3% to $108 a barrell.

Prices have risen this week after the ⁠world’s biggest ​crude ‌oil exporter, Saudi Aramco, ‌closed its East-West ‌pipeline due to an attack by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis. Aramco had increased ⁠use of the ​Yanbu terminal since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran in late February.

blocks.caption: A screen grab from a Houthi video released earlier this week purporting to show militants on an armoured personnel carrier during an offensive near Yemen’s Red Sea city of Mocha. Photograph: Houthi Military Media Center Handout/EPA

blocks.text: Qatar, acting as a mediator in the Iran war, is still trying to revive a postponed meeting planned for Monday between Iran and most Gulf Cooperation Council countries. The planned talks in Oman were delayed at the insistence of Saudi Arabia in protest at what it regarded as Iranian-inspired Houthis attacks on Saudi cities.

The Houthis had claimed responsibility for a new “large-scale” attack using “dozens of ballistic missiles and drones” against King Khalid airbase in Khamis Mushait, southern Saudi Arabia, on Monday. Air raid sirens were activated in six governorates including Jeddah on Tuesday. The warnings were lifted relatively quickly, but reflect an unprecedented new state of insecurity across Saudi Arabia.

The Oman meeting had been organised with the intention of reaching a regional agreement on an authorised route for commercial shipping through the strait of Hormuz. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, spoke with Oman’s foreign minister, Sayyid Badr Albusaidi, on Tuesday amid US concern that Oman will cede excessive control of the waterway to Iran.

blocks.caption: A shipping vessel anchored off Yemen's coast in the Bab al-Mandab strait, pictured earlier this week. Qatar has warned a blockade of the waterway could have a significant impact on world trade. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The prospect of the strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab strait both being under the long-term control of anti-western forces would be a significant strategic reversal for the US and Europe.

Qatar foreign ministry official Ibrahim al-Hashmi told reporters: “The world is suffering enough with the closure of the strait of Hormuz, so we cannot also afford to add the Bab al-Mandab into that equation.” He added that the closure of the southern entrance to the Red Sea would be “catastrophic for the entire world … and we are already seeing the consequences”.

The strait of Hormuz remained largely closed for commercial traffic on Monday and Tuesday, with a Qatar ship disabled by Iran and only four ships recorded as crossing the strait on Monday compared with a prewar average of about 130 ships.

So far Donald Trump has rejected Saudi pleas to join the fight to drive the Houthis back north up the coast of the Red Sea. Houthi leaders have also spoken to the US vice-president, JD Vance, reassuring the White House that their forces are seeking only to hinder Saudi-owned shipping, and that their overall goal is to end what they regard as a Saudi blockade of Houthi-controlled areas. The Houthis have signed a ceasefire agreement with the US, but are still subject to US sanctions.

The UK is unlikely to offer direct military, as opposed to political, support to Saudi Arabia unless there is a clear instruction from Washington to do so. Inside Yemen the next military engagement is likely to focus on the city of Marib where Saudi air raids have been trying to weaken Houthi formations.
Yemen’s ministry of foreign affairs and expatriates said: “If the world wants stability and calm in the region, it must tell the Saudis: enough interference in the Yemeni affair.”

Rather than giving direct military help, western governments are providing intelligence, including targeting advice as well as strategic help in the task of trying to integrate the disparate anti-Houthi forces in Yemen.

But Maysaa Shuja al-Deen from the Sana’a Centre said: “Any renewed military campaign must be accompanied by a serious reassessment of past mistakes, meaningful reform of the Yemeni government, stronger coordination among anti-Houthi forces, and a more balanced relationship between Yemeni actors and their regional partners.”

She added: “In many cases, the Saudis choose Yemeni figures who are weak, easily manipulated, and willing to follow their orders. If they instead chose competent, strong actors who could implement a shared agenda, they would also gain the respect of other competent Yemeni figures.

“This approach contrasts with the Iranian and Emirati models, which have generally given their local allies more room to manoeuvre while building relationships around specific objectives and clearer mandates.”

Due to the weakness of the UN-recognised government in Yemen, various militias with different ideological or regional loyalties operate alongside the official national army. Together on paper, the number of anti-Houthi forces could reach as many as 500,000 troops but in practice not all these forces cooperate or are willing to fight outside their area.

Saudi Arabia gives support to Yemen’s Homeland Shield Forces while the United Arab Emirates had backed both the 80,000-strong Southern Transitional Council’s Giants Brigade and a 20,000-strong force led by Tareq Saleh. But the UAE, after backing separatist forces in the south, has now pulled out of Yemen.

articles.title: Leader of Reform UK in Wales stands down after arrest on suspicion of assault
articles.summary:
Dan Thomas, elected in May, says he does not wish to be a ‘distraction’ on same day Reform MS defects to Plaid Cymru

The leader of Reform UK in Wales is standing down after he was arrested…

blocks.text: The leader of Reform UK in Wales is standing down after he was arrested and bailed on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour.
Dan Thomas, a former Tory councillor, had only been announced as Reform UK’s Welsh leader by Nigel Farage in February.
He was elected to the Senedd as leader of the opposition in May’s election to the Welsh parliament, when Reform UK emerged as the second largest party.

However, it emerged on Tuesday that Thomas would not be taking part in the first plenary session of the new Senedd term and questions for the first minister on Tuesday afternoon. Reform said he was absent for “personal reasons”.

In a statement later on Tuesday afternoon, Thomas said: “Over the weekend, I was reported to the police and was released without charge. I stress that I have done nothing wrong, but I do not want the coming headlines to be a distraction from the fantastic work our Senedd team is doing in holding this government to account.”

blocks.caption: Dan Thomas, left, and Nigel Farage at the Reform Wales manifesto launch in March. Photograph: Jon Rowley/Getty Images

blocks.text: Gwent police said: “On Sunday 13 September, a 45-year-old man, from the Aberbargoed area, was arrested on suspicion of assault and engaging in controlling/coercive behaviour. He has been bailed pending further inquiries.”
Thomas, a former Conservative leader of Barnet council in north London, is originally from Blackwood, Caerphilly.

Eyebrows had been raised on Monday when Thomas was notably quiet when it came to commenting on the meeting of the nationalist first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, who had declared that: “Westminster’s time is coming to an end.”
His resignation comes as a heavy blow to Reform, which has poured significant resources into Wales, where it believes further inroads could be made in traditional Labour strongholds.
However, the perception of Thomas as a figure who was parachuted in by Reform headquarters has caused tensions.

It is believed Farage chose an outsider to the Welsh branch of the party in an effort to distance Reform from its former Welsh leader, Nathan Gill, who was jailed for accepting bribes to make pro-Russia statements in the European parliament.
Since the new Senedd opened in May, there have been frequent reports of infighting in the Reform group, and its performance in the Siambr so far has been notable for unparliamentary conduct.
Thomas previously led Barnet council between 2019 and 2022, when the north London council was seized by Labour, and defected to Farage’s Reform party last summer.
He stood down in December as a councillor for Finchley Church End – long synonymous with Margaret Thatcher – to move back to his south Wales valleys home town.
In May, Reform won 34 seats at the expense of Labour and the Conservatives in the newly expanded 96-seat chamber of the Welsh parliament, behind Plaid Cymru’s 43.

Reform had been aiming to become Wales’s biggest party, Thomas said, but it still performed better than any Welsh Conservative result on record and managed to increase its vote share from 1% in 2021 to 29% in 2026. With more than a third of the seats, the Senedd is the biggest political platform Reform has had to date.

At almost exactly the same time that Thomas announced his resignation, the Reform MS Sarah Cooper-Lesadd said she was defecting to Plaid Cymru – a party nearly on the opposite end of the political spectrum.

blocks.caption: Sarah Cooper-Lesadd accused her former party of not being serious about governing in Wales. Photograph: Senedd

blocks.text: She said in a statement: “[Reform UK] … are not serious about governing Wales. They are far more interested in division, opposition and headlines than in finding solutions.
“Their Senedd group is a staging post in the effort to get Nigel Farage into Downing Street and that was glaringly obvious at its conference this week.”

Ken Skates, the leader of the Labour Senedd group, said: “Nigel Farage chose to make Nathan Gill his leader in Wales and he turned out to be a Russian asset. He chose to take £5m from a crypto billionaire that triggered an investigation.
“He chose to meet two men in a pub in Clacton to discuss breaching electoral law. And he chose to make Dan Thomas his leader in Wales, who has now quit suddenly.
“That Farage and Reform are in such a dire mess is bad enough, but it’s also bad for Plaid, welcoming a Reform defector who just a few weeks ago characterised herself as being rightwing.”

articles.title: Ministers vow sweeping NHS changes after ‘devastating’ report on Lucy Letby hospital
articles.summary:
Lady Justice Thirlwall’s report concludes three babies might have survived if hospital had acted on concerns about nurse

Ministers have promised sweeping changes to the NHS after a…
articles.byline: Josh Halliday North of England editor

blocks.text: Ministers have promised sweeping changes to the NHS after a “devastating” official review concluded that three babies might have survived if hospital bosses and doctors had acted on concerns about the nurse Lucy Letby.
A public inquiry found a “complete failure” to protect babies on the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester hospital in north-west England.

In a series of findings, the inquiry chair, Lady Justice Thirlwall, said two newborn twins would not have died and five others would not have been harmed if Letby had been removed from the unit sooner.

Thirlwall said a third baby who died, a two-month-old girl, and two others who suffered unexplained collapses might have been protected if a doctor had detected an earlier insulin poisoning on the unit. One of those infants, now aged 11, suffered a lifelong brain injury and needs 24-hour care.

Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, said she was “profoundly sorry” for the “devastating” failures revealed in the report, telling MPs: “This must be a turning point for the NHS.” She said she had asked officials to urgently take forward plans for “cot cam” monitors for neonatal units in line with Thirlwall’s recommendation.
However, Letby’s barrister, Mark McDonald, told the Guardian the government had “moved with too much haste” and acted before the outcome of her challenge to her convictions was known.
Letby, 36, is serving 15 whole-life prison terms after being convicted of the murder of seven babies and attempted murder of seven other newborns at the hospital in the year to June 2016.
The former neonatal nurse is fighting to overturn her convictions, which have been described by the senior Conservative MP David Davis as a “clear miscarriage of justice”.

The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC), which investigates potential miscarriages of justice, is reviewing a dossier of evidence submitted by experts on her behalf before deciding whether to refer the case back to the court of appeal, which has twice rejected her legal challenges.

Delivering her report at Liverpool town hall on Tuesday, where families of some of the babies had gathered, Thirlwall said: “My report describes dysfunctional management and governance; a gulf between hospital leadership and clinicians; and failure to understand the fundamentals of safeguarding.

“There was a complete failure to protect babies on the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester hospital. This was because no one seems to have understood that safeguarding action is required when a member of staff is suspected of causing deliberate harm and does not require colleagues to be sure of guilt.”
Families of the babies who died or were injured said the report painted a “damning picture of what happens when concerns over patient safety are not listened to and acted on”.
Tamlin Bolton, a solicitor at Irwin Mitchell representing seven of the families, urged ministers and the NHS to act on the report’s recommendations, saying: “It cannot be the end of the matter.”

Richard Scorer, of the law firm Slater and Gordon, which represents three of the families, said: “Far too often public inquiry recommendations are left to gather dust. This cannot be allowed to happen again.”

blocks.caption: Bosses at the Countess of Chester hospital did not contact police until nearly two years after the unexplained increase in deaths.  Photograph: Brian Hickey/Alamy

blocks.text: In her 822-page report, Thirlwall said it was “inexcusable” that successive governments had failed to act on reforms proposed by other public inquiries into NHS scandals stretching back 30 years.

Thirlwall is said to believe that “cot cams” – allowing parents to monitor their newborn around-the-clock – could have prevented all seven of the deaths as medics would know they were being monitored.

Samantha Dixon, the Labour MP for Chester North, whose constituency includes the hospital, said the inquiry revealed a “truly appalling state of affairs” that needed “the firmest response possible from government”.

Ministers are working on the urgent introduction of other CCTV in hospital neonatal units as well as cot cams, in line with Thirlwall’s recommendation, as well as stricter rules on the storage of insulin.

Hospital executives who are found to have failed in their responsibilities will be prevented from working again in the NHS under new regulation to stop managers being transferred to another part of the country.
And they will roll out a single tracker to monitor the delivery of recommendations made by inquiries into maternity and neonatal scandals.
McDonald, Letby’s barrister, said: “The government has moved with too much haste. They have made the same mistake as Thirlwall not to pause and wait for the new evidence to be considered.”
However, others said the inquiry’s findings and recommendations must be taken seriously irrespective of Letby’s legal challenge.
Dr Tom Dolphin, chair of the British Medical Association (BMA), said it stemmed from “system reform” within the NHS and that it required “major reforms” to the culture of the health service.

Leaders of NHS trusts and other bodies said the inquiry had shone a light on the “upheaval caused by successive reorganisations, the complex regulatory landscape, staff shortages, unacceptable ‘revolving door’ appointments and the inadequacies of under-funded NHS IT systems”.

Letby was first linked to baby deaths in June 2015. In less than two weeks that month, three newborns died in unexplained circumstances within two weeks – the number usually expected on the neonatal unit in a year.

Senior doctors became concerned about Letby’s connection to the unusual rise in deaths and serious incidents over the following months and raised their fears with executives. However, the inquiry found that senior nurses effectively dismissed the concerns about Letby and that there was a “prolonged delay” in calling the police.

Rather than being believed, Thirlwall said, clinicians were themselves made the subject of investigation in a “deplorable” grievance process brought by Letby when she was finally removed from the neonatal unit in July 2016.

Parents were “kept in the dark” for years about what happened to their babies and the concerns they may have been deliberately harmed, the inquiry found. Thirlwall described their treatment as “reprehensible”.

The inquiry chair accused hospital executives of overseeing “an exercise in spin” by downplaying the rise in deaths to the board of directors. Their failure to contact police before April 2017 – nearly two years after the unexplained increase in deaths – suggested that protecting the hospital’s reputation was “prized more highly” than the doctors’ concerns, she found.

blocks.caption: The Thirlwall inquiry’s 822-page report was published on Tuesday. Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty Images

blocks.text: Three hospital executives, who have not been named, were arrested last year on suspicion of gross negligence manslaughter. Cheshire police said its investigation into the former bosses, and a parallel investigation into corporate manslaughter, was ongoing.

Thirlwall, a court of appeal judge, said it was “clear that some babies would have been saved and some attacks would have been prevented if action was taken earlier”. She said the precise number of deaths that might have been prevented would never be known for sure.

However, the inquiry concluded that if Letby had been removed from duties in October 2015 – when senior managers were made aware of the concerns – then the twin boys known as babies O and P would not have died in June 2016 and five further babies would not have suffered harm.

Thirlwall said it was possible that three newborns would not have died and seven others would have been protected if a senior doctor had not “disregarded” an insulin result for a week-old baby boy in August 2015, whom Letby was later convicted of attempting to murder by poisoning him.

articles.title: Ed Sheeran responds to backlash over removing Macklemore from tour after ‘Free Palestine’ comments
articles.summary: English singer outlined his position after US stadium owners refused to let rapper perform after political speech

blocks.text: Singer Ed Sheeran has responded to the backlash over the removal of Macklemore from his North American Loop tour, following the rapper’s “Free Palestine” speech on stage at MetLife stadium in New Jersey.

In a two-minute speech on 4 September, the Grammy-winning artist told the audience he wanted the people of Gaza and “the occupied West Bank” to know “we have not forgotten about them”, prompting owners of subsequent stadium tour venues – including Robert Kraft, the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots and a prominent supporter of and donor to Israel – to object to Macklemore’s appearance on the tour.

Messina Touring Group, the promoter of the US leg of Sheeran’s tour, confirmed Macklemore’s removal from the eight planned subsequent dates on Monday; hours later, Macklemore posted a lengthy statement reiterating his support of Palestine and the people of Gaza and outlining conversations about political activism with Sheeran, prompting criticism of the English singer’s apolitical stance.
On Tuesday, Sheeran responded with a lengthy Instagram post captioned: “It’s important that I set out some facts.”

“I am appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine,” he wrote in the first of several bullet-point statements. “The suffering and pain caused on both sides is a human tragedy. There are too many wars across the world causing immeasurable pain, none of which should be tolerated.”

According to Sheeran, Macklemore “asked to join my tour last year and I agreed, because I respect him as an artist”. He went on to say that he allowed the Thrift Shop singer to perform a set list of his choosing, “as with all my support acts”.
The Seattle-bred rapper, long an outspoken supporter of the rights of Palestinians and those in Gaza, delivered the brief remarks between songs during his first appearance on tour.

“A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: Free Palestine,” he said. “I said: Free Palestine! I want those words to be loud and clear, so that people all the way in Gaza to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten about them.”

He also played his protest anthem Hind’s Hall, which celebrated protesters’ occupation of a building they named in honor of Hind Rajab, a six-year-old killed by the Israeli military in 2024, accompanied by images of the Israeli military’s destruction of Gaza, which killed more than 75,000 people in 16 months, according to some estimates.

At the second of his appearances at MetLife on 5 September, Macklemore reiterated his support for Palestine and addressed Jewish members of the audience: “Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you. My message is for peace, love; for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect and equality.”

Following those comments, which prompted the Israeli American Council to launch a petition calling for Macklemore’s removal from the tour, US venues communicated to Sheeran that they would refuse to host the show if the rapper was still a supporting act.

“I was informed this stance was based on how Macklemore conveyed part of his message during his performance, rather than on everything that was said,” he wrote. Though Sheeran said that he attempted to broker conversations between the promoters, venue owners such as Kraft and activists “on both sides”, the “venue’s and the promoter’s decision was final”.
after newsletter promotion

“Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter’s decision, it was not mine,” he said. “I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living.”

Sheeran went on to outline his larger view on the use of his platform, which Macklemore had described the day prior as “his typical apolitical stance” that “was being challenged in a way it had never been before”.

“I have always used my platform and music to bring people from all backgrounds and cultures together and this won’t ever change,” he wrote, later adding: “I choose to use my fame and platform to be a place of safety and sanctuary, to maintain diplomacy and keep the conversations open, not closed.”

“I am not complicit,” he added. “I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn’t mean I don’t have them, and it doesn’t mean that I don’t care. Nor does it mean that I don’t support causes in my own, personal way.”

As of now, the North American leg of Sheeran’s tour will conclude in November at Raymond James Stadium in Tampa, Florida, which earlier this year hosted two shows by Ye, the rapper formerly known as Kanye West, who has a history of antisemitic statements.

“I have spent this week trying to build bridges, to find a solution and unfortunately, was unable to do so,” Sheeran concluded his post. “I know who I am, both as a person and as an artist, and those who know my heart know my values too.”

articles.title: Army officers ‘let down’ soldier over sexual assault claim before she killed herself, court martial told
articles.summary:
Court hears that two officers did not deal properly with allegation Jaysley Beck made against a superior

Two army officers “let down” a teenage soldier who went on to kill herself when they…

blocks.text: Two army officers “let down” a teenage soldier who went on to kill herself when they did not deal properly with a sexual assault allegation she made against a superior, a court martial has heard.
Jaysley Beck, 19, told Col Samantha Shepherd that she had been touched on the leg by a warrant officer during a social event at an adventure training exercise, the court was told.
But Shepherd allegedly misrepresented what Beck had told her when she reported the claim, falsely saying there had not been physical contact.
The second officer, Maj James Hook, failed to take the incident seriously and was sceptical of what Beck had reported, believing she wanted to leave the training package, the court heard.

Shepherd and Hook deny “conduct prejudicial to good order and service discipline”. Shepherd is accused of misreporting what she had been told by Beck while Hook allegedly did not treat information passed to him in a manner “consistent with its seriousness”.

At the start of the trial, the assistant judge advocate general Edward Legard said he expected the board hearing the case – an RAF air commodore, navy captain and army colonel – almost certainly knew of the Beck case.
He told them she had taken her own life and there had been significant press interest but they should put anything they had heard about it to one side.
Legard also instructed them not to be influenced by anyone’s views – including their chain of command – on the subject of unacceptable sexual behaviour in the armed forces.
Cdr Paul Patterson, for the crown, said Beck was taking part in the training package in Hampshire in July 2021. Hook was running the exercise while Shepherd was the regimental colonel.

Following a social function, Beck was found distressed and sleeping in her car early in the morning by a colleague, L/Cpl Drew Tudor. She told him there had been an incident the night before with a warrant officer, Michael Webber, who was senior in rank to her.
Hook was alerted and Beck expressed concern over what would happen if she made a complaint. He gave her until noon to decide what she wanted to do.
The court was told he was sceptical as Beck was not enjoying the adventure package and he thought she may be wanting to leave.
Patterson said rather than empowering her, Hook could be seen as “leaning on her”. He said an issue for the board to consider was if Hook knew he was dealing with a potential sexual assault.
Shepherd was told of the incident later. She went for a walk with Beck, who told her Webber had touched her leg and tried to kiss her, the court heard.

Patterson said when she went to speak to an adjutant, whose role includes advising on discipline, about the incident, Shepherd was asked if there had been physical contact and allegedly replied that there had not been.

The prosecutor said that the colonel “edited the information” when she “should have told the truth”. He told the court it was the crown’s case that Shepherd deliberately tried to suppress the detail about touching, knowing that if she did report this it would go to service police.
Patterson said Beck told each of the officers enough to understand that she may have been sexually assaulted and she had been let down by them.

Tudor became emotional as he gave his evidence. He said when he found Beck in her car she was distressed and told him that Webber had “tried something on with her”. He said he could not now remember Beck’s exact words but added: “I was concerned enough to want to report it.”
The adjutant, Maj Mae King, told the court Shepherd had told her Webber had attempted to kiss Beck but Beck had leant away. She said: “My understanding was no physical contact had been made.”
King said incidents such as this were “relatively normal” and it was not the most serious she had dealt with.

King told the court that Webber’s wife worked in the same building as her and there was concern about her welfare. She said she did not know if the wife knew about what had allegedly happened during the adventure package. “It wasn’t our business to tell her,” King said.
Beck’s mother, Leighann McCready, from Cumbria, sat in the front row of the public gallery, holding her daughter’s army cap.
The trial at Catterick in North Yorkshire continues.

articles.title: Catnapped bodega cat in Brooklyn reunited with owner after intense grassroots campaign
articles.summary:
Three-month-old Jabal was returned to Park Slope bodega after community rallied to rescue purloined kitty

The owner of a New York…

blocks.text: The owner of a New York City bodega on Tuesday was reunited with the store’s cat after a couple passing by the establishment five days earlier appeared to abduct the feline in plain view of a surveillance camera and ignited an intense grassroots search effort.

The plight of three-month-old Jabal began on Thursday morning in Brooklyn, when he went just outside the Eighth Street Mini Market where he lives as it opened for the day. A man walking alongside a woman passed the Park Slope market then picked up Jabal, and the pair took off as the kitten visibly squirmed, according to store surveillance video which the bodega’s owner, Imad “Jimmy” Innab, reviewed after he noticed the cat had gone missing.

Dan Janzen, who lives across the street from the Eighth Street Mini Market and is one of its regular customers, said someone immediately ran after the couple and told them the kitten belonged to the bodega – but they were unmoved, stuffed Jabal into a bag and left with him anyway.

As the New York Post and the local CBS affiliate soon reported, Innab and his family subsequently offered a $500, no questions asked reward for Jabal’s safe return, which was announced on a poster. Supporters of the bodega also canvassed the streets of Park Slope for Jabal while the neighborhood’s forum on the Reddit platform provided updates on the search efforts.

One thread dedicated to Jabal’s disappearance had a photo of the couple who took the kitten and was titled, “Anyone Know These Two?” It generated about 1,000 upvotes – which indicate Reddit users’ approval of a thread – and more than 240 comments, with many aiming to help reunite Jabal with the Innabs.

Another thread titled “Stolen Bodega Cat?!?” also called attention to Jabal’s catnapping, along with the news media coverage, which publicized the shocking surveillance footage of the kitten being brazenly snatched.

The campaign paid dividends by Monday, when Janzen – speaking on behalf of Innab’s store – said the bodega had received a call from someone claiming to know who had Jabal. That person said Jabal would be brought back to the store from the Brooklyn neighborhood of Bushwick, according to both Janzen and Innab.
Janzen on Tuesday afternoon then followed up with pictures of Innab holding Jabal, including one in which the bodega owner was planting a kiss on the top of the kitten’s head.
Janzen sent the joyous pictures after spending part of Monday and Tuesday at the store with Innab eagerly awaiting Jabal’s return.
“As much as we love the kitten, we love him more,” Janzen said of Innab. “We were rallying around him to keep his hopes up.”

Innab said he had been particularly affected by Jabal’s snatching because the Eighth Street Mini Market’s prior bodega cat, Victoria, had died in June after living there for 17 years. Innab took in Jabal to succeed Victoria, and the kitten was soon due to be given a microchip, which is injected subcutaneously and contains scannable owner and home address information.

Bodega cats are deeply embedded in the fabric of New York City, serving to help keep vermin under control while also acting as living mascots for the stores where they reside. They can be seen lounging among store offerings or roaming along the freezer cases – among assorted other activities – in pictures on certain widely followed social media accounts, including @bodegacatsofnewyork on Instagram.
Janzen on Monday made it a point to say that Innab refused to entertain the thought of not getting Jabal back. As Janzen put, Innab “always said, ‘I have a feeling he’s coming back.’”
“I wish all the stories in the world could end this happily,” Janzen said on Tuesday.
Innab said the way the neighborhood where his store had stood for 39 years supported him after Jabal’s temporary abduction “means everything” to him.
“The people are very beautiful – very good – here,” Innab said of Park Slope. “And I thank everybody who tried to help me.”

articles.title: Kash Patel defends FBI hiring policy on applicants who have engaged in bestiality
articles.summary: Senators question FBI chief on move to cut restrictions on agent applicants who have engaged in bestiality

blocks.text: FBI director Kash Patel defended his agency’s decision to roll back restrictions on agent applicants who have previously engaged in bestiality, arguing the FBI “did not want to punish victims of bestiality” by automatically disqualifying them.

The unusual topic of bestiality emerged during a Senate judiciary committee oversight hearing on Tuesday after Democrat Dick Durbin and Republican John Kennedy questioned Patel’s decision to remove barriers that previously prevented applicants who engaged in prostitution and bestiality from being qualified for a job at the FBI.
“I’m trying to understand why you did this,” Kennedy told Patel. “We’re having a tough time attracting agents, good quality agents we all can trust … why would you even get into bestiality?”

Patel said the change was recommended to him after he saw various “cases” in which qualified FBI applicants were denied consideration because they had been forced into bestiality as a result of human trafficking.
“I say this with respect to the person who recommended it, why didn’t you just say: ‘What planet did you parachute in from?’” Kennedy replied.
It is unclear how many FBI applicants have fallen into this category. The Guardian has contacted the FBI to provide data supporting Patel’s claim.

“They showed me cases in which people were forced into it and had applied to the FBI, and so I thought: ‘They should be considered. It’s not an automatic disqualification.’ That’s all,” Patel told Kennedy.

The rule change, first reported by CBS News in August, allows the FBI to consider candidates who hired a sex worker under specific circumstances, a person who stole from an employer under certain circumstances and engaged in bestiality or animal cruelty – so long as the incident took place before they were 18 years old.
Kennedy, generally an ally of Donald Trump’s administration, grilled Patel on the hiring qualification change, arguing that it “really hurt” the FBI’s reputation.
At one point, the Republican senator from Louisiana asked Patel whether the change “disqualified the animal” from FBI service.
While Patel characterized the change as nondiscriminatory toward victims, Durbin refuted the notion and claimed it was a way to protect those who engaged in bestiality.
“You dropped automatic disqualification for applicants who have been engaged in bestiality, not victims of bestiality, applicants who have engaged,” Durbin said to Patel.
Patel responded: “Applicants who have engaged in bestiality means they were victims of bestiality because they were forced to do so.”
Democrats sent a letter to Patel on Monday requesting more information about the rule change and applicants who fell into the categories.

articles.title: ‘This should be condemned by any thinking human’: film industry rallies behind NAZA directors
articles.summary:
Backing comes after Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor were threatened with having their citizenship revoked and accused of treason

Film industry heavyweights across the globe have expressed…
articles.byline: Catherine Shoard in London and Lorenzo Tondo in Jerusalem

blocks.text: Film industry heavyweights across the globe have expressed solidarity with Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, the Oscar-winning Israeli directors of documentary NAZA, who have been threatened with having their citizenship revoked by Israel’s culture minister, who accused them of “treason against the state”.

NAZA, which was produced by the Guardian, is named for an acronym euphemistically used by Israel’s intelligence service to indicate how many civilians it expects to die in an airstrike on Gaza. It includes interviews with 24 Israeli military or intelligence soldiers and officers who outlined the AI-powered targeting systems used to bombard Gaza, resulting in the mass killing of Palestinian civilians.
The film builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and the Guardian between 2023 and 2025.

The 80-minute documentary won the special jury prize at this year’s Venice film festival on Saturday, after receiving a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record. On Sunday, Israel’s culture minister, Miki Zohar, accused the directors of being willing to “harm their homeland in order to receive applause from antisemites around the world”.

blocks.caption: Jonathan Glazer, Rachel Szor, Yuval Abraham and James Wilson in Venice.  Photograph: Stefano Rellandini/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “I will act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship of these despicable creators for treason against the state,” Zohar wrote on X.

Representatives for Venice, or the jury headed by Maggie Gyllenhaal, have not yet commented on these threats, but the artistic director of the Telluride film festival – widely acknowledged as the foremost Oscars launchpad – was swift to voice her outrage.

“Documentary film-makers are among the best long-form journalists working and critical to our understanding of the world,” said Julie Huntsinger. “To even threaten their citizenship standing is unacceptable. This should be condemned by any thinking human.”

Her words were echoed by the heads of the Locarno film festival, who said they stood “firmly in support of film-makers’ right to pursue difficult and urgent subjects without fear of reprisal. Artistic and journalistic freedom are the very foundation of what cinema can be: a space for dialogue which engages critically with the world we live in.”
They added that they “reaffirm our support for film-makers who ask difficult questions and help us reflect”.

NAZA will screen at the San Sebastián film festival next week. In a statement, its festival directors said the film “exposes the systematic genocide of the Palestinian people by the Israeli government” and that they stand “in solidarity” with the film’s makers as well as “the Palestinian people”. The documentary will show at the Bologna film festival tonight, before its North American premiere, at the New York film festival, later this month.

Tricia Tuttle, director of the Berlin film festival, said: “Artists must be free to critically examine the world. Films can provoke discussion, disagreement and criticism, but in a democratic society, the response to art must be dialogue and scrutiny, not intimidation or punishment by the state. Our team at the Berlinale stands with Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and all artists who exercise these rights.”

Abraham and Szor won the documentary Oscar in 2025 for No Other Land, about Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank, alongside their Palestinian co-directors Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal. That film premiered at Berlin the previous year, where it won a prize. Following this victory, Abraham’s family home was targeted by a rightwing mob. “For me, that was the worst moment of all,” he told the Guardian last week. “My mum is hoping it doesn’t happen again.”

Earlier this year, Tuttle’s position came under threat after several prize winners condemned Israel’s actions against Palestinians from the stage at the closing night awards gala. In the wake of this, the German culture minister, Wolfram Weimer, convened a crisis meeting as the Bild tabloid reported Tuttle was to be fired over giving “hate speech” an airing. In response, hundreds of prominent film-makers worldwide, including from Israel, rallied around Tuttle.

blocks.caption: Laura Poitras in Venice last week.  Photograph: Alessandra Benedetti/Corbis/Getty Images

blocks.text: In Israel, more than 1,500 film-makers have signed a petition in support of the directors, and refuting the accusation that they have sought to damage the country’s image internationally.
Signatories include film-makers Liran Atzmor, one of the petition’s initiators, Nadav Lapid, Orna Ben Dor, Netalie Braun, Rani Blair, Hagai Levi, Shai Carmeli-Pollak and Shlomi Elkabetz.
The petition calls on those who support freedom of expression and artistic freedom to stand in solidarity with Abraham and Szor.

“In recent days, we have witnessed an unprecedented campaign of vilification and incitement against the film’s creators,” it says, warning that the rhetoric was moving increasingly close to “effectively sanctioning violence” and posed a physical threat to their lives.
So far the Academy of Motion Pictures and Sciences has not commented on the situation in which its recent winners find themselves. However, previous recipients of the documentary award have done so.
Laura Poitras, who won the documentary Oscar in 2015 for Citizenfour, about the WikiLeaks whistleblower Edward Snowden, defended the film’s factual credentials.

“The facts about the mass killing of civilians in NAZA have been reported by the Guardian in dozens of rigorously fact-checked articles, and every assertion in the film is based on multiple sources,” said Poitras, who acted as a consultant on NAZA.

blocks.caption: No Other Land co-director Hamdan Ballal with his Oscar in March 2025, shortly after he had been attacked by Israeli settlers at his home, in his village of Susya in the occupied West Bank.  Photograph: Hazem Bader/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: She called the threats by Israeli government officials “a threat to journalists worldwide. They are also familiar – my reporting with the Guardian on the National Security Authority’s illegal global mass surveillance was met with similar denials and attacks by the US government.
“Despite the alarming nature of these current threats, it is important to emphasise that Israel has killed over 200 Palestinian journalists in Gaza and has normalised the murder of journalists.”

Meanwhile Nan Goldin, the US photographer and activist who worked with Poitras on the 2022 Oscar-nominated documentary All the Beauty and Bloodshed, said she applauded NAZA’s directors “for their enormous courage in presenting a film that shows irrefutable proof of Israel’s war crimes at their own great risk.”

British film industry veterans offering their support include director Richard Eyre, who said he was “beyond shocked by anything that the Israeli government does”, and the novelist and screenwriter Hanif Kureishi, who called the pair “both brave and admirable, standing up to state oppression, steadfast in their pursuit of the truth”.

Israeli attacks in Gaza since 2023 have killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, the majority of them civilians, and injured more than 174,000 others, together representing more than 10% of Gaza’s prewar population. Israel launched its war after the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, when more than 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken to Gaza by militants. The majority of the dead and hostages were civilians.
Additional reporting by Andrew Pulver and Philip Oltermann

articles.title: High fuel prices challenge the German government
articles.summary: Chancellor Friedrich Merz wants to provide relief to motorists. But exactly how this is to happen remains unclear.

image.caption: In Germany, a liter of fuel now costs about three euros — that is over €11 for a gallonImage: Marc John/Bonn.digital/picture alliance

blocks.text: Gas stations in Germany are only allowed to raise their fuel prices once a day, at 12 noon. In Berlin, on the morning of September 15, E10 gasoline cost about €2.25 ($2.60) per liter and diesel about €2.37. At noon, prices rose by about €0.20 per liter. The highest prices were recorded at a highway gas station in southern Berlin, where Super Plus cost €3.03 per liter.

Drivers are angry. While it's possible to use public transportation in large cities, residents of rural areas have hardly any realistic alternative to driving. Those living in regions near national borders have an advantage. On September 7, filling up a 60-liter tank with E10 gasoline cost about €31 less in the Czech Republic and Poland than in Germany. In Luxembourg, the difference was €28, and in Austria, €25. These figures were calculated by the Federal Statistical Office.

Germany has nine neighboring countries. Gasoline is significantly cheaper in seven of them, and diesel is cheaper in six. Only in the Netherlands and Denmark do drivers have to pay more for fuel than in Germany.
German government expresses 'great and growing' concern

But relief is in sight. That's what Chancellor Friedrich Merz(CDU) has promised. "Many people who need their cars every day, have reached their breaking point," Merz said Tuesday at an event hosted by the German Foreign Trade Association (BGA) in Berlin. "I believe we must take action." However, the chancellor added that the "exact measures" have not yet been determined. "We are therefore in close dialogue within the federal government and with the German states." A proposal will be announced "very soon," he assured.

But what might that look like? On Monday (Sept. 14) in Berlin, Deputy Government Spokesperson Steffen Meyer rejected any government responsibility for the high prices. "So, it's not the actions of the federal government or anything like that causing prices to rise so sharply. Rather, it's largely due to the escalating situation in the Middle East, attacks on oil pipelines and the blockade of shipping lanes," Meyer explained.

The fact is, however, that Germany imposes higher taxes and levies on fuels. The ADAC automobile club has pointed out that while the oil price remains below previous peaks, E10 gasoline is more expensive than ever before. "From the ADAC's perspective, there is therefore a need to provide greater clarity, especially regarding refinery and wholesale markets," said an ADAC spokeswoman.
Donald Trump blames Ukraine for record US diesel prices
Price gouging at the pumps

Herbert Rabl of the Gas Station Interest Group (TIV) puts it more bluntly. "They're raking it in. The oil companies aren't cutting into their profit margins at all," Rabl told the Rheinische Post newspaper. He said that this is an issue that has long been the subject of political debate, but that the federal government remains divided on what, if anything, can be done about it.

However, the problem that the conservative bloc of Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) face as coalition partners is that the state coffers are empty, and the federal government cannot cover its budget shortfall without taking on a historically high level of new debt. "Ultimately, the only way to bring these prices down is to end the hostilities and ensure the freedom of navigation," said spokesperson Meyer.
A new fuel rebate or tax relief?

Faced with rising oil prices that followed the outbreak of the war on Iran, the German government introduced a fuel rebate in the spring. From May 1 through June 30, 2026, the energy tax on gasoline and diesel was temporarily reduced. Factoring in value-added tax, this was expected to lower fuel prices by about €0.17 per liter.

"We had a fuel rebate; we subsidized prices," Federal Economy Minister Katherina Reiche (CDU) told the n-tv network. But she says that won't be possible again. "Together, we in the coalition have decided that we don't have the financial scope for that at the moment." As an alternative, the Conservatives are exploring the possibility of at least providing tax relief for commuters or supporting low-income earners with direct payments.

But that's not enough for the SPD. It is proposing a completely different approach and, as it did shortly after the outbreak of the Iran war, is advocating for a government-imposed cap on fuel prices. One of the ways they plan to finance this relief is through an excess profit tax on energy companies. In addition, the SPD supports a temporary reduction in energy taxes to deal with crisis situations. Their goal is an immediate price reduction at the gas pump.
Saudi oil pipeline attack could raise global gas prices
AfD standing to profit from bickering

But while the federal government continues to debate and weigh its options amid internal disagreements, other parties feel time is running out. Regional elections will be held in two states on September 20.

In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, SPD Premier Manuela Schwesig is fighting to stave off a win for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD). In the latest polls, the AfD was in the lead with 38%, while the SPD has recently gained ground, and is now polling at 34%.

The AfD wants to drastically lower fuel prices by abolishing the CO₂ tax on fossil fuels and reducing the energy tax to the European minimum. It also proposes lowering the German value-added tax on gasoline and diesel from 19% to 7%.

"There is the option of introducing a fuel cap and, at the same time, an excess profit tax, as in Luxembourg," Schwesig said on Monday (Sept. 14) in Schwerin. She criticized the federal government's inaction. "The chancellor is just allowing this to drag on, and that is causing frustration."
A solution from the EU?

According to the SPD-led Federal Finance Ministry, Minister Lars Klingbeil will "strongly push" for the introduction of an excess profits tax at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin this coming Friday.

Officials in Berlin point out that an excess profits tax is currently being discussed at the European level. "Large member states such as Spain and Poland are on our side," said a spokesperson for the finance ministry on Monday (Sept. 14) in Berlin.

"Such an excess profits tax would be one way to use the excessive profits that oil companies are reaping during this crisis — by fleecing consumers and imposing excessive price hikes — to provide targeted relief for the people who are particularly affected by these high gas prices," he added.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Knobloch: 'It is a very dangerous situation at the moment'
articles.summary: Charlotte Knobloch survived the Holocaust by passing as the daughter of non-Jewish farmers. She recently spoke with DW to express her shock following the AfD victory in Saxony-Anhalt's state election.

image.caption: Charlotte Knobloch is appalled by the AfD's election victory in Saxony-AnhaltImage: DW

blocks.text: Charlotte Knobloch, president of the Jewish Community of Munich and Upper Bavaria, is dismayed by the electoral victory of the nationalist Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in the Saxony-Anhalt state election. Knobloch told DW that there were now once again a number of Jewish people who, in the wake of such events, were considering leaving Germany.
It took decades, Knobloch said, for Jews in Germany to regain trust in the country after the Holocaust. That had ultimately been achieved.

But now, there were great fears again: "That is, in sum, the biggest problem for me, because we successfully tried to rebuild the Jewish communities after 1945, to give the Jewish people a home again, which they hadn't had for a long time..."

blocks.caption: AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund's (center) party received nearly 44% of the vote in Saxony-AnhaltImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Standing up against the far-right 'requires some courage'

In Saxony-Anhalt's September 6 state election, the AfD, classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" by the state's Office for the Protection of the Constitution, had received almost 44% of the vote. Although AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund fell short of an absolute majority, he still has a good chance of becoming the next premier in the state parliament, meaning he'd become the first head of a state government from a right-wing extremist party after World War II.

Charlotte Knobloch issues a stark warning: "We can't allow any of those people to become state premier. It is a very dangerous situation at the moment, in my view. I hope the other parties realize that and stand up against it. They can do it. It requires some courage of course."

blocks.caption: The nonagenarian, seen here with Chancellor Friedrich Merz, is still present in Germany's public lifeImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Charlotte Knobloch, who is almost 94 years old, is one of the most prominent and well-known representatives of Jewish life in Germany and one of the last surviving witnesses of Nazi dictatorship between 1933 and 1945. Born in 1932, she was initially raised by her grandmother, who was deported to the Theresienstadt concentration camp in 1942 and died there. A family acquaintance saved the girl by accommodating her on her farm in Middle Franconia and passing her off as her own child.
Knobloch: 'danger looming' today did not exist like this 10 years ago

Asked by DW when and how she still thinks about that horrible era, she said: "There were times when this happened only rarely. When it was mentioned by the media from time to time, but not permanently. These days, I wake up thinking about it, and I also go to bed thinking about it."

blocks.caption: Knobloch spoke to DW correspondent Tina Gerhäusser in MunichImage: DW

blocks.text: Knobloch served as vice president of the World Jewish Congress between 2005 and 2013, and as president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany from 2006 to 2010. For a long time, she has been warning against growing antisemitism in Germany. However, she herself did not foresee the rise of far-right extremist parties like the AfD.
"There's a danger looming that did not exist in this form ten years ago," Knobloch said. "There have always been Nazis, there have always been Jew haters, but not in the way as it's the case today."

In Knobloch's view, the established parties have up to now failed to speak out decisively against the AfD: "Today's political parties must jointly, not alone, address the issue. I still see a chance here, that people will at least be willing to listen and discuss it. And that's very, very important."
Young people need to be included in the conversation
Politicians have to speak to young people in particular more intensively and address their fears, which isn't happening enough, Knobloch says.

"There's talk about it, but there is no real discussion, because young people are naturally afraid that what they say will become public. What I want to say is, we'll have to find ways to bring young people back into the fold."

Last week, Knobloch received death threats. On Thursday, a witness discovered the scrawled threats on a park bench and a rubbish bin in the English Garden in Munich and informed the police, according to a police headquarters statement. Knobloch subsequently canceled her attendance at an event. The threats were directly linked to the AfD's election victory in Saxony-Anhalt, a spokeswoman said in response to a query from the dpa news agency.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: South Africa probes deaths of 7 women near Johannesburg
articles.summary: Police have warned women to take extra care in parts of Johannesburg as similarities between seven deaths fuel fears that the cases could be connected.

image.caption: South African police have warned women to exercise caution amid fears the cases could be connectedImage: AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: South African police are investigating the deaths of seven women found east of Johannesburg over the past two months, after another body was discovered on Tuesday and an earlier case was added to the widening investigation.

The deaths have raised fears that a serial killer or group of killers could be operating in the area. Several of the victims were found naked or partially clothed, with some showing signs of sexual violence.
What have South African police said?
The South African Police Service (SAPS) has issued a public warning urging women to exercise caution when jogging or carrying out similar activities in the area.

"While investigations are still underway and SAPS has not, at this stage, confirmed that the deaths are linked to a serial killer, the similarities are sufficiently concerning for the police to issue a public warning and intensify investigations," police spokesperson Athlenda Mathe said.
President Cyril Ramaphosa on Tuesday ordered police to prioritize the investigations, saying the deaths were causing "fear and uncertainty" and promising that "no stone will be left unturned."
What do we know about the victims?
The bodies have been discovered at several locations across the Ekurhuleni municipality, east of Johannesburg.
Police said the first victim, a 37-year-old woman, was found naked and bound with cable ties on July 15. A suspect was arrested two days later.
A 32-year-old woman was found partially clothed on August 24. Another woman's body, found in a river near the Tembisa township on September 7, has now been included in the wider investigation.
One of the victims, aged 38, disappeared after leaving her eight-year-old daughter at home to go jogging. Her partially clothed body was found behind a hotel on September 12.
Another woman's body was discovered in the Kwa-Thema township on Tuesday.
Why are women still unsafe in South Africa?
Are South African police investigating a serial killer?
Police have not confirmed that the deaths are the work of a serial killer.
"We are still investigating whether we are dealing with one perpetrator or a group of men that are behind the murders of these women," police spokesperson Athlenda Mathe said.
Police said similarities between the cases were sufficiently concerning to issue a public warning, including advising women to exercise caution while jogging in the area.
How serious is violence against women in South Africa?
Violence against women is a longstanding problem in South Africa. UN Women says the country has some of the world's highest rates of violence against women and children.
Around one in three South African women experience physical or sexual violence during their lifetime, according to the United Nations.
The killings come as violent crime remains a major source of public concern ahead of municipal elections in November.
