articles.title: Spanish scientists find first evidence of Diplodocus dinosaur in Europe
articles.summary: Paleontologists in Spain say they have found the first evidence of the long-necked Diplodocus genus of dinosaur outside of North America. They found bones at the rich La Tejeria fossil site in Teruel…

image.caption: 'Dippy' the Diplodocus in the British Natural History Museum contributed to making the giant herbivore one of the most recognizable Jurassic creatures of them all [FILE: September 2016]Image: Travelshots/Visually/picture alliance

blocks.text: Researchers writing in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology this week say they have found the first skeletal evidence of the Diplodocus dinosaur outside of North America, uncovering various vertebrae and chevron bones dating back around 150 million years at a site in eastern Spain.

The team from the Dinopolis Foundation in Teruel, studying the rich La Tejeria fossil site in the El Castellar municipality, said the dinosaur joined a growing list of giant sauropods found in the area.
Although the long-necked herbivore with its vast tail is one of the world's most recognizable dinosaurs, fossilized remains had until this point only been recovered in North America.

blocks.caption: Dinosaurs like the Diplodocus and Stegosaurus were once thought to have lived exclusively on the North American continent but more and more evidence to the contrary is now being unearthedImage: Andia.fr/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: What did the researchers say about the find?
The paper published on Monday concluded that the find was "one of the most complete diplodocid skeletons from Europe."

It said that systematic study and analysis of 14 caudal vertebrae and several chevron bones "reveals that it can be confidently referred to as Diplodocus," one of several genuses in the diplodocid family of sauropod dinosaurs.

"This discovery consists of the first evidence of Diplodocus outside North America (Morrison Formation) and is one of the strongest piece of evidence that supports the exchange of continental faunas between North America and Europe during the Late Jurassic," the authors wrote.

Although the diplodocus is well known worldwide, not least thanks to the famous skeletal cast nicknamed "Dippy" that for years greeted visitors entering the British Natural History Museum, the researchers said that the "European diplodocid fossil record is scarce and fragmentary."
How could dinsoaurs cross an ocean?

During the time of the dinosaurs the continents were only just starting to drift apart. In recent decades scientists have begun to theorize that the proto-Atlantic Ocean still had ephemeral land bridges or episodic sea regressions or some other temporary means of crossing that occassionally enabled land-based dinosaurs to move vast distances between the separating continents.

Recent fossil finds, not least in Spain and Portugal near the Atlantic coast, have been further reinforcing this notion. This is part of a land bridge thought to have connected Iberia to what's now Canada.

The authors said the find "constitutes one of the strongest pieces of evidence of episodic dispersal events and faunal exchanges across the proto-North Atlantic Ocean during the late Kimmeridgian–early Tithonian" period, approximated 150 million years ago.
Another route linked North America with Scandinavia, and one much further south connected what's now Brazil to Cameroon.
Why did the dinosaurs grow so big?

articles.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial Day 25: SALNs show no cash or stock shares in multiple years
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte"s declarations in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN) took the spotlight on Day 25 of her impeachment trial.

blocks.text: Vice President Sara Duterte’s declarations in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN) took the spotlight on Day 25 of her impeachment trial.

This developed after the prosecution panel presented Ombudsman Records Division officer-in-charge Karen Batu to testify on the contents of the SALNs that the Vice President submitted in her years as a public official from 2007 to 2013 and from 2016 to 2025.

Batu said that the Vice President did not declare shares of stock in her SALNs in 2007, 2008 to 2013 and 2016 to 2025, although she declared that she and her husband, Manases Carpio, were either incorporators or stockholders in various businesses in the same years.
The businesses include:

items: Sgt. Fortune Horse Corp.
3Kids Inc. Trucking Services Inc.
Davao Bounty Times Food Corp.
Davao Emerging Taipan Corp.
Davao New Royal Taipan Corp., allegedly retired and formerly Davao Emerging Taipans Corp.
Timesquare Bee Foods Corp., formerly Great Jolly Times Foods Corp.
Gencorp Industries Inc., formerly Timesquare Bee Foods Corp.
City Hall King Chow Foods Corp.
Metro City Chow Foods Corp., allegedly formerly known as City Hall King Chow Foods Corp.
Tapang at Malasakit Alliance for the Philippines Inc.
Cykt Inc.
Zelta Matiem Salon, under Carpio
Carpio Lawyers
888 Bistro
Cale88 Foods Corp.
Madayaw Fisheries Corp.
Mati City Ice Plant and Cold Storage Inc.
Amianan Shores Inc.
Geometry Security and Investigation Agency Inc.
Cabletow 88 Shipping and Marine Services Inc.

blocks.text: Private prosecutor James Alih said the Vice President should have declared her shares of stock in her SALN for personal properties, which provides for an acquisition cost column to determine the value of each listed personal property.

Senator-judge Sherwin Gatchalian also raised the possibility that the Vice President’s net worth was underdeclared, noting that she did not indicate the value of her shares of stock in various businesses.
Batu, a lawyer, also said that the Vice President did not declare any cash on hand and in bank from 2019 to 2025.
Batu also testified that the Vice President did not file an exit SALN as required for government officials when her first term as Davao City mayor ended on June 30, 2013.
Duterte was not a public official from 2013 to 2016, but she was again elected as Davao City mayor in 2016 and 2019 before being elected Vice President in 2022.
This prompted senator Judge Lito Lapid to ask Batu if politicians or government workers really tell the whole truth in their SALNs.

“Meron po kasi akong napanood na isang abogado na in-interview sa TV. Ang sabi niya, ewan ko lang po kung tama ito, walang politiko o magsa-submit ng SALN na nagtatrabaho sa gobyerno na totoo. Ang sabi niya, isang kalokohan ‘yan kung magsasabi sila ng totoo. Tama po ba ’yun?” Lapid asked.

(I saw a lawyer being interviewed on TV. I don't know if this is true, but he said there is no politician or government employee who submits a truthful SALN. He said it would be foolish for them to tell the truth. Is that correct?)
Batu chuckled before replying, “Kami po, ako po, nagsa-submit po ako ng totoong SALN ko, Your Honor.” (I myself submit a truthful SALN, Your Honor.)

Later in the day, the prosecution panel said that the Vice President’s zero declaration of cash and shares of stock, as well as her increased wealth, raises questions as to whether these will match her legitimate sources of income and income tax filings.
The defense team, in response, said it has strategies to explain the movement of figures in her SALN.

"We have a strategy on that matter, actually. Obviously, without disclosing the specifics, I will also not deny na siyempre napag-isipan na ng depensa kung paano natin gagawin 'yan," defense team spokesperson Michael Poa said.
(We actually have a strategy on that matter. Obviously, without disclosing the specifics, I will also not deny that the defense has naturally thought about how we will handle that.)

Before the trial ended, the impeachment court issued a modified order for Gerardo del Rosario, Company Registration and Monitoring Department (CRMD) Director of the state-run Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), to testify before the impeachment trial of Vice President Duterte on September 21st and 22nd.
Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero reissued the subpoena upon the request of House prosecutor Terry Ridon of Bicol Saro party-list, citing voluminous documents involved.

In addition, the court encouraged the public to submit questions for the retired Supreme Court justices who will appear as amici curiae (friends of the court) to help resolve questions on the voting threshold for convicting Duterte.
In a press conference, court spokesperson lawyer Regie Tongol said the public may submit questions through the Senate of the Philippines’ official Facebook page.
The Senate impeachment court will hear the amici curiae on Wednesday, September 16.

Under the Constitution, the Senate has the sole power to try and decide all cases of impeachment and no person shall be convicted without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the members of the Senate.
There are 24 senators, meaning a two-thirds majority requires 16 votes.
At least four of the 24 senators, however, have not been able to participate in the impeachment trial proceedings for quite a while now.
Senators Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta are detained on plunder and other related charges due to their alleged involvement in flood control and undeclared campaign donations, respectively.
Senator Ronald dela Rosa is nowhere to be found amid a standing warrant of arrest issued against him by the International Criminal Court due to his alleged involvement in the drug war deaths.
Senator Loren Legarda is on an extended medical leave abroad due to a lung ailment. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Ash from Mount Etna grounds flights at Sicily airport
articles.summary: All flights are suspended from one of Italy's busiest airports until Tuesday night.

blocks.text: All flights have been suspended from one of Italy's busiest airports because of volcanic ash released from nearby Mount Etna.

It is the second time in recent months that Catania International Airport, on the island of Sicily, has stopped flights due to emissions from Etna, which is Europe's tallest active volcano and erupts frequently.
Airport officials said arrivals and departures, which were first halted on Monday, would be suspended until 22:00 (20:00 GMT) on Tuesday.
Ongoing activity at Etna prompted the INGV Etneo Observatory to issue a red aviation alert on Monday.
In a statement on its website on Tuesday, Catania - Italy's fifth-busiest airport by passenger traffic - said further updates would follow.
It also advised passengers due to fly from Catania to check with their airline for updates before travelling to the airport.
Catania, which usually serves about 12 million passengers each year, was closed for almost a week during the peak summer season last month because of volcanic activity.
There have been calls for the airport to shut and other facilities in Sicily to be expanded because of its proximity to Etna.
The volcano, which stands at 3,324 metres (10,906ft), is about 40km (25 miles) away from the airport.
Despite air traffic disruption, August's eruption drew large crowds of onlookers to Etna's lava flows. About 1.5 million people visit Etna every year.

articles.title: Democrat sends letter to White House over Trump Jr wedding bankrolled by Russian oligarch
articles.summary:
Robert Garcia expresses concern over ‘any possible foreign entanglement’ between White House and Umar Kremlev

Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House oversight committee, is…

blocks.text: Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House oversight committee, is investigating potential ties between the White House and a Russian oligarch who paid for a portion of Donald Trump Jr’s wedding.

In a letter sent to Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, on Monday, Garcia expressed concern about “any possible foreign entanglement” between the president’s son and the oligarch, Umar Kremlev. Garcia asked Wiles to provide documents, records and communications between the White House and Trump Jr about Kremlev, among other requests.

“As the son of President Donald Trump and the part-owner and major investor of multiple companies with extensive Department of Defense contracts, any apparent ties to members of Russian President Vladimir Putin’s inner circle raises serious questions about pay-to-play schemes and foreign intelligence infiltration of the President’s family,” Garcia wrote in the letter.

In a separate letter addressed to Trump Jr, Garcia expressed similar worries and asked the president’s son to provide more details about his wedding events bankrolled by Kremlev, including: all dates of communication between Trump Jr and Kremlev, any communications Trump Jr may have had with the White House about Kremlev, financial records of purchases made by foreign nationals and a complete list of wedding gifts from foreign nationals.

It came just hours after ProPublica revealed that the Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on wedding celebrations for Trump Jr and his wife, Bettina, earlier this year. The couple also confirmed Kremlev’s financial involvement on Monday.

“I have no idea who Umar is, never heard of him, and he didn’t pay for Don and Bettina’s wedding, which took place at a totally different location, and on a different day from the wedding. It was an ‘afterparty’ given in their honor. Not a big deal! I was not present at the party,” the US president said in a statement in response to the report.
“Why did a Russian oligarch close to Putin fund Trump Jr.’s wedding in the Bahamas?” Garcia wrote on X after the ProPublica report was published.
Garcia added: “Umar Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the President’s son. What did he get in return? We need answers.”
Axios was the first to report on Garcia’s letter.

The investigation into Trump Jr’s wedding is part of the House Oversight Committee Democrats’ larger investigation into the ways the Trump family has allegedly enriched themselves since President Donald Trump took office last year.
The Guardian reached out to Garcia’s office and the White House for further comment.

articles.title: What weapon could the US have put into space?
articles.summary: The announcement by the US points to a developing field of modern warfare in the Earth's orbit.

blocks.text: The announcement by the United States that it has deployed a space weapon in Earth's orbit has raised questions about what weaponry is actually in space, and what role it could play in efforts by great powers to dominate that arena.

Washington has given away little in its announcement. Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the "on orbit" weapon was necessary to safeguard US forces against hostile enemy action, but gave no details about the weapon's capabilities or when it was put into orbit.
So what could this weapon be, and what is wider picture like for military developments in space? Who else could have similar weaponry?

Advanced militaries already deploy satellites in space for range of purposes, from supplying secure communications to reconnaissance, and providing precise location information for targeted strikes and detecting missile launches.
As warfare become more technologically advanced, analysts expect the use of military hardware in space to increase.

Dr Bleddyn Bowen, an associate fellow in military sciences at the Royal United Services Institute and associate professor in astropolitics at Durham University, said he was only able to hazard a guess about the weapon announced by the US.
"I would expect there to be some kind of electronic warfare or radio-jamming platform, possibly, this would be a non-destructive kind of anti-satellite weapon," he told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
Such weaponry already exists on Earth and can disrupt satellite communications, he said. "If you take out the radio links then your satellite is very useless."
Bowen also would not rule out some sort of more disruptive and riskier weaponry, which could create a lot of debris and destruction.
"Less likely would be a kinetic kill vehicle of some sort, so a vehicle that would release a projectile of some sort that could ram into a satellite and destroy it," he said.
"Possibly some sort of close inspection and grappling satellite would be another possibility as well."
But while the weapon placed in orbit appears to be a first, the US - and indeed its Russian and Chinese rivals - have had weapons that can be pointed and shot into space for some time.
In fact in the last 10 years, Russia and China have been doing a lot more manoeuvres in space, known as rendezvous and proximity operations (RPOs) - "buzzing" Western satellites.

"Theoretically, these RPO sats can become hunter-killer satellites by physically colliding with them or by nudging them out of orbit," Dr Rod Thornton, reader in Russian Defence and Security Studies at King's College, London, told the BBC.
Bowen adds that the Chinese have demonstrated "space tug capability", saying: "A vehicle can go up to a satellite, can grapple it and move it into a different orbit."
This, he says, can be a positive development - a way of removing space junk as well as knocking out working satellites.
Thornton says that what Russia lacks in space weaponry and satellites, it makes up for in missile capability.

"The Russians... have ground-based missiles which can be launched into space to strike sats in low Earth orbit. They also have ASAT missiles that can be launched from a great height by aircraft," he says.

"From the Russian point of view they see Nato as having much better and more sats than the Russian military can call up, therefore they have invested heavily in ASATs in order to 'level the battlefield' somewhat."
Thornton adds a sobering thought: "As a last resort, the Russians can also launch nuclear weapons into space and the EPM blast would 'fry' any unhardened sats over a wide expanse."

He says that, having so few satellites, Russia would be the "big winner" in any space war, which would involve "missiles fired up into space, manoeuvring sats designed to nudge/destroy them and ground-based lasers".

articles.summary: Experts tell BBC Verify the pipeline's closure could cut oil supplies by as much as 3.6 million barrels per day.

blocks.text: Satellite imagery shows a key oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia has been badly damaged after a strike last week, which experts have told BBC Verify could take more than a month to repair and force oil prices even higher.

The image shows the most significant damage is at a pumping station along the East-West Pipeline, which Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on to export crude oil via the Red Sea rather than through the Strait of Hormuz, where ships have been attacked by Iran and the US during their six-month war.

The Saudi government has accused Iranian-backed militias in Iraq of the pipeline strike, which followed days of renewed missile and drone attacks on south-western Saudi Arabia by Yemen's Houthi group - which is also backed by Iran. Saudi Arabia has retaliated by carrying out strikes on Houthi-controlled areas of western Yemen.
New satellite images also show damage to Saudi Arabia's King Khalid Air Base after a Houthi strike last week.
The Saudi government said on Tuesday it would respond "firmly" to attacks by the Houthis.
While the Houthis have been fighting a long-running civil war against Saudi-backed Yemeni pro-government forces, the group has stepped up its campaign in recent weeks.

It seized control of significant new territory across Yemen's south-western coast last week, including areas overlooking the crucial Bab al-Mandab waterway, strengthening its ability to enforce its declared blockade of Saudi shipping.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia faces hard choices as Houthis gain in Yemen
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia faces growing security and economic problems as it seeks to balance deterrence and diplomacy during its escalating conflict with the Iran-backed Houthis in neighboring Yemen.

image.caption: Saudi Arabia is increasingly affected by Yemen's civil war in which it backs the Yemeni governmentImage: Ansarullah Media Centre/AFP

blocks.text: Saudi Arabia is being increasingly affected by the rapidly escalating conflict across its southern border in Yemen, where the Iran-backed Houthis are fighting Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces.
Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia injured another 13 people on Monday night bringing the total number of people injured since the conflict escalated in July to about 100.

In July, the Houthis also blocked Saudi oil shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key waterway that had been serving as an alternative route for Saudi oil exports amid Iran's blockade of the nearby Strait of Hormuz.

Last week, Saudi Arabia's alternative lifeline for oil export, the East-West pipeline, was allegedly targeted by Iranian proxy militias in Iraq. On Tuesday, officials said that it might take weeks to repair the damage to the pipeline which runs 1,200 kilometers (745 miles) across the country and ends at the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea.

"Riyadh faces a genuine dilemma," Neil Quilliam, associate fellow of the Middle East and North Africa program at the London-based think tank Chatham House, told DW. "The Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is trying to protect both Saudi security and Saudi economic development simultaneously," he said. "The difficulty is that the Houthis are increasingly able to threaten both."

blocks.caption: After attacks on Saudi Arabia's alternative export hub, the East-West oil export pipeline will be closed for weeks for repairImage: Vantor/AFP

blocks.text: Saudi Arabia seeks to balance deterrence and diplomacy
Saudi Arabia has one of the most heavily armed and technologically sophisticated militaries in the Middle East, especially in combat aviation and air defense.
But the country is "reluctant to become drawn back into a costly military campaign in Yemen," Quilliam said.

A Saudi-led military coalition intervened in Yemen in 2015 to support the government's fight against Houthi insurgents. After seven years of intense war between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed government, the fighting eased in 2022 with a UN-brokered truce.

The latest Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and the Saudi-backed government in Yemen aim to pressure Saudi Arabia to end its air and sea blockades on Houthi-held territory which have not been fully lifted despite the 2022 truce.
"Saudi Arabia is now in a very complicated situation," Sebastian Sons, Middle East observer at the German Middle East Research Center CARPO, said.

"On the one hand, it needs to make it clear to the Houthis that a red line has been crossed and that there must also be a military response, particularly in coordination with Yemen's internationally recognized government.
"But on the other hand, it also needs to keep the lines of communication open in order to get back to the negotiating table and to de-escalate the situation."

In his view, Riyadh's goal is to balance deterrence and diplomacy. "The argument is very clear," he said, adding that "the Houthis are not only a threat to Saudi Arabia but to the global economy as a whole."

After Houthi advances in southern Yemen last week, including the seizure of port cities and Perim Island in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the rebels are now able to exert even more pressure on global oil supply.
This strategy could lend more leverage to Iran in its war with the United States.

According to the maritime data and analytics firm Kpler, only 21 commodity vessels transited the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on Monday. Before the crisis, the narrow waterway handled roughly 30% of global container traffic.

blocks.caption: US President Donald Trump, (right), seen with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, is reportedly resisting pressure to get involved in the renewed fighting in YemenImage: Evelyn Hockstein/REUTERS

blocks.text: Saudi Arabia's 'new level of vulnerability'
"The current conflict exposes a new level of vulnerability for Saudi Arabia," Quilliam from Chatham House said. "And it's being tested from all sides."

While Saudi Arabia is a close US ally, three sources told the Reuters news agency that Saudi Arabia's de facto ruler, Mohammed bin Salman, or MBS, phoned US President Donald Trump last Thursday, asking for military aid to fight the advancing Houthis.
The sources said that he was only offered intelligence support for now as Trump hesitated to join another front in the ongoing US war in Iran.

The recently signed Mecca Joint Defense Agreement between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan has also yet to be activated. So far, Pakistan, an Iranian ally and mediator in the current US war in Iran, has been reluctant to directly join the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis.
"The untested nature of the Mecca Pact adds to Saudi Arabia's challenges," Quilliam said.

blocks.caption: The escalating conflict in Yemen has displaced around 85,000 people, warned the International Organization for Migration this weekImage: Marwan Abdullah Yahya Saeed Al-Shabi/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: Saudi Arabia's silencing of dissent
Meanwhile, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman faces growing domestic pressure.
"People expect economic progress," Sons told DW. For Saudi Arabia's population, this means "affordable housing, jobs and protection from additional attacks from Yemen," he said.

On top of this, Saudi Arabia needs stability to continue progressing its costly Vision 2030 reform. The sweeping diversification agenda aims to reduce the kingdom's reliance on oil and to transform the economy and society but the foreign investment, tourism and investor confidence all depend on a stable security situation, Quilliam points out.
Other major planned events in Saudi Arabia, such as the Expo 2030 and the 2034 FIFA World Cup depend on geopolitical stability as well.
In turn, as security threats grow and economic pressures mount, human rights observers say Saudi authorities are becoming increasingly sensitive to criticism of their handling of the crisis.

"Since MBS rose to power, there has been a strong crackdown on freedom of expression, especially regarding criticism of Saudi foreign policy," Yahya Al-Asiri, founder of the London-based Saudi rights organization ALQST for Human Rights, told DW.

"Critics and individuals calling for peace are dealt with harshly," he said, highlighting that people are charged under the country's counter-terrorism laws and sentenced to lengthy prison terms or even to death for nonviolent actions.
In 2025, Saudi Arabia carried out at least 356 executions, the highest annual total recorded by ALQST.

This week, the rights watchdog warned that Saudi authorities executed at least 154 people between January and September 2026. Of the 154 executions, 101 were carried out for drug-related crimes while nine executions took place for terrorism-related offenses "which according to the vague and overly broad definition in Saudi law can include a wide range of non-lethal acts," the report states.

articles.title: More than 100,000 people in Japan are now aged 100 or older
articles.summary: Figures show 88% of the centenarians are women as the population continues to age and shrink.

blocks.text: The number of people aged 100 or more in Japan has exceeded 100,000 for the first time, according to the health ministry.

Figures show Japan is now home to 107,677 centenarians, the highest number in the world, of which 88% are women. The oldest woman is Kishimoto Fuyo, a 114-year-old from Kyoto City and the oldest man is Kato Hikaru, a 112-year-old from Kumamoto.
Health Minister Kenichiro Ueno said he was "delighted that so many people are living long, healthy and active lives", citing progress in medicine and technology.
But Kenichiri also warned of the challenge the country faces in maintaining a sustainable social security system.
Experts put the long lives of the Japanese down to several factors, including a healthy diet and an active lifestyle.
The island nation's cuisine predominantly consists of fish, vegetables, and rice - and less saturated fat than many Western diets.
Older people also regularly walk, use public transport, cycle and stretch.
Japan has been aging for years and sales of adult nappies have been higher than those for babies for more than a decade.
Companies have also developed new products for the older population, including a powered exoskeleton to support moving various parts of the body and eyewear that automatically adjusts its focus.
For a population to replace itself, each woman needs to give birth to 2.1 children on average. Last year Japan's total fertility rate dropped to a record low of 1.14.

The total population is estimated to drop to 87 million by 2070, representing a 30% decline from its peak of 128 million in 2008, according to data from the National Institute of Population and Social Security research.
Residents aged 65 and older currently make up around 30% of the population and are expected to make up nearly 40% by 2070.
Japanese authorities have called the trend an "existential crisis" with Prime Minister Sanae Takichi describing the decline as a "quiet emergency".
In 2025 Japan's total population decreased in all 47 prefectures but two, and the rate of decline is accelerating.
The government's many programmes and subsidies to encourage young people to have more children do not appear to be boosting birth rates.
Experts say the reasons are complex, ranging from lower marriage rates and more women joining the workforce to the increased costs of raising children.
While immigration has risen in previous years, foreigners only make up around 3% of the population and opposition to accepting more has grown.

articles.title: Canada is a 'safe harbour' for global finance, Carney says
articles.summary: The prime minister is hosting a major global investment summit, with the goal of attracting investment amid a trade war with the US.

blocks.text: Prime Minister Mark Carney has pitched Canada as a "safe harbour" for some of the world's largest investors to spend their money in an era of geopolitical and economic uncertainty.

The country is "perfectly situated to build in the new global economic order", he told more than 100 global investors and sovereign wealth fund representatives gathered in Toronto for a major investment summit.
The group represent more than C$120tn ($86tn; £64tn) of assets. Carney's ambition is that they will invest in sectors like defence, energy, mining, AI and infrastructure.
Ottawa hopes they can be sold on more than 160 projects, from data centres to pipelines, and help Canada weather its trade war with the US.

Canada's dispute with its largest trade partner has prompted Carney to look to expand economic partnerships with Europe, Asia and the Middle East as he seeks to reduce his country's reliance on its neighbour to the south.
"Our goal is simple: to make Canada the most attractive place in the G7 to invest," Carney said on Tuesday morning.

As part of that move, Carney announced plans to privatise operations for four of the country's largest airports, saying it would raise billions of dollars that could be reinvested in transport infrastructure.

Many of the business leaders attending the event in Toronto received a personal invitation from the prime minister, who worked in the top tiers of global finance and was a central banker before turning to politics.
Much of the action will take place in private sessions and bilateral meetings over the course of the day.
There will, however, be panels with speakers including Deutsche Bank AG CEO Christian Sewing, Bombardier executive Eric Martel, and BlackRock CEO Larry Fink and Blackstone president Jon Gray.
For Carney, the event will be a test of whether he can deliver on his promise to strengthen the country's economic resilience.
Trade talks between Ottawa and Washington collapsed last month and the two countries have since imposed tit-for-tat tariffs.
On Tuesday, new US tariffs came into effect on a number of Canadian goods while some others were lifted, and bans on goods like alcohol and motorcycles are due to come into force next week.
On Tuesday, Carney addressed the American executives in Toronto directly.
"To our American friends, let me say this. We will always be neighbours, and Canada will continue to be the US's most important partner in many key areas," he said.
"After all, even at times of disagreement during our long history, we have always maintained deep ties."

Meanwhile, protestors on Monday accused the Carney government of organising a "great Canadian sell-off" of public resources and infrastructure to corporate interests, and hundreds appeared outside the opening night gala at a downtown museum.
"Half the buyers that he has invited here to Toronto are American," said Kai Nagata, with advocacy group Dogwood, on Monday.
"Let's be clear, every piece of our country that we sell off to American billionaires brings us closer to becoming the 51st state."

blocks.text: Published September 15, 2026 9:38pm
The Sandiganbayan Third Division has allowed former Speaker Ferdinand Martin Romualdez to attend his arraignment and pre-trial via videoconference on Wednesday.
According to Third Division clerk of court Atty. Dennis Pulma, the tribunal granted Romualdez's urgent motion "to allow attendance for arraignment and pre-trial via videoconference."
Romualdez's arraignment has been set at 8:30 a.m. on Wednesday, September 16.
The Leyte congressman is facing plunder charges in connection with P7.2 billion in alleged kickbacks from allocations for infrastructure projects.
His co-accused, former Ako Bicol party-list Rep. Zaldy Co, Samchan Foreign Exchange Corp. president Felicito Guevarra, and Romualdez's personal assistant Joselyn Sereño, all remain at large.

Romualdez was committed to the Quezon City Jail in Payatas on Monday. He was taken to the facility in the evening and was placed in the jail infirmary together with inmates who also need medical monitoring.
The former Speaker was placed under arrest at the Cardinal Santos Medical Center before he was transferred to the Philippine General Hospital.
Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said Romualdez had suffered a cardiovascular event and an anxiety attack.

Romualdez was placed under hospital detention until Monday, when doctors told the Sandiganbayan that he was in stable condition despite his illnesses and didn't need hospital confinement. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Prosecution flags VP Sara's 'tanging yaman' over years of zero cash declaration
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel flagged Vice President Sara Duterte"s non-declaration of cash in her SALN for seven years amid the exponential increase in her net worth.

blocks.text: The House prosecution panel on Tuesday flagged Vice President Sara Duterte’s non-declaration of cash in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN) for seven years amid the exponential increase in her net worth, saying these should match the Vice President’s tax payments and source of income.

“For Day 25 of the impeachment trial, this is titled Ang Tanging Yaman ni VP Sara. Pitong taong walang cash na idineklara. Ang nakalagay sa batas, ang cash on hand at cash in bank ay dapat [ideklara], at ito ay dapat tukoy na idineklara sa ilalim ng RA 6713,” lawyer Hez Montalan, deputy spokesperson of the House prosecution panel, said, referring to the Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees.
(Seven years of no cash declared. In the law, the cash on hand and cash in bank must be declared and identified under RA 6713.)

Montalan was referring to the testimony of Ombudsman Records Division officer-in-charge Karen Batu, who told the Senate impeachment court that the Vice President’s SALN filings from 2019 to 2025 did not include declarations of cash on hand or in bank.

Specifically, Section 8 of the said law states that “All public officials and employees, except those who serve in an honorary capacity, laborers and casual or temporary workers, shall file under oath their Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth and a Disclosure of Business Interests and Financial Connections and those of their spouses and unmarried children under 18 years of age living in their households.”

Likewise, the same provision states that the SALN entries should include the following: (a) real property, its improvements, acquisition costs, assessed value and current fair market value; (b) personal property and acquisition cost; (c) all other assets such as investments, cash on hand or in banks, stocks, bonds, and the like; (d) liabilities, and; (e) all business interests and financial connections.
“This [cash] should not be lumped together with other personal properties,” Montalan pointed out.

He also cited Batu's testimony that confirmed that the Vice President did not declare shares of stocks in her SALNs even as she declared that she was an incorporator or a stockholder of multiple businesses in various years.
“Under our laws, SALN is not a mere form. This should be submitted under oath,” he added.
But wait, there’s more?

Private prosecutor Benjamin Tolosa, Jr., for his part, said that the Vice President’s net worth climbing from P7.2 million in 2007 to at least P98 million as of end-2025 based on her declared SALN raises questions of whether this will match her income tax filings and other sources of income.

“We are talking about unexplained wealth here. Iyong nadeklarang yaman dito sa kanyang mga SALNs, ito ba ay tutugma doon sa kanyang income na puwede niyang kitain as government official? And if so, does she have other legitimate sources, and if those are allowed considering the restrictions of the law since she is already a Vice President?” Tolosa said.
(Will her declared wealth match with her income as a government official?)

“Are these income sources declared in her BIR (Bureau of Internal Revenue) filings? Secondly, iyong mga nadeklarang yaman na ‘yan, ‘yan lang ba talaga ang kabuuang yaman niya, o mayroon pang mas malaking yaman na hindi pa naipapakita at hindi nadeklara? There are really questions that need to be answered here,” he added.
(Besides, is her declared wealth all there is? Or does she have higher amount of wealth that is yet to be declared or was not declared?)

It was Senator judge and Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian who cited the possibility of the Vice President's net worth being undervalued since she did not indicate the amount of her shares of stock in various businesses she was involved in based on her SALN declaration.
Why not 'yaman'?

House prosecutor Terry Ridon of Bicol Saro party-list and House prosecution panel adviser and former Surigao del Norte congressman Ace Barbers, on the other hand, said that the defense’s refusal to use the word "yaman" to translate net worth during the proceedings is puzzling because there was no other way to translate net worth with a word that is understandable.
“Anything you possess, properties, cases, whatever…assets mo ‘yun. Yaman mo ‘yun. Hindi naman puedeng tawagin na hirap [mo yun],” Barbers said.
(That is your wealth. You cannot call it your scarce wealth.)
Ridon then said translating net worth to the word "yaman," which also translates to wealth in English, is merely calling spade a spade.
“Tama rin iyong sinabi ni presiding officer [Francis Escudero] na kabuuang pag-aari pero ultimately, yaman pa rin talaga. Huwag na natin pag-iba ibahin. A duck is a duck,” Ridon added.
Defense lawyer Michael Poa, in response, said they will address these allegations of the prosecution in due time.

“The witness was a mere custodian of the SALNs and she cannot testify on whether there is ill-gotten wealth there. If we need to explain the increase in net worth [of the Vice President, we will have our turn for that,” Poa said.
“That will come later with other witnesses or other evidence to be presented by the defense,” Poa added. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Family wants killing of young engineer linked with case of kidnapped Canadian mining firm workers
articles.summary: The family of Pablo Osorio Sánchez is calling on federal authorities in Mexico to link the killing of the 26-year-old engineer with the ongoing investigation into the January kidnapping of 10…

image.caption: Pablo Osorio Sánchez, 26, was kidnapped in the same town and around the same time that armed men abducted 10 employees of a Canadian mining firm. (Courtesy of Mauricio Osorio Sánchez)

blocks.text: The family of Pablo Osorio Sánchez is calling on federal authorities in Mexico to link the killing of the 26-year-old engineer with the ongoing investigation into the January kidnapping of 10 Canadian mining firm workers.

Osorio Sánchez was kidnapped in the same town and around the same time that armed men seized the Vizsla Silver Corp. employees and contractors. His body was buried in the same clandestine graves where federal authorities located nine of the 10 kidnapped workers.
The family believes the facts around the Vizsla Silver kidnappings could also reveal the truth behind Osorio Sánchez's fate.

"We want answers, we need them to explain to us who kidnapped him, for what reason. Who were they? We have so many questions and so few answers," said Jaime López, Osorio Sánchez’s uncle, in a phone interview with CBC News from Florida.

Between 6 a.m. and 7 a.m. on Jan. 23, armed men, allegedly aligned with a Sinaloa cartel faction, stormed a gated compound in Concordia, Sinaloa, called La Clementina where Vizsla Silver housed its workers and parked some of its vehicles.

Around 7:30 that same morning, Osorio Sánchez walked from his residence in Concordia, a municipality roughly 50 kilometres east of the Pacific Coast city of Mazatlan, to a bus stop. He called his girlfriend while waiting for his regular weekday ride to his worksite at a highway tunnel several kilometres to the east.

During the phone conversation, his partner suddenly heard male voices. One said, "We can fix this." Then the line went dead. That was the last time she ever spoke to him, according to family testimony and filings from the UN Committee on Enforced Disappearances and the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.
'Indicio C'

Federal authorities located the body of Osorio Sánchez, originally from Taxiaco, Oaxaca, about two weeks later. He was buried at a depth of two metres along with an unknown number of other bodies in one of at least two unmarked, clandestine graves dug into an open field in El Verde, a village about 19 km northwest of Concordia.

Authorities identified the spot where Osorio Sánchez was found as "fosa 2," or Grave 2, according to investigative records obtained by CBC News. They wrapped Osorio Sánchez's body in a blue surgical sheet and tagged his body bag with the label "Indicio C" to identify it among the other bodies found in the same area on Feb. 6.

Post-mortem examinations determined he died from a gunshot wound to the upper right side of the head and that his body suffered severe blunt-force trauma before his death. A suspected bullet wound was also found on his right jaw, with no exit point.
"We are destroyed, mentally, because this is a very big loss for us," said López.
Osorio Sánchez was the oldest of three brothers.

items: Vancouver-based mining company confirms the deaths of 9 of 10 workers kidnapped in Mexico
Canadian mining company employees worked amid gunfire, Mexican cartel checkpoints, says family member
Local management had dealings with armed group before kidnapping at Canadian mining company, say ex-workers

blocks.text: The El Verde gravesites also included the remains of nine of the 10 men kidnapped from the Vizsla Silver compound. Some of the other bodies were found with similar signs of blunt-force trauma with gunshot wounds to the head, according to information obtained by CBC News.
The whereabouts of the 10th kidnapped Vizsla Silver worker, Francisco Antonio Esparza Yáñez, who was responsible for community relations, remains unknown.

Maurillo Santiago, a lead lawyer with the Centre for Human Rights and Legal Council for Indigenous Peoples in Oaxaca, said separate branches of the federal Attorney General’s Office are handling Osorio Sánchez’s case and the Vizsla Silver workers investigation.

Santiago, who is representing the family, said that investigators with the forced disappearances unit are managing Osorio Sánchez’s case, while the organized crime branch holds the Vizsla Silver file.
The Attorney General's Office did not respond to a CBC News request for comment.
'A gap that we can't cross'

Yetzy Santiago Lorenzo, a lawyer with the same human rights group that's also handling the case, said there are still outstanding questions around how the clandestine graves were found, who found them and who was buried alongside Osorio Sánchez.
She said it remains unclear whether it was federal and state authorities that found the graves in El Verde or civilian collectives that search for disappeared persons.
"There is a strange secrecy around this, because the moment the graves were found, federal authorities, the Attorney General’s office, took over and guarded the area," said Santiago Lorenzo.
"Why does the Attorney General’s Office separate Pablo’s investigation from the group? There is a space, a gap that we can’t cross yet."

Osorio Sánchez and the Vizsla Silver workers were kidnapped and killed amid a more than two-year-long civil war within the Sinaloa cartel between La Chapiza, those still loyal to the sons of Joaquín "El Chapo" Guzmán Loera, and La Mayiza, those loyal to the son of Ismael "El Mayo" Zambado, who once co-led the Sinaloa cartel with El Chapo.

The civil war, which has left thousands of people dead and disappeared across the state, flared after one of El Chapo’s sons lured El Mayo to a July 2024 meeting on the outskirts of the Sinaloan capital of Culiacan to have him kidnapped and turned over to U.S. authorities.
Mexican federal authorities have said a cell linked to the La Chapiza faction was responsible for the kidnapping and killings of Vizsla Silver's workers.

items: Sinaloa cartel faction linked to kidnapping of Canadian mining firm's workers: top official

blocks.text: In June, a local, La Chapiza-aligned boss named Gabriel Nicolás "El Gabito, El 80" Martínez Larios was arrested in connection with the Vizsla Silver kidnapping. This month, federal authorities announced the arrests of Angel Gabriel, known as "El Tronco," and Milton Yair, along with 11 other people, including two minors, who were part of the La Chapiza cell linked to the case.
Gabriel and Yair were reportedly members of a La Chapiza commando unit known as Los Menores.
In the middle of conflict territory

A July report from International Crisis Group on the civil war said hundreds of families fled the Concordia region in September 2024 as the conflict exploded and La Mayiza gunmen "dislodged the local strongman" affiliated with La Chapiza.

Vizsla Silver’s exploration operations are in the middle of this conflict territory. The Canadian mining firm is conducting exploration work across 35,000 hectares in a remote and mountainous area as part of its flagship Panuco Project, roughly 25 km east of Concordia’s urban centre.
"Dozens [of families] have since returned … Many services, however, are now controlled by [La Mayiza], including public transport," said the report.

The deaths, violence and chaos of the conflict in Sinaloa have likely played a role in the decision by federal authorities to treat Osorio Sánchez’s case differently from that of the Vizsla Silver workers, which received widespread coverage, said Mexico City lawyer Cesar Gutiérrez Priego, a specialist in national security and military affairs.

"That has created enormous legal uncertainty and problems. No matter how hard the federal government tries to show results, the reality is that Pablo’s case, for example, is just one more among many that keep piling up," he said.
"It isn’t a priority for the media or authorities. They simply haven’t placed the necessary emphasis on conducting the investigation as it should be done."
Gutiérrez Priego said the family’s lawyers should petition a federal judge to join the cases.

Santiago Lorenzo said that at the moment, they are focused on convincing the Attorney General’s Office to add the case to the one involving the Vizsla Silver workers before making any applications to the court.
The wait for answers weighs heavily on Osorio Sánchez’s family.
"I call on the Mexican authorities not to let this become normalized," said Lopez.
"There are many young people, students, who want to become engineers, too, and it would be sad if [their careers] ended in the same way."

articles.title: Why the era of cheap government debt is over
articles.summary: US debt has topped $40 trillion. How risky is the growing debt burden, and will investors keep funding Washington's deficits?

image.caption: If bond yields continue to rise, a stock market correction looms, many financial analysts warnImage: Brendan McDermid/REUTERS

blocks.text: When the world's largest pension fund changes its investment strategy, the financial world pays close attention, especially when it plans to drastically reduce its holdings of US government bonds.
According to Reuters, Norway's sovereign wealth fund wants to cut its US bond holdings, which totalled around $215 billion (€186 billion) at the end of June, by $80 billion.

Global investors are increasingly viewing the US debt binge with suspicion, especially as the country's national debt surpassed $40 trillion in August. This week, the yield on 30-year US Treasury bonds climbed to nearly 5.4%, the highest level since 2007.
How much debt is too much?

For highly indebted countries like Japan, where debt exceeds 200% of economic output, borrowing money on capital markets is getting increasingly expensive. The same applies to Italy, France and the UK.
Germany is in a much better position. At around 65% of gross domestic product (GDP), its debt-to-GDP ratio is only about half that of the US.
Borrowing to modernize its armed forces and infrastructure, however, means that ratio is set to move toward 80% over the coming years.
Why US debt keeps rising

The US now spends over $1 trillion annually on interest payments — more than $3 billion per day — according to calculations by the Congressional Budget Office. Since 2024, Washington has spent more annually on servicing its debt than on its entire military.
The Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis calculated that the US national debt has risen by around 650% over the past 30 years, from $5.2 trillion in 1996.

blocks.caption: Can US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calm the bond markets?Image: Kyodo/picture alliance

blocks.text: This year, the US budget deficit is on course to reach nearly 6%. Yet, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent aims to cut it by half — a goal seen as unrealistic given the huge cost of the Iran war plus a shortfall in revenue due to corporate tax cuts and the tariffs struck down by the Supreme Court.

"That is a very difficult path," Carsten Roemheld, capital market strategist at Fidelity International, told DW. "Nervousness is also rising sharply within the US administration — that is clearly evident. If this trajectory continues, it will be very difficult to sustain."
This is particularly striking when you consider how rapidly US debt is rising.

The $10 trillion mark was surpassed during the 2008 financial crisis, while $20 trillion was reached in 2017. By early 2022, the figure had already hit $30 trillion. It took just four and a half years to reach the next record high of $40 trillion this summer.
Why bond investors are worried
Bessent has therefore resorted to a special measure to drive down US bond yields.
On September 9, he announced he would triple the volume of long-term US government bond buybacks from the previous $2 billion to as much as $6 billion.
"The measure is, of course, far too small on its own to truly keep yields in check over the long term," said Roemheld.
"The bond market [now] demands discipline," Kim Crawford, global fixed income portfolio manager at JPMorgan Asset Management, told the Financial Times.
That discipline is, however, sorely lacking and many analysts say governments have shown little appetite for spending cuts.
What's behind the US government's bond buyback scheme?
US still dominates capital markets
Despite all the problems, most economists agree that there is currently no way for investors to bypass the US.

"The European capital market is not yet an alternative to the US market," said Carsten Brzeski, chief economist at ING Bank, noting that China and other emerging markets are neither able nor willing to take over this role.

"That is why I believe investors — even though they currently fear higher inflation and question the sustainability of US sovereign debt — will not turn away from the US," Brzeski told DW. "At least not as long as the US economy is growing."
Fidelity's Roemheld also sees no immediate danger for the US, which he says is unlikely to default and can simply print money to pay off the debt.

"But this course of action will undermine confidence," Roemheld said. "And one outlet for this is the dollar exchange rate, which suffers when international investors become less willing to continue providing dollars to the US."

blocks.caption: Amazon and others are investing hundreds of billions in AI infrastructure — partly funded by bondsImage: Noah Berger/AP Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: AI investment drives up interest rates
However long the US war against Iran drags on — driving up military spending and energy prices — there are strong indications that the US will have to pay higher interest rates on capital markets

According to Robert Sockin, chief US economist at asset manager PGIM, this is partly due to artificial intelligence or "AI-related corporate bonds increasingly crowding out government bonds," as he put it.
Roemheld agrees that as major tech companies issue bonds to finance AI infrastructure they are creating competition for government debt.

"The four major 'hyperscalers' alone — the companies building platforms for the US AI industry — have already raised over $800 billion in debt this year, a figure expected to rise further over the next year or two," he told DW.
This is an attractive alternative for many investors who previously held US Treasuries for safety only to see their outlook deteriorate in recent years, says Roemheld.

If as an investor I can now get "long-term bonds from high-quality companies like Alphabet or Microsoft, sometimes with spreads of 100 basis points over Treasuries, then that represents genuine competition," he told DW.
This piece was originally published in German.

articles.title: Fearing retaliation, drug war victims urge ICC to keep Rodrigo Duterte detained
articles.summary: Lawyers representing victims in the International Criminal Court (ICC) case against former President Rodrigo Duterte have asked Trial Chamber III to keep him in detention, saying the circumstances…
articles.byline: JAY-VEE MARASIGAN PANGAN, ANDY PEÑAFUERTE III

blocks.text: Published September 15, 2026 9:15pm

Families and relatives of extrajudicial killing victims hold a protest rally inside the University of the Philippines in Quezon City on Friday, February 28, 2026, the last day of the confirmation of charges hearing against former President Rodrigo Duterte in the International Criminal Court in the Netherlands. DANNY PATA/File photo

Lawyers representing victims in the International Criminal Court (ICC) case against former President Rodrigo Duterte have asked Trial Chamber III to keep him in detention, saying the circumstances previously cited by the court remain unchanged.

In a public redacted filing dated September 15, Atty. Gilbert Andres, Atty. Joel Butuyan, and Paolina Massidda of the Common Legal Representatives of Victims (CLRV) argued that Duterte’s continued detention “remains necessary and warranted” to ensure his appearance at trial and prevent possible intimidation or interference with victims and witnesses.
“Victims expect to finally see Mr. Duterte appear in person in the courtroom,” the lawyers said.
The victims’ lawyers also said the latest medical assessment of Duterte does not alter earlier findings that he remains a flight risk.
“The independent medical expertise does not affect the prior judicial determination that Mr. Duterte continues to pose a significant flight risk,” they said.
According to the CLRV, Duterte remains capable of absconding, interfering with the investigation and proceedings, and relying on a network of supporters and resources to achieve them.
The CLRV said drug war victims and their families continue to fear “threats, retaliation, and stigmatization in the communities due to Mr. Duterte’s continuing influence.”
The filing comes as Trial Chamber III reviews Duterte’s continued detention, while a ruling on his fitness to stand trial remains pending.
The prosecution has likewise asked the Chamber to maintain his detention, while the defense has questioned the medical experts’ findings and sought further examinations. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Two sailors missing after tanker attacked in Strait of Hormuz, Oman says
articles.summary: Iran says El Gaia caught fire after hitting mines, but the US says the oil tanker was struck by a missile and then a drone.

blocks.text: Two sailors are missing and 23 others have been rescued following an attack on an oil tanker in the Strait of Hormuz, Oman says.

Oman's Maritime Security Centre said the Panama-flagged El Gaia was being towed to an Omani port on Tuesday after a fire broke out in its engine room, adding that the vessel was targeted 1.3 nautical miles (2.4km) north of the Musandam peninsula.
On Monday, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said the tanker hit naval mines and caught fire while passing through what they described as a restricted and unsafe route.
But the US military insisted the Iranian report was false. It said the tanker was struck by an Iranian missile last month and again by a drone over the weekend.

The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre, meanwhile, said it had received a report of a fire breaking out on board a vessel that was struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz in the early hours of Sunday.
Earlier this month, Iran made a similar claim about an incident that killed two Filipino sailors on a Saudi-owned oil supertanker in the crucial waterway.

The Revolutionary Guards said the vessel, Sidr, caught fire after hitting a naval mine. But Saudi authorities said it was targeted by Iran and maritime security firms reported that it was hit by projectiles north of Musandam.

The International Maritime Organization says at least 22 seafarers have been killed in 79 confirmed incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and the rest of the Middle East since the start of the US and Israel's war with Iran at the end of February.

The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, has effectively been closed due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after the Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

Iran has insisted it will not give up some measure of control over the waterway and has targeted vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.

articles.title: Colombian ex-foreign minister charged over nanny's lie detector test
articles.summary: Laura Sarabia is accused of ordering police to interrogate her nanny after cash allegedly went missing from her flat.

blocks.text: Prosecutors in Colombia have accused former foreign minister Laura Sarabia of abusing her power after she made her nanny take a lie detector test.

The scandal erupted in 2023, when Colombian news weekly Semana reported that a woman Sarabia had employed to look after her son had been hooked up to a polygraph and questioned over the alleged disappearance of a case full of cash from Sarabia's flat.

Sarabia, who was the chief of staff for President Gustavo Petro at the time, resigned in June 2023 but was later appointed as foreign minister and, following her resignation from that post, as Colombia's ambassador to the United Kingdom.
She has denied any wrongdoing.
The 32-year-old was one of the closest advisers of Gustavo Petro, Colombia's first left-wing president, who governed from 2022 to August this year.

Prosecutors said Sarabia abused her position as his chief of staff by ordering police to question her nanny, Marelbys Meza, over the alleged disappearance of the cash, which was said to amount to several thousands of dollars.
Meza told Semana that she was taken by Sarabia's driver to an official building opposite the presidential palace, saying it felt like "a kidnapping".
Police officers then attached her to a polygraph machine and questioned her about the alleged disappearance of the money.
Meza denied having stolen any money during the test, and has consistently denied any wrongdoing in media interviews since.
Prosecutors allege that in ordering police to question Meza, Sarabia improperly used state resources to investigate a matter which was not related to her official post.
Sarabia rejected the accusation during a hearing, without going into further details.
She had earlier said in a social media post that her lawyers were dealing with the issue and that she respected the judicial authorities and trusted their decisions.

articles.title: US allies in Asia alarmed as think tank calls for pullback
articles.summary: Analysts warn that a US withdrawal from the western Pacific, as recently suggested by a think tank, would weaken deterrence and strengthen China's position.

image.caption: The report calls for shifting US forces from the 'vulnerable' first island chain in the Pacific to the 'more defensible' second island chainImage: Daniel Ceng/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: A study by a US foreign policy think tank advocates a major military pullback from the western Pacific, prompting concern among long-standing allies of the United States across the Indo-Pacific, analysts say.

The report was authored by Jennifer Kavanagh, a senior fellow and director of military analysis at the right-of-center Defense Priorities Foundation. Kavanagh calls for the US to "narrow its defense commitments in the region" by ending mutual defense alliances with South Korea, Japan, Australia and the Philippines.

The priority for Washington, she states, is to defend the US homeland and safeguard access to key economic markets and trade routes. That would be best served by pulling back from the "first island chain," which runs from Okinawa in southern Japan, through Taiwan and on to the Philippines.

Kavanagh writes that US forces should be pared back and moved to the "second island chain," which runs from eastern Japan to the Northern Marianas Islands in the central Pacific, Guam, Palau and on to Papua New Guinea.
The report states that moving the troops back would make their positions easier to defend and "reduce the risk of a catastrophic war with China."
Taiwan in the crosshairs
Such a withdrawal would arguably be most keenly felt in Taiwan, which Beijing views as a renegade province that must one day be assimilated into greater China.

In her report, Kavanagh notes that the US has no formal commitment to come to the assistance of Taiwan in the event of an attack by China. She warns that any armed clash "would come at an exorbitant cost for the United States, far in excess of any benefits."

"With a cost-benefit calculation this lopsided, a change in the US commitment to Taiwan seems wise," she said. "The United States should shift from strategic ambiguity to a clear non-intervention policy in the event of any military confrontation over Taiwan."
As China threat looms, US pausing arms sales to Taiwan

The countries named in the report have made no formal comments on the think tank's proposals, but its conclusions "will be viewed with shock," William Yang, a Taiwan-based security analyst for the International Crisis Group, told DW.

The concern will be even deeper given that the Defense Priorities Foundation is known for its isolationist foreign and defense policy positions and is reputed to have ties with a number of senior and like-minded decision-makers in the White House, Yang said.
Pullout 'seems to be very accommodating to China'

Yang noted that US President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened to withdraw troops from allied nations in Europe and Asia if his demands for larger payments or concessions in some other area of the bilateral relationship were not met, Yang said.
"This is a venture into a fully restrained agenda and seems to be very accommodating to China," Yang said.

Though there is no indication that the White House is about to adopt the foundation's proposals, Yang said, they do mesh with many of the administration's isolationist and transactional principles. And, if the plans were to find favor with Trump, he said, the consequences would be "earthquake-level."
The Defense Priorities report was published amid broader regional concerns about the durability of US security commitments in Asia, specifically tensions over Taiwan and the South China Sea.

Despite Kavanagh's reassurances, many analysts suggest that a withdrawal of US support in the region would prompt China to quickly seize Taiwan and nuclear-armed North Korea to make greater demands on South Korea. It is also likely to trigger a region-wide spike in defense spending and, ultimately, a rupture in regional nuclear non-proliferation efforts.
Report plays down China fears

Kavanagh's report plays down those fears, concluding that "China's path to regional hegemony would be a difficult one, threats to the US homeland emanating from Asia are few, and challenges to US economic interests are unlikely and to some extent self-deterring."
Why are China and the US so fixated on Taiwan?

Garren Mulloy, a professor of international relations at Daito Bunka University and a specialist in military issues, described the study as "one of the more cogent and informed versions of what Trump and those around him have been arguing inconsistently for years: The idea is that the US has a priority to defend the homeland and all costs incurred in other missions are a waste."

"In my view, this is seeing the cost of everything and the value of nothing," Mulloy said. He pointed out a number of "obvious problems": notably that the United States would leave a void that China and, to a lesser extent, Russia would step in to fill, and the US would have no influence on the region's geopolitics — including "the shaping of norms, standards and laws."

"Is this worth saving money for that Trump would give away in a tax cut or election bribe?" Mulloy asked, in reference to the president's promise of $5,000 (€4,300) for every US adult if his party wins midterm congressional elections in November.
"This is the ultimate short-term vision that haunts diplomats around the world," Mulloy said.
Dan Pinkston, a professor of international relations at the Seoul campus of Troy University, echoes those concerns, describing the plan as "flawed and unrealistic."

"The whole premise of the report is completely different to how collective and cooperative international security has been practiced for decades," Pinkston said. "These people have a very different worldview, and you wonder if they won't stop at the second island chain and go all the way back to the US mainland."
Fears of a stronger China
US isolationists see NATO and America's other allies "purely as a burden and a cost," Pinkston said, which is "too simplistic."

By withdrawing from security alliances in the Indo-Pacific, the US jeopardizes its trade relationships and largely gives up any influence it presently has over "complex issues" that range from combating piracy, breaches of international sanctions, efforts to combat cybercrime and espionage, smuggling, climate change, fisheries, cross-border financial crime, and a host of other critical matters, Pinkston said.

"It's naive to believe that China is going to be benevolent if the US withdraws and will act in anyone else's best interests when it comes to the rule of law, peaceful settlements of territorial disputes or human rights," he said.
More and more US military members don't want to go to war

articles.title: 'Woman, Life, Freedom' spirit lives on as Iran war drags on
articles.summary: The 2022 death of Jina Mahsa Amini in police custody triggered a resistance movement in Iran. Four years later, the Iranian regime endures — but so does the legacy of the "Woman, Life, Freedom"…

image.caption: The protests brought 'fundamental' changes to Iran, an activist told DWImage: Anonymous/Middle East Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: On September 16, 2022, Jina Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman, died away in a Tehran hospital . She had left her home in northwestern Iran to visit the capital and was then confronted by Tehran's morality police, who claimed the she was violating the mandate for women to cover their hair. The police arrested her. Three days later, she was declared dead.

For many Iranians, the brutality of law enforcement officers toward women accused of violating hijab rules was nothing new. And yet, Amini's death triggered an unprecedented outpouring of anger. Protesters all across the country took to the streets under the slogan "Woman, Life, Freedom." They marched for months, but the regime eventually managed to suppress the movement with a violent clampdown.
"From my perspective, the movement 'Woman, Life, Freedom' is the biggest social and cultural change in Iran in decades," the writer, poet and activist Pouran Nazemi told DW.
Iran uprising seen through the eyes of Iranian women
Nazemi's work as a women's rights activist has gotten her arrested several times in recent years. Still, she refuses to be intimidated.

She said the movement had clear goals right from the start: ending the hijab mandate and ending state violence against Iran's population. Though those goals were ultimately not met, the protests did lead many people to recognize their own power within the society.
"The institutions still use physical violence and occasional arrests against us," Nazemi said. "But something fundamental has changed."
Hijab law still under debate

Even now, amid the ongoing war with the United States, parts of the Iranian regime are still focusing on the hijab mandate. Many politicians are supporting a new bill which would introduce significantly stricter punishments for women violating the hijab order in public places.
One lawmaker described the missing head coverings as a "deep wound in the body of society."
Iranian women unveiled: A shift in hijab enforcement?
The proposed law has been in limbo for years and marked by wrangling between various state institutions.
I a virtual parliamentary session on September 6, several lawmakers urged Parliamentary Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf to pass the proposed legislation to the president for signing.
New normal for young Iranians

A 17-year-old female student told DW that she doesn't even think about wearing a hijab in public. Like many other young women, the pupil is posting pictures and videos of herself in colorful skirts and summer clothing on social media. To her, this is the new normal.
"My mother is not wearing a hijab either," the student said. "She is still a bit afraid and always carries a scarf so she can cover up in an emergency."

Even this degree of freedom would be hard to imagine just a few years ago. It was only after the 2022 protests that many woman started openly defying the government regulations and deciding for themselves if they wanted to cover up.
Decades of female resistance

Iranian women's resistance to the regime did not start with the "Woman, Life, Freedom" protests. An important phase in the long history of dissidenceplayed out 20 years ago, the women's rights activist and writer Mansoureh Shojaee told DW.

Along with other Iranian activists and feminists, Shojaee started the "One Million Signatures" campaign in 2006. The goal was for a million people to sign a petition to change laws that discriminate against women. This campaign became an important role model for feminist activism and societal mobilization in Iran.

Activists went into the streets — and to universities, neighborhoods and private homes. They talked to people about divorce, custody, inheritance, court testimony, and polygamy. They also set up workshops, study groups and other cultural and media events.
Nobel Prize winners among activists facing repression

From the very beginning, the initiative was met with massive state repression. Activists were summoned by the police, arrested and dragged through courts. In the years that followed, authorities raided and shut down a rights NGO run by Shirin Ebadi, a lawyer and advocate for women and children who in 2003 became the first Iranian to win the Nobel Peace Prize. Ebadi's deputy at the Defenders of Human Rights Center, Narges Mohammadi — the winner of the 2023 Nobel Peace Prize — was arrested multiple times over the years. The women's rights activist and journalist Mansoureh Shojaee fled the country in 2011, as have many dissidents over the years.
Fleeing Iran for freedom
Shojaee now lives in the Netherlands.

The activists never met their goal of reaching 1 million signatures. Still, they managed to change the conversation about the legal and social position of women. For this reason, Shojaee does not see the "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement as a full-on break with the past, but only as one of the chapters in the much longer story of Iran's resistance.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Bangladesh court sentences 7 Hasina allies to death
articles.summary: The latest verdict brings to 22 the number of death sentences handed down in cases stemming from the 2024 uprising that ended Sheikh Hasina's 15-year rule.

image.caption: The International Crimes Tribunal sentenced seven senior figures to death over the deadly crackdown on the 2024 uprising (FILE: 17/11/2025)Image: Mamunur Rashid/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: A court in Bangladesh on Tuesday sentenced seven senior figures from ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina's former ruling party to death in absentia over their role in the deadly crackdown on anti-government protests in 2024.
The seven former officials and Awami League leaders were convicted of crimes against humanity, including inciting and ordering killings during the uprising that ultimately forced Hasina from power.
The United Nations estimates that as many as 1,400 people, most of them civilians, were killed during the unrest in July and August 2024.
Who was sentenced to death?
Those convicted include former Awami League Secretary-General Obaidul Quader and former Information Minister Mohammad Ali Arafat.
The other five all held positions within the Awami League.
All seven remain at large.
Prosecutor Mohammad Aminul Islam welcomed the verdict, saying most of the charges had been proven beyond reasonable doubt.
The court also ordered the seizure of half of the defendants' assets to provide compensation to the families of people killed or injured during the protests.
A court-appointed defense lawyer, M Hasan Imam, argued that the men had not been directly involved in the killings and should have received less severe sentences.
What happened during the 2024 uprising?
The protests began as a student-led movement and developed into a nationwide revolt against Hasina's government.
Hasina fled Bangladesh by helicopter for neighboring India on August 5, 2024, ending more than 15 years in power.
Bangladesh lacks women in politics
She was herself convicted of crimes against humanity in November 2025 and sentenced to death in absentia for her role in the crackdown.
Hasina and the Awami League have rejected the proceedings against them as politically biased.
How many people have now been convicted?

Tuesday's verdict brings the number of people convicted in trials connected with the 2024 uprising to 68, according to the AFP news agency. Twenty-two have received death sentences, while only four of those convicted are in custody.
Bangladesh's government, led by Tarique Rahman following elections in February, has requested Hasina's extradition from India.
The 78-year-old former prime minister remains in exile there and has said she intends to return to Bangladesh in December.
