articles.title: UN rights chief says uncovered remains in Gaza raise concerns of war crimes
articles.summary: The recovery of hundreds of bodies from the rubble of buildings destroyed by Israeli strikes in Gaza during the war that began nearly three years ago has raised fresh concerns about possible war…

image.caption: Palestinians attend a mass funeral in Gaza City on Sept. 6 for those who were killed in a 2023 Israeli strike and whose remains were recently recovered from beneath the rubble, according to Gaza’s Civil Defence. (Dawoud Abu Alkas/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·Updated

The recovery of hundreds of bodies from the rubble of buildings destroyed by Israeli strikes in Gaza during the war that began nearly three years ago has raised fresh concerns about possible war crimes, the United Nations human rights chief said Tuesday.
Volker Türk calls for full access in Gaza for international investigators to help preserve evidence
Volker Türk said the remains of what appeared to be entire families were being unearthed from sites destroyed during Israeli attacks, adding that many victims were women and children.
"It is heartbreaking that the loved ones of those missing for so long are only now having their worst fears confirmed," he said in a statement.

He said the discoveries revived concerns raised in a 2024 UN report that found Israeli strikes on residential buildings and other civilian sites during the early weeks of the war may have violated international humanitarian law.

The Israeli Prime Minister's Office and Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Israel has repeatedly rejected allegations that it deliberately targets civilians and says it acted in accordance with international law while fighting Hamas militants in Gaza.

Israel's assault on Gaza — launched after Hamas's deadly raid into Israel in October 2023 — has generated around 61 million tons of wreckage and debris that could take seven years to clear, according to the United ​Nations.
These families waited three years to bury loved ones in Gaza
A U.S.-brokered ceasefire brought an end to full-scale fighting in October 2025, but has failed to halt regular Israeli strikes, as both sides accuse each other of violating the truce.
The Palestinian Civil Defence says more than 630 bodies and human remains have been recovered from beneath destroyed buildings across Gaza since November 2025.
Palestinian authorities estimate more than 8,000 people remain buried in the ​wreckage.

Türk said he feared the remains recovered so far could be "only the tip of the iceberg," noting that large parts of Gaza had been flattened by Israeli bombing or later demolition and clearance operations.
He also accused Israel of continuing to level some areas of Gaza where its forces remain deployed, saying bulldozers were operating "with no respect for the dead under the rubble."
Israeli restrictions impeding recovery efforts

Ajith Sunghay, head of the UN human rights office for the Occupied Palestinian Territory, said that Israeli restrictions on items like DNA kits and excavators were impeding recovery and identification efforts.
"The collective impact of Israel's conduct is making any systematic, large-scale search, recovery, and identification work nearly impossible," he told a Geneva news briefing on Tuesday.
Sometimes, Palestinian teams were having to dig through rubble with their bare hands, he added.

Israeli authorities did not immediately respond to the UN allegations on supply restrictions. Israel's COGAT military agency, which controls access to Gaza, has previously justified long-held restrictions on items it said could be used for a "terrorist buildup."
The 2023 Hamas-led attacks killed 1,200 people in Israel while another 251 were taken hostage, according to Israeli tallies.
More than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israel's military campaign, ​according to Gaza health authorities.

items: Israeli strike kills 2 people in Gaza, medics say
Israeli clearance of Gaza rubble could destroy evidence of 'atrocity crimes,' says UN expert

blocks.text: Israel says it has gone to great lengths to avoid civilian ​casualties and ⁠that Hamas uses Gaza's civilians as human shields in densely populated areas — an accusation Hamas denies.
The UN rights chief called for international investigators to be granted access to all parts of Gaza to help preserve evidence, citing ongoing legal proceedings examining conduct during the war.
Israel has blocked the entry of heavy machinery needed to remove rubble, according to Türk's statement.
Francesca Albanese, the UN expert on the Palestinian territories, has said evidence should be gathered and human remains identified ​before full clearance starts.
This month, the Palestinian Civil Defence said 96 bodies and human remains had been recovered from a single site in the Zeitoun area of Gaza City, including 58 children and 23 women.

articles.title: Remembering Eggie Apostol, purveyor of truth, independence
articles.summary: 'Eugenia Apostol’s passing marks the end of an era, but her legacy endures in every journalist who continues to defend truth, independence, and the people’s right to know,' the UP College of Mass…

blocks.text: REST IN PEACE. Eugenia Apostol was a pioneering journalist and press freedom advocate who founded the Philippine Daily Inquirer.
Ramon Magsaysay Foundation

'Eugenia Apostol’s passing marks the end of an era, but her legacy endures in every journalist who continues to defend truth, independence, and the people’s right to know,' the UP College of Mass Communication writes

items: Eugenia 'Eggie' Apostol, a prominent Filipino journalist and founder of the Philippine Daily Inquirer, passed away at the age of 100, leaving a legacy of truth and fearless journalism.
Apostol was known for her strong advocacy for press freedom and her role in the 'mosquito press' during the Marcos dictatorship, which aimed to expose government corruption and uphold democracy.

Her contributions to journalism were recognized with numerous awards, including the Gawad Plaridel and the Ramon Magsaysay Award, and she is remembered by peers for her unwavering commitment to independent reporting.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – As the Filipino journalism community mourns the passing of Eugenia “Eggie” Apostol, the late veteran’s peers are choosing to remember her for her fierce stance on truth and the freedom to do powerful reportage.

Apostol, a renowned publisher and veteran journalist, founded the Philippine Daily Inquirer in 1985, just a few months shy of the 1986 People Power Revolution. She was well-known in the world of the “mosquito press” — newspapers and media outlets that were vocal about their criticism toward Ferdinand E. Marcos and his dictatorship.

According to Marixi Prieto, the former chair of the Philippine Daily Inquirer’s board of directors, Apostol had always been known to stand up for reporters, editors, and their work when it came to doing hard-hitting reportage. “Those moments captured so much of who she was — strong, principled, courageous, and unwavering in what she believed was right.”

“Eggie was a woman of extraordinary strength and courage, someone I had the privilege of knowing. She built the Inquirer on a foundation of truth and independence and fiercely protected those values through the years,” Prieto said in her statement.

Apostol, who died at 100, was the first-ever awardee of the Gawad Plaridel, the highest honor the University of the Philippines confers to media practitioners who strive to make a difference in their line of work and contribute to shaping the Philippine media landscape.

“Eugenia Apostol’s passing marks the end of an era, but her legacy endures in every journalist who continues to defend truth, independence, and the people’s right to know. She is survived by her family, colleagues, and generations of media practitioners who carry forward her vision of fearless journalism,” the UP College of Mass Communication said in its statement.
She was the publisher of Mr. & Ms. Special Edition, a weekly tabloid that would carry reports against the Marcos administration.

“MR. & MS. became our Facebook or our social media when it was not there yet, so the Filipino people will know the TRUTH about our country and more about our aspirations for our people and our country,” wrote the August Twenty-One Movement, a civil rights group established after the assassination of former president Benigno “Ninoy” Aquino Jr.
In 1999, Apostol would then go on to establish Pinoy Times, another tabloid that would publish exposés about then-president Joseph “Erap” Estrada’s administration.

“I join the many mourning the passing of Eggy Apostol who came into the lives of people like me through Mr. & Ms. And then the Inquirer. She very kindly asked me to join her venture, the Pinoy Times where I wrote a column in Filipino. When the country needed fighting journalism, she was there,” historian and veteran writer Manolo Quezon shared.
Historian Xiao Chua, meanwhile, lauded Apostol for her work at Mr. & Ms. Special Edition, PDI, and the Pinoy Times Special Edition, and her overall dedication to press freedom and democracy.

“Nagpakita ng tapang at malayang pamamahayag bilang saligan ng kapayapaan at demokrasya. Paalam po (She showed that courage and freedom of the press are the foundation of peace and democracy. Farewell),” Chua said about Apostol in a Facebook tribute.
Hailing from Sorsogon, Apostol received the Ramon Magsaysay Award for Journalism, Literature and Creative Communication Arts in 2006.

In 1948, she completed her journalism degree at the University of Santo Tomas, where she graduated magna cum laude. She was also the editor of the women’s sections of The Manila Times and The Manila Chronicle. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Leading legal experts say sanctions on Israel ‘fall far short’ of UK obligations
articles.summary:
More than 130 counsels and KCs sign letter to PM saying international law requires further measures to stop illegal settlements

More than 130 legal experts, including 18 king’s counsel…

blocks.text: More than 130 legal experts, including 18 king’s counsel (KCs), have written to Andy Burnham saying that sanctions on Israeli settlements “fall far short” of Britain’s obligations under the international court of justice’s (ICJ’s) finding that the occupation is unlawful.

The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband last week announced an import ban on goods from illegal Israeli settlements in Palestine and other measures. Signatories to the letter to the prime minister, including the leading lawyers Michael Mansfield KC and Imran Khan KC, and the former lord justice of appeal Alan Moses, say it is not enough.

In a 2024 advisory opinion, the ICJ, which is the UN’s top court, ordered Israel to end the occupation “as rapidly as possible” and said other countries were under an obligation not to recognise the occupation as lawful nor aid or assist it.

The letter, sent on Tuesday, says the ICJ’s findings have “not had an impact on Israel’s apartheid practice” and, while the UK sanctions are “a necessary corrective”, they are “improperly narrow” when compared with sanctions on Russia, which are not limited to economic activity in occupied Ukrainian territory but apply to wider economic structures supporting the unlawful conduct.

It says: “We ask it to commit to further and more rigorous measures to ensure that no part of the UK’s economic relationship with Israel continues to sustain the illegal occupation itself, and the settlements and other serious violations of fundamental rules of international law perpetrated through its conduct, and to build on this to adopt robust coercive measures to seek to bring all these serious violations of international law, and the practices they sustain, including, fundamentally, the occupation itself, to an end.

The letter, also signed by legal academics, calls for a range of additional measures including a full arms embargo on Israel. When announcing the sanctions, Miliband accused Israel of ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, and the signatories say article 6(3) of the arms trade treaty prohibits transfers of arms where a state has knowledge of such a crime.

The sanctions were announced after escalating attacks by Israeli settlers against Palestinian villages in the West Bank and an Israeli tender was issued for 1,200 homes in the E1 settlement, east of Jerusalem, which could in effect cut off the north from the south of the West Bank, threatening the viability of any future Palestinian state.

The signatories want extension of the sanctions to cover insurance, accountancy services and digital infrastructure as well as public confirmation that no UK public body, pension scheme or sovereign fund holds settlement investments.

One of the letter’s signatories and drafters, Ralph Wilde, a professor of international law at University College London, welcomed the UK’s recent recognition of Israel’s occupation of the West Bank as unlawful as an “important shift”, but said it fell short in its focus on the settlements and settlers.

“The elephant in the room is the illegality of the occupation itself,” said Wilde, who acted as senior counsel and legal adviser to the Arab League in the case before the ICJ. “It’s not just simply the settlements and the abuse of treatment and the genocide, which of course are also wrong, it’s Israel’s very presence.”

He added: “There’s a mismatch between saying Israel’s very presence there is illegal, but then only focusing on the question of the settlers and the settlements. If the problem is with the settlements themselves, then the problem is with the state that establishes them.”

A government spokesperson said: “This is the biggest reset in the UK’s approach to protecting and securing the two-state solution in a generation. We have shown our commitment to international law and our refusal to be bystanders to further suffering.
“We have taken concrete action, supported accountability, pledged to galvanise the international community and acted with our partners across the globe.”
In response to the sanctions, the Israeli foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, accused Miliband of “outrageous lies” and said the UK government was “systematically working against the state of Israel”.

articles.title: Socialist Left leads far-right AfD ahead of Berlin vote
articles.summary: The results of the Berlin election are as hard to predict as ever. Three parties are vying for first place, including the socialist Left Party and the far-right AfD. But one issue is most important…

image.caption: The Berlin election race is now increasingly between the socialist Left and the conservative CDUImage: dts Nachrichtenagentur/IMAGO

blocks.text: Berlin, a city-state of 3.9 million people, is famously diverse, but it's also very atomized — a city of villages, where people often don't stray beyond their district, or Kiez, as Berliners like to call them.

That atomization extends to its political landscape: While the central districts of Berlin have recently voted Green or for the socialist Left Party, the outskirts — where in fact most Berliners live — is dominated by the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), and, in certain districts, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD). That makes it notoriously difficult to predict Berlin's elections, particularly in the past few years, when more parties have crowded onto the city's lampposts at election time.

Ahead of Berlin's state election on September 20 (when Berliners will elect the state parliament, which decides who is the next mayor) three parties are neck and neck: The Left Party, the CDU and the AfD. In the latest infratest dimap poll, the Left Party has a slim lead: They're at 21%, with the CDU at 20% and the AfD at 18%. Not far behind are the Greens, with 16%, while the center-left Social Democrats, for so long a party of government in Berlin, is currently mustering just 12%.

The AfD's relative weakness in Berlin means the situation is not as dramatic as it was in Saxony-Anhalt on September 6, where the scale of the far-right victory likely means it will be impossible to keep them out of government.

Nevertheless, a victory for the Left Party — and yet another defeat for Friedrich Merz's CDU — would both transform the politics of Berlin, where the CDU are currently in government, and increase the pressure on the chancellor.
How to fight for election victory in a polarized city
The capital's disparate political scene makes running an election campaign in Berlin tricky, especially for a conservative party like the CDU.
"Berlin is indeed particularly challenging," Lukas Krieger, the CDU's general secretary in Berlin, told DW.

Krieger is in a perfect position to understand the national implications of regional elections, as he is also a member of the federal parliament, where the CDU is still digesting the result in Saxony-Anhalt.
But, he insists, "Berlin isn't comparable to the country as a whole or to Saxony-Anhalt."
Dressed in a neat suit and about to enter a post-mortem meeting of CDU parliamentarians, Krieger remained bullish about the fight in Berlin, and said it was clear who the main opponent was.

"It's crystallizing more and more as a duel between the CDU and the Left Party," he said. "The AfD in Berlin has no option to negotiate a government. There's no one who wants to work with them. We have a very radical Left Party in Berlin, and that's why we say: Berlin will stay stable, and the CDU is the only party that guarantees that Berlin will stay in the middle of the political spectrum."

Another challenge for the Berlin CDU is dealing with the loss of their incumbent mayor, Kai Wegner, who is still in office but is not running again thanks to his decision to play tennis in the middle of Berlin's biggest power outage since World War II.

blocks.caption: Lukas Krieger says Berliners must vote for the CDU if they want to avoid the socialist Left, but his party also has to face the far-right AfDImage: Ben Knight/DW

blocks.text: Instead, the party was forced to hastily present a new candidate, Wegner's Finance Minister Stefan Evers, who now has to navigate a course between two very different political threats: The super-confident AfD and the surging Left Party, both of whom look set to make significant gains on their 2023 election results in the city.

Evers' main opponent is another new face: Elif Eralp, a lawyer born in Munich in 1980 just weeks after her parents fled a military putsch in Turkey. But Berliners are used to mayoral candidates not being natives of the city: Evers was born in North Rhine-Westphalia. In fact, polls show that none of the leading mayoral candidates are particularly well-known: In one recent poll, around half of Berliners said they didn't have any strong opinion on any of them.
Tiny rooms at sky-high prices — Berlin's rental rip-off
Be credible and make offers

The CDU's problem is that German politics is increasingly radical — as the Saxony-Anhalt election showed — and observers say this is partly because of the perceived failure of the centrist parties of government to present new solutions to the electorate.
"The question is: Do you have your own political offers? Are you trying to unlock new groups?" said Julia Reuschenbach, political scientist at Hamburg University.

She thinks that the Left Party has established itself in Berlin as the most "credible" opposition to the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD). That's partly, she says, because it's the only one of the left-of-center parties not willing to support the CDU (nor is the CDU willing to collaborate with the Left).

But the Left Party has its own disadvantage: The party has been pursued by accusations of antisemitism after a rapper performing at a campaign event in Neukölln, where many of Berlin's large Palestinian community live, chanted "Death to the IDF," referring to the Israeli military. Eralp condemned the performance and promised an internal investigation, but Gaza has become vital to the Left Party's supporters: In June, the party officially resolved to consider Israel's military action in Gaza a genocide.
Nevertheless, Reuschenbach thinks the Left Party's strength is that it is able to make tangible political offers.

"Of course, they're populist," she said. "They formulate maximalist positions: 'We want to socialize. we want to expropriate.' But it's straight. I'd say that for many people, the Left have more clarity, more of their own proposals."

The pundit was referring specifically to what many consider the Left's most radical demand, an idea that has been at the heart of Berlin's politics for at least half a decade: The Left Party is the only one of the major parties that promises to implement the result of a referendum carried out in 2021, when 59% of Berliners voted to expropriate real estate companies that own more than 3,000 units in the city and transfer their property to public ownership.

Since then, successive Berlin governments, led by center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) and then the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), have dragged their feet on the implementation, by setting up commissions on the question.

blocks.caption: Kerstin Wolter says one issue dominates Berlin: rentsImage: Ben Knight/DW

blocks.text: It's the rents, stupid

Kerstin Wolter, co-leader of the socialist Left Party in Berlin and candidate in the upcoming state election, rejects the idea that expropriating landlords should be considered "populist." After all, she said, the idea was written into the German constitution, or Basic Law, at the founding of West Germany in 1949 — though the expropriation article has never actually been invoked.
As far as Wolter is concerned, there's one reason why the Berlin population became so "radicalized," and made her party so strong.

"All the polls, all the surveys, all the conversations we have with voters ourselves, it's always the same: The rent situation is catastrophic," she told DW. "People can't find an apartment, people are scared of rent increases, people are losing their apartments because the landlords are claiming them for their own use."

Housing, according to a recent Berlin Trend poll, is indeed by far the most important issue in this election: Some 32% of Berliners said it was the city's most important problem — way more than the 10% who said immigration and asylum, or the 9% who said security/crime/terrorism.

Perhaps adding to this taste for revolutionary ideas is that this is the first election in Berlin's history where the voting age has been lowered to 16, and young Germans have become increasingly politicized in the last few years.

"I think a lot of young people — much more than when I was young — are concerned with questions like climate change, will I still get a job," said Wolter. "Even pensions: At an info-stand I had a girl, she seemed about 14, asking me about our pensions policy."

Berlin, which has always been its own mix of conservatism and radicalism, is now also becoming more and more economically diverse, according to Wolter: "We have an increasing number of millionaires in Berlin, as well as an increasing number of people living in poverty."
That contributes to making the city a unique political challenge.
Edited by Rina Goldenberg

articles.title: Several U.S. military bases, diplomatic buildings have been damaged in Iran war: inspector general report
articles.summary: A U.S. government watchdog has released its first report on the impact of the Iran war, acknowledging the military's advanced weapons shortfalls and offering the first public look at the damage to…

image.caption: A U.S. Air Force KC-135 Stratotanker aircraft refuels a U.S. Air Force F-35A Lightning II aircraft during an Operation Epic Fury attack on Iran, at an undisclosed location on April 5. Seven KC-135 refuelling aircraft have been damaged or destroyed since Feb. 28, a report from the Pentagon inspector

blocks.text: World·New

A U.S. government watchdog has released its first report on the impact of the Iran war, acknowledging the military's advanced weapons shortfalls and offering the first public look at the damage to American aircraft, bases and diplomatic outposts in the Middle East.
Operation Epic Fury estimated to have cost $33.4B US over first 4 months

The Pentagon inspector general's report on Monday offered the fullest official accounting so far of the conflict's costs in American lives, taxpayer dollars and physical damage as a result of Operation Epic Fury, which was estimated to have cost $33.4 billion US as of June 29. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth testified in Congress in late July that the war had cost $37.5 billion so far.

The report noted that the U.S. war with Iran "has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply" in regard to advanced weapons. Experts have previously said it will take about three years for military contractors to replenish advanced missiles and defensive missile interceptors to prewar levels.

The Pentagon has repeatedly pushed back against reports of any munitions shortage, saying the U.S. military has all the weapons it needs to fight any conflict. U.S. President Donald Trump said in a social media post Monday that the U.S. is "producing more exquisite and elite weapons than at any time in our history."
Trump says U.S. brimming with weapons, vows to 'hunt down' leakers
Multiple U.S. bases, diplomatic buildings struck

The watchdog report, which covers April 1 to June 30, also acknowledged that Iranian strikes damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and other structures at U.S. bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan.

It noted that the U.S. naval base in Bahrain, a Navy logistics hub in the region, was targeted with Iranian drones and ballistic missiles. U.S. Central Command had to shift to supply lines to alternate hubs that were much farther away, including Diego Garcia, a U.S.-U.K. base on an island in the Indian Ocean.

Hung Cao, the acting U.S. navy secretary, acknowledged in an interview with The Epoch Times last week that "they blew the hell out of Bahrain" and said he has a task force looking into whether the navy would need to repair the base in Bahrain to sustain its forces in the region.
Monday's report also included information from the watchdogs for the Defence and State departments, as well as the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID).

U.S. diplomatic facilities in Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Iraq suffered physical damage from Iran's strikes, costing $184 million US. In addition, the war has resulted in construction project delays at several other U.S. outposts in several countries, including in Israel, Egypt and Oman.

The State Department reported in early June that its other costs from the conflict came to $113 million US, with nearly $80 million used to respond to contingency plans, including evacuation expenses for U.S. personnel and their families, as well as other American citizens and eligible third-country nationals.

items: Who are the Houthis? How they could send oil prices surging even further
Diesel prices soar. Here are the potential impacts

blocks.text: The State Department reported that in the weeks and months after the U.S. and Israel first struck Iran on Feb. 28, the Trump administration evacuated about 9,000 U.S. citizens from countries in the Middle East and Europe. Through private and commercial flights as well as land and water travel, the cost of the department's evacuation operation was more than $11 million US as of late June.

The majority of the evacuations were made from Israel, with Iraq and Jordan following shortly behind. While the U.S. only evacuated 1,200 Americans from the United Arab Emirates, those trips to Istanbul, Athens and Washington cost the most, at more than $4 million US.
Weapons shortfalls, weapons sales

Dozens of American aircraft and drones also were destroyed or damaged by Iran, including the destruction of as many as 30 MQ-9 Reaper drones that cost around $30 million US apiece, the report said. Seven KC-135 refuelling aircraft were damaged or destroyed, including five that were struck by Iranian munitions while on the ground in Saudi Arabia.

Another KC-135 crashed in Iraq, killing six service members, following a collision with another KC-135. Those deaths, and the death of a pilot of a helicopter that crashed into the Arabian Sea, are listed as occurring during non-hostile events. Eleven other service members are listed as "killed in action" in Kuwait, Iraq, Jordan and Saudi Arabia.

items: Is the U.S. military running out of weapons?

blocks.text: The State Department reported that more than $44 billion US in emergency and non-emergency military sales also were made in that span of time, with the majority of sales going to Saudi Arabia. Sales included military helicopters, munitions and munitions support as well as advanced precision weapons systems.

Other regional countries, including Qatar, Kuwait, the U.A.E. and Israel, also received billions in sales, as Iran retaliated against nearly every country in the region that hosted a U.S. military base.

articles.title: Court orders SEC official to testify on records of VP Sara's business interests
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court has issued a modified order for SEC official Gerardo del Rosario to testify before the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

blocks.text: Published September 15, 2026 7:45pm

The Senate impeachment court has issued a modified order for Gerardo del Rosario, Company Registration and Monitoring Department (CRMD) Director of the state-run Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), to testify before the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero reissued the subpoena upon the request of House prosecutor Terry Ridon of Bicol Saro party-list on Tuesday, after Ridon asked for the rescheduling of del Rosario’s testimony to next week, citing voluminous documents involved.

Had del Rosario proceeded to take the witness stand in Tuesday, September 15, he could have only testified for one hour since the previous witness for the prosecution, Office of the Ombudsman official Karen Batu, was only discharged shortly before 2 p.m.
“Attorney Del Rosario will appear [for his testimony] on 21st and 22nd [of September at 10 in the morning,” Escudero said.

During the House justice panel deliberations on the impeachment complaints against the Vice President, Gerardo said that Vice President Sara Duterte was listed as a stockholder and member of the board of directors of a Davao-based private company from 2022 to 2025 while she is already the Vice President.

Citing the General Information Sheet (GIS) of Metro City Chow Foods Corp., del Rosario said then that the name “Sara Z. Duterte” appeared as a stockholder holding 500 shares and as a member of the board of directors during the period.
Del Rosario will serve as a witness for Article 2 of the impeachment case which accuses the Vice President of accumulating unexplained wealth through the following:

items: failure to fully and truthfully disclose all her and her spouse's assets, liabilities, and net worth in her statement of assets, liabilities, and net worth (SALN) including in her SALN for the years 2022, 2023, and 2024; and
failure to divest, and instead, willfully continued, all her business interests during her tenure as vice president for the years 2022, 2023, 2024, and 2025.

blocks.text: Article 7, Section 13 of the 1987 Constitution states that the President, Vice President, Cabinet members, and their deputies or assistants “shall not hold any other office or employment during their tenure, unless otherwise provided in the Constitution.”

It also prohibits them from practicing any profession, participating in any business, or having a financial interest in contracts, franchises, or special privileges granted by the government or its subdivisions, agencies, or instrumentalities, including government-owned or controlled corporations and their subsidiaries. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Reporting a two-hour firefight behind a concrete wall
articles.summary: Maguindanao del Sur, a province mired in decades-old armed conflicts, was ominously peaceful the whole morning of Monday, September 14, 2026, a historic day in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in…

blocks.text: Maguindanao del Sur, a province mired in decades-old armed conflicts, was ominously peaceful the whole morning of Monday, September 14, 2026, a historic day in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao with voters casting their ballots for the first-ever parliamentary elections.
My team and I moved from one town to the next in search of stories. Everything seemed in order, a pleasant surprise for voters and even for the media covering the historic event.
“Sana ganito lagi sa mga susunod na eleksyon (Hopefully, succeeding elections will be like this),” a village chief, who had just voted, told us.

But the momentary peace was quickly shattered. We were at a voting place in the town of Shariff Aguak when we got wind of reports of an ongoing firefight in Shariff Saydona Mustapha, a town more than 20 kilometers from our location.

blocks.caption: Two armored personnel carriers and Special Action Force troopers stand guard several meters from a polling center in Shariff Saydona Mustaphaa

blocks.text: Two armored personnel carriers and Special Action Force troopers stand guard several meters from a polling center in Shariff Saydona Mustapha.
We boarded our vehicle, and rushed to the town, stopping in front of a polling center where the sound of sporadic gunfire could be heard from a distance.
“Around 700 meters ang labanan, sir (The firefight is about 700 meters),” a police intelligence officer whispered to me.
According to initial reports, armed supporters of two contending political parties gunning for parliamentary seats were locked in a fierce gunbattle for reasons still unknown.

blocks.caption: Cops launch a drone to check the gunbattle between two armed groups supporting rival political parties taking part in the BARMM parliamentary elections.

blocks.text: Cops launch a drone to check the gunbattle between two armed groups supporting rival political parties taking part in the BARMM parliamentary elections.
10 arrested
As the sound of gunshots continued to fill the air, a tense moment ensued when a speeding tricycle passed by, refusing to stop as ordered by cops manning the street.
But the driver and the passengers were eventually surrounded by the security forces with their guns in shooting position.
“Dapa, dapa (face down, face down),” the cops shouted.

blocks.caption: With guns drawn, police officers command the suspects to remain on the ground following their arrest.

blocks.text: With guns drawn, police officers command the suspects to remain on the ground following their arrest.
Among the items found in their possession was a small sack filled with spent bullet casings, raising suspicion that they could be involved in the ongoing firefight.
“Bakit may mga basyo kayo ng bala (Why do you have spent shells),” a cop asked.

blocks.caption: Cops stop at gunpoint a speeding mini van loaded with passengers along the main road of the town of Shariff Saydona Mustapha.

blocks.text: Cops stop at gunpoint a speeding mini van loaded with passengers along the main road of the town of Shariff Saydona Mustapha.

Just seconds later, a mini van loaded with passengers also ignored the cops who had flagged them down. The police personnel blocked their path, and with guns pointed at them, the driver and the passengers were ordered to get out of the vehicle and drop to the ground.
Upon inspection, cops saw a pistol inside the bag of one of the passengers.
A total of 10 individuals were apprehended and immediately brought to the police station for investigation and possible filing of charges.
Combat zone
After the tense arrest, the security forces began to move toward the direction of the conflict area.
We were at the tailend of the convoy, and as we traveled closer and closer to the combat zone, the gunshots sounded louder, the volume of fire getting heavier.

Then the convoy came to a halt along the highway, some of the vehicles backed up and entered the municipal compound of Shariff Saydona Mustapha, while we remained parked on the roadside. Only then we realized that the fighting between the two warring groups was just a couple of hundred meters away.
“Tara na (Let's go),” I told my team.

blocks.caption: Behind a concrete wall, GMA News senior reporter Jun Veneracion filming a recorded (not live) blow-by-blow selfie report of the early part of the firefight between government troops and armed groups in Maguindanao del Sur.

blocks.text: Behind a concrete wall, GMA News senior reporter Jun Veneracion filming a recorded (not live) blow-by-blow selfie report of the early part of the firefight between government troops and armed groups in Maguindanao del Sur.
In a low-crouch position, we ran for cover, and found a relatively safe place behind a concrete wall inside the municipal complex.

blocks.caption: PNP officers planning their next move as fighting intensifies.

blocks.text: PNP officers planning their next move as fighting intensifies.

But the situation would turn from bad to worse as the fighting shifted, dragging the police to the fray. The volley of fire from the armed groups were now being aimed at the position of the government forces inside the compound.

Though protected by the solid wall, we were from being safe given the heavy volume of fire the compound was taking. Bullets whizzing and ricocheting, tree branches snapping as the armed groups pressed on with their relentless attack.
“Ginagapang na nila tayo papalapit (They are crawling near to us),” one cop said in a concerned tone.
SAF troopers fight back
Armed with modern fighting equipment, the elite troopers of the Philippine National Police-Special Action Force (PNP-SAF) decided to fight back, taking turns in firing to repel the advancing enemy.

blocks.caption: SAF member fires a machine gun in an effort to thwart the advance of the armed group.

blocks.text: SAF member fires a machine gun in an effort to thwart the advance of the armed group.
Outside the compound, two armored personnel carriers of the SAF unleashed heavy fire from 50-caliber machine guns, each shot reverberated with deafening noise.
While from the top of a building, SAF snipers took aim at their targets, pressing the trigger whenever there’s a clear shot in the crosshair.

blocks.caption: SAF sniper positions himself on the top floor of a building to get a clear view of the surrounding and enemy targets.

blocks.text: SAF sniper positions himself on the top floor of a building to get a clear view of the surrounding and enemy targets.
But the enemy was no pushover. Despite the counter-offensive by government forces, they refused to back down, taking even more pot shots as if they’d never run out of ammunitions.
It was a back-and-forth exchange, with each side standing their ground.

blocks.caption: Cops shoot grenade launchers against as part of their counter-offensive against the enemy.

blocks.text: Cops shoot grenade launchers against as part of their counter-offensive against the enemy.
In the middle of the fighting, a SAF trooper got wounded after being hit by a shrapnel.
“Okay naman siya. Tinamaan ng nag-ricochet na bala (He's okay. He was hit when a bullet ricocheted),” an officer told me.
Newsmen in the middle of a firefight
Caught in the middle of the firefight with nowhere to go, me and my team had no other recourse but to film the encounter as it unfolded.

blocks.caption: GMA News cameraman Joseph Salazar takes cover behind a tree while filming the gunbattle.

blocks.text: GMA News cameraman Joseph Salazar takes cover behind a tree while filming the gunbattle.
Joseph Salazar, who has been my cameraman for many years, documented everything he could while moving from one area to another, at times taking refuge behind tree trunks.
Alfredo Loresto, our assistant cameraman, would sprint to our vehicle to get batteries and other equipment and run back to our coverage position behind the concrete wall.

Amid the chaos, our systems engineer, JC Navarro, managed to set up our satellite internet equipment, enabling us to remain online while covering and reporting about the armed encounter. While the gunbattle was happening, he was transmitting all the gathered video materials to our news base.
Exit move

It was around 4 p.m. when the police provincial director of Maguindanao del Sur, Police Colonel Michael John Mangahis, gathered his men to map out their next plan of action. He asked if there was another gate that could be used for safe exit.
“Meron sa likod, sir (There's another one at the back, sir),” a policeman replied.
Mangahis then ordered his troops to immediately move. “Lahat ng tropa prepare papunta doon (All troops prepare to go there),” he instructed men.

blocks.caption: The police provincial director of Maguindanao del Sur in a huddle with his troops.

blocks.text: The police provincial director of Maguindanao del Sur in a huddle with his troops.

We took it as a cue to extricate ourselves as well. So, we rushed to our respective vehicles and loaded all our things. But a long queue of cars clogged the road leading to the exit gate at the back of the municipal compound.

At 4:10 p.m., vehicles packed with people with their heads down began speeding away from the compound. We joined the convoy and made it to a safe ground two hours after getting trapped in the middle of an intense firefight.

blocks.caption: GMA News personnel safely exit the combat zone in Shariff Saydona Mustapha after two hours inside the municipal compound.

But far more important than the story, is the fact that we all made through…unscathed. — RSJ, GMA News

blocks.text: September 15, 2026
Brandenburg BSW state lawmaker quits the leftist party, becoming the 6th to do so in 10 months

blocks.caption: Oliver Skopec said he wanted to remain a lawmaker, as an independent at firstImage: Marc-Oliver von Riegen/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The left-wing populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) contingent of lawmakers in Brandenburg continues to shrink.
Oliver Skopec announced on Tuesday he was quitting the party, becoming the 6th of what was once 15 BSW parliamentarians to do so since November last year.

The first four left last November. When the former party leader at the state level, Robert Crumbach, quit in January, the state coalition between the BSW and senior partners the Social Democrats lost its majority and fell apart.
Skopec, a 41-year-old businessman said he wanted to retain his place in the state parliament and operate as an independent, at least at first.
He linked his decision to quit with the BSW's character as what he termed a party of protest. "For me personally, that is not enough," he said.
Tensions are high in the party as it wrangles with questions like how, or whether, to deal with the far-right AfD — particularly in Saxony-Anhalt after the recent election.
A senior BSW politician at the federal level, Niels-Olaf Lüders, said it was "regrettable" that Skopec was leaving, "but of course it doesn't topple us either."
The party's chairwoman in Brandenburg, Friederike Benda expressed anything but regret at seeing Skopec go, saying it was "not a loss."
"Separating the chaff from the wheat will help us," Benda said, accusing Skopec of using his seat in parliament "as a comfortable, state-financed pillow" to rest on at the taxpayer's expense.
In another eastern state, Thurinigia, the BSW group of parliamentarians has dissolved itself altogether and set up a rival group at the state level.
In Brandenburg, two of the six defectors left for the more centrist Social Democrats (SPD), and four set up a group they call "We for Brandenburg."
Skopec did not say he planned to join them, but said "we will surely speak to each other."

The BSW surfed a brief wave of popularity fairly soon after its foundation — and enjoyed big state election results in Thuringia and Brandeburg in 2024 as a result. But it has since lost almost all of its momentum and is fighting to survive, in large part because of the relative resurgence of the more traditional socialist Left Party in the run-up to last year's federal elections.

“The Department confirms that subpoenas were served on Sen. Robinhood Padilla and Lt. Col. Jean Alla Yasin Robles at around 2:30 pm today at the Senate, in connection with the pending complaint against them for alleged violation of PD 1829 (Obstruction of Justice),” DOJ spokesperson Raphael Martinez said.
Based on the subpoena, Padilla was directed to appear before state prosecutors on September 25 and October 9 at the DOJ headquarters in Ermita, Manila.
Rappler reached out to Padilla for comment, but he has yet to respond as of this writing. He seemingly alluded to the subpoena in an earlier Facebook post.
“A subpoena has arrived,” his post read.

In May, the DOJ’s National Prosecution Service confirmed that the police had referred an obstruction of justice complaint against Padilla and other individuals for allegedly “facilitating” Dela Rosa’s escape from the Senate.

It can be recalled that Dela Rosa initially went into hiding to evade an International Criminal Court warrant over his alleged crimes against humanity in connection with former president Rodrigo Duterte’s war on drugs and the Davao Death Squad killings.

He reappeared on May 11 to back Senator Alan Peter Cayetano’s bid for Senate presidency and sought refuge inside the Senate. However, he left the premises on May 14, hours after a shooting incident inside the Senate, and has remained out of public view.
Padilla was named a person of interest by the National Bureau of Investigation on May 15 after it was revealed that Dela Rosa had left the Senate compound with him at around 2:30 am on May 14.

On May 22, the lawmaker said his ally had merely asked him for a ride and that Dela Rosa got off somewhere in Makati City, where a vehicle was already waiting for the former Philippine National Police chief. – Rappler.com

articles.title: LGUs to seek P58.53-B local funding via online portal -- DBM
articles.summary: Local government units (LGUs) must directly apply for government funding through a digital platform, bypassing political intermediaries and ensuring greater transparency in the allocation of public…

blocks.text: Published September 15, 2026 7:24pm

Local government units (LGUs) must directly apply for government funding through a digital platform, bypassing political intermediaries and ensuring greater transparency in the allocation of public funds, the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) said on Tuesday.

During the Development Budget Coordination Committee briefing at the House of Representatives, DBM Secretary Kim Robert De Leon, through House Appropriations Committee Chair Mikaela Angela Suansing, said the government has proposed P58.53 billion for the Local Government Support Fund (LGSF) under the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP).
"We are proposing Php 58.53 billion for the (LGSF), covering financial assistance to LGUs, the Growth Equity Fund, and the Barangay Development Program," she said.
"By strengthening local fiscal capacity, we bring resources and decision-making closer to communities and give every region a stronger voice in the nation's development," the DBM added.
Under DBM Local Budget Circular No. 169, local chief executives must apply directly through the digital Ugnayang Bayan Portal.

Suansing, who was defending the committee report on the 2027 General Appropriations Bill, said LGUs must submit their funding requests directly to the DBM through the portal, ensuring that allocations are based on local priorities rather than requests coursed through third parties.
The circular eliminates intermediaries, while submission of an application does not guarantee that an LGU will receive funding, she said.

The proposed P58.53-billion allocation for 2027 is reportedly 1.14% higher than the 2026 budget. The DBM said the proposal incorporated inputs from groups such as the Union of Local Authorities of the Philippines (ULAP) and various LGU leagues to better address local infrastructure and social development priorities.

In a separate statement, the DBM said funding requests are evaluated based on several criteria, including governance standards, fiscal management, transparency, absorptive capacity, service delivery, economic development, environmental management, public safety and citizen engagement.

"The evaluation considers governance standards; financial management, fiscal transparency, and absorptive capacity; service delivery; economic development; environmental management; public safety; and citizen engagement," it said.
"DBM also considers the necessity of the proposed assistance, just and equitable distribution of funds among LGUs, and availability of funds," the DBM added.

During the House hearing, Suansing also noted that the Supreme Court had previously affirmed the constitutionality of the LGSF, saying it serves a clear policy purpose and is governed by sufficient legal standards.

"The ruling reinforces that LGSF releases operate within defined purposes, eligibility requirements, evaluation criteria, and accountability mechanisms. LGUs themselves identify and request assistance based on local needs, while approved funds remain subject to transparency, monitoring, audit, and applicable government rules," she said.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Imran Khan’s sons accuse Pakistani army chief of vendetta against imprisoned father
articles.summary:
Kasim and Sulaiman Khan tell Guardian they believe ex-PM is being ‘slowly killed’ by harsh treatment, driven by Asim Munir

The sons of Imran Khan have accused Pakistan’s powerful army chief…
articles.byline: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi and Shah Meer Baloch in Islamabad

blocks.text: The sons of Imran Khan have accused Pakistan’s powerful army chief of a “personal vendetta” against the incarcerated former prime minister and expressed fears their father is being “slowly killed” in jail, as international pressure mounts over his prison conditions.

Kasim Khan, 27, and Sulaiman Khan, 29, have become strong advocates for the release of their father, who has been held in Adiala prison in Rawalpindi since his arrest in 2023, and is serving a 14-year sentence on corruption charges.
They have not been allowed to speak to Khan for more than six months and have been prevented from travelling from the UK to Pakistan to lobby for his release.

On Wednesday, the supreme court will rule on a case alleging the Pakistan government has been in contempt of court by denying Khan private hospital treatment for a worsening eye condition and preventing family from visiting him or speaking with him in jail for more than six months, in violation of a court order. Khan is being held in solitary confinement, in a cell alleged to be 6ft by 8ft.

blocks.caption: Imran Khan outside court in Lahore after a hearing in February 2023. Photograph: Mohsin Raza/Reuters

blocks.text: Later this month, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) – the political party Khan founded in 1996, four years after retiring from international cricket – is planning a nationwide march demanding his release.

Speaking to the Guardian from London, Khan’s sons – from his first marriage to Jemima Goldsmith – said they were “deeply, deeply concerned” about their father’s health, and that the conditions he was being kept in amounted to “a form of mental and physical torture”.

“The reality is that he is locked in a tiny 6x8ft cell without human contact,” said Sulaiman. “He hasn’t been allowed new books for months and he’s not been allowed to see or speak to his family or a neutral doctor. He has an eye condition which was neglected for months and has meant he’s probably almost lost sight in one eye.”

blocks.caption: Left to right: Sulaiman Khan, Jemima Khan, Imran Khan’s daughter Tyrian White and Kasim Khan at a film premiere in London in February 2023. Photograph: PA Images/Alamy

blocks.text: Late last month, Sky Sports aired an interview with Khasim and Sulaiman during its coverage of a test match between England and Pakistan. The Pakistan Cricket Board, which has close links to the government and whose chair is also the interior minister, made a formal complaint to Sky Sports after the broadcast and the Pakistani team threatened to refuse to return to the field after the lunch break.

“It shows how out of touch they are with the rest of the world, that they thought they could silence media like they do at home,” Sulaiman said of the complaint. “It just exposed them for the authoritarian regime that they are.”

The UN has said Khan’s prolonged detention violates international law and the UN’s special rapporteur on torture said his solitary confinement and detention conditions could amount to psychological torture.
Sulaiman said the family had been told their father, 73, had also been diagnosed with high blood pressure. “More than anything, we just want to speak to him and make sure he’s OK,” he said.
Khan’s sons said they were particularly concerned that the “cruel” treatment was being driven by a “personal grudge” by Asim Munir, Pakistan’s chief of defence forces and army chief.

blocks.caption: Asim Munir praying after laying a wreath on the martyrs’ monument during a ceremony in Rawalpindi last year. Photograph: AP

blocks.text: When Khan was the prime minister, he unceremoniously demoted Munir, and the bad blood between them was well known. When Munir was made army chief in 2023, the persecution of Khan increased notably.

“It’s very clear this is being driven by personal grudge and that’s one of the reasons he’s being treated so harshly, on the orders of Asim Munir,” said Sulaiman. Munir’s powers expanded over the past year as he established himself as a close ally of Donald Trump, who referred to him as “my favourite field marshal”.

Last month, the supreme court ruled that Khan should be taken to a private hospital for treatment for a blood clot in his retinal vein, believed to have destroyed 85% of the sight in his right eye because of a prolonged lack of medical attention.
Khan was instead taken briefly to a government hospital, where he was given several injections and ruled fit to return to prison, prompting outrage from his family and political party.

“There’s still been no light shed on our father’s real condition from an unbiased, neutral physician,” said Kasim. “We believe they’re trying to slowly kill him in there. Just as soon as there’s less pressure, we are sure they will put even harsher restrictions on him and try to finish him off.
“The one with the real vendetta here is the army chief Asim Munir.”

In a statement, the Pakistan government called the allegations around Khan “fake propaganda” and said he was being kept in adequate conditions, with access to home-cooked food, nuts, bottled water, exercise equipment, family visits and regular medical examinations.
“The government of Pakistan categorically rejects allegations that the convicted prisoner is being subjected to punitive solitary confinement, cruelty or deprivation,” the statement said.

It was widely acknowledged that Khan came to power in 2018 with the backing of Pakistan’s military, widely referred to as the “establishment”, which has long held an oversized role in the country’s governance. Khan had promised to build a “naya Pakistan” (new Pakistan), which would end corruption and follow the rule of law. However, his time in power was plagued by allegations of corruption, press censorship and persecution of his opponents.
He was toppled in 2022 after falling out with his military benefactors. He then began a campaign calling for the generals to be kept out of government.

By 2023, as his accusations against the military grew, Khan turned from alleged persecutor to the persecuted. He was arrested and charged with more than 100 crimes, including alleged corruption and sedition, which he claims are trumped up to keep him out of power.
Despite his toppling and imprisonment, Khan still remains popular. “They want to do everything they can to sideline him and disappear him from public life,” Kasim said.

blocks.caption: Supporters of Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf display a poster of Imran Khan at a rally in February on the second anniversary of the 2024 general elections, which the party alleges were rigged. Photograph: Bilawal Arbab/EPA

blocks.text: Sulaiman said that while it was “clear the establishment think they can get away with it without any kind of repercussions”, it was also evident the government had been rattled by international coverage of Khan’s case.
Khan’s sons said that while they were keen to travel to Pakistan, their visas had still not been granted more than nine months after applying.
They emphasised they had no interest in entering politics in Pakistan or leading Khan’s PTI party in his absence.

“We definitely don’t want to get involved in politics in Pakistan in the long term,” said Sulaiman. “Our father always said that one of the biggest problems with Pakistani politics is this dynastic nepotism; that power’s been held by just two families for the last 40 years. It’s a sign of what’s wrong with the political system in Pakistan.”

Speculation has abounded on whether Khan would strike a deal with the military to secure his release. Khan’s closest aide, Zulfi Bukhari, said: “There is only one deal Khan would ever accept: the restoration of democracy, the rule of law and the people’s mandate in Pakistan. If they’re genuinely willing to do that, then fine – let’s talk.”

Kasim and Sulaiman said they did not believe Khan would give up his politics to secure his release. “He’s a very single-minded person,” said Kasim. “I don’t think there’s a chance that he’d ever give it up.”

articles.title: No sign of drilling from Chinese ship lurking in Bajo de Masinloc - AFP
articles.summary: The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) on Tuesday said the Chinese vessel that was spotted in Bajo de Masinloc for 28 days was conducting research and surveillance, but did not conduct any…

blocks.text: Published September 15, 2026 7:17pm

The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) on Tuesday said the Chinese vessel that was spotted in Bajo de Masinloc for 28 days was conducting research and surveillance, but did not conduct any drilling.

AFP Special Spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea Rear Admiral Roy Vincent Trinidad reiterated the country’s claim over the disputed waters, particularly Bajo de Masinloc, also known as the Panatag Shoal.

“On the Chinese research vessel that was spotted for 25 days...28 days in Bajo de Masinloc, the presence and the track would indicate that they were conducting surveillance or research activities,” Trinidad told reporters.
“As to any report of drilling activities, there was none that was confirmed, nor were there any reports given by our monitoring capabilities,” he added.
Trinidad explained that for the vessel to be able to drill, it needed to remain stationary. He said the AFP also has other sensors to determine such activities.
“The tracks indicated not a continuous pattern. It was not only transiting. But to be able to conduct drilling activities, it should be stationary,” the Navy officer added.
The presence of the Chinese vessel was initially called out by Philippine Coast Guard spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela.

China has continuously laid its claim to Philippine waters despite the 2016 ruling of the Permanent Court of Arbitration, with numerous maritime encounters between Filipino and Chinese personnel. —Jean Mangaluz/RF, GMA News

articles.title: SPD governor campaigns as one-woman bulwark against AfD
articles.summary: Manuela Schwesig, of the center-left SPD, has governed the state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, on the Baltic Sea coast, since 2017. Ahead of this weekend's election, she is campaigning against…

image.caption: Manuela Schwesig has made a point of meeting as many voters personally as she canImage: Philip Dulian/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The late-summer warmth is lingering in the countryside of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Lavender-infused cocktails and savory onion cakes are being served on the spacious terrace of Hasenwinkel Castle, an old country house turned conference hotel not far from the Baltic coast. The largest business association in this northeastern German state has invited members and guests from the political world to a convivial gathering. State Premier Manuela Schwesig, of the Social Democratic Party (SPD), is also in attendance.

It could be a relaxed evening, were it not for the upcoming state election on September 20. "We live in politically turbulent times," says association president Lars Schwarz in his welcoming remarks. But the evening is also meant to serve as an opportunity to "recharge," he says. Days before the election, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is leading in the polls with around 37%. But the SPD is not far behind, with 33%, and has narrowed the gap in recent weeks. The conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which leads the federal government with the SPD under Chancellor Friedrich Merz, is far behind and hoping to remain above the 5% threshold to enter parliament.
The economy needs immigration, the AfD opposes it

The term "remigration" is playing a major role in the AfD's campaign. But as far as the state's business leaders are concerned, sending people of immigrant background out of Germany would be a disaster for the economy.

Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania has a significantly older population than most other German states. It's also less densely populated and more severely affected by demographic change. "International skilled workers and laborers have long been an important part of our economic future," said Schwarz. "Openness to the world is not an abstract political formula, but a concrete prerequisite for ensuring that businesses in our state can continue to produce, offer services, train employees, and grow."

In a brief speech at the event, Schwesig recounted encounters she had during the election campaign. She speaks of a conversation with a baker who is concerned not only about high energy prices but also about her employees. "She said, 'Ms. Schwesig, I have employees with immigrant backgrounds working here, and I'm very worried that I'll lose them — because I value them, and because I care about them as people.'"

The head of a planning firm approached the state premier and explained that his Moroccan employee wanted to leave the country. "Because when he goes to the café at the market in Stralsund and waits for his German friends, the people sitting near him either make snide remarks or move to another table." Who, Schwesig asks, would want to live in such a climate?
Fear of social division

Preventing the AfD's victory — that is what the 52-year-old Schwesig has made her stated goal. In the final stretch of the campaign, her posters feature just her face on a red background — no name — above the slogan "The Woman Against Blue" — a reference to the AfD's party color.

"The situation is serious," Schwesig told DW. "The AfD would harm our economy; they would harm our social cohesion. Their crude way of speaking, their hate and incitement, is tearing our society apart; there's a renewed propensity for violence, and that will affect us women in particular."
Anyone who doesn't want those things must support her, she says. "To do that, you have to go to the polls and vote for the SPD — and that's why I'm the woman against blue."

Perhaps tellingly, the SPD isn't mentioned on most of her campaign posters, however. Only Schwesig herself is visible, dressed in red. The SPD's party color must suffice as a reference. Schwesig is the driving force: She represents the political comeback of the past twelve months. In September 2025, the SPD in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania was languishing at just 19% in opinion polls, while the AfD stood at 38%.
Recipe for success: Close to the people and distance from Berlin

Manuela Schwesig managed to close the gap, in part, by trying to stay closely connected to the people of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, seeking direct dialogue with voters as often as possible. She is friendly and approachable, yet also firm. Schwesig listens, answers questions with confidence, marshals the facts, and engages in discussions where she attempts to demonstrate that she is well-informed about everything happening in the state.

Above all, however, she scored points by maintaining maximum distance from the federal government — and thus from her own party too. In Berlin, the SPD governs as the junior partner in a coalition with the conservative bloc of Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) parties, and the government is more unpopular than any before it. As Schwesig has gained ground, the SPD's support at the federal level has plummeted to 12%.
Imported care giver: Skilled, needed, stalled by bureaucracy
Strong criticism of Friedrich Merz

Schwesig believes much of what is decided in Berlin is wrong — and she says so. "I expect the chancellor and the entire federal government to chart a new political course,” she demanded following the AfD's victory in Saxony-Anhalt in early September.

She has long believed that the reform of the social welfare systems planned by the CDU/CSU and the SPD is heading in the wrong direction. "I expect that the reforms will ensure that those who have worked their entire lives and made contributions are not the ones who bear the heaviest burdens," she says regarding the plans to eliminate the retirement age of 63 for people who have contributed to the pension fund for a particularly long time. "And I'm glad that my criticism is now receiving a lot of support."
Will Manuela Schwesig become SPD leader?

She also receives support from within her own party. Discontent is growing within the federal SPD over the two co-chairs, Lars Klingbeil and Bärbel Bas. There is open speculation about whether Manuela Schwesig should replace them at the party's helm. Amid the SPD's crisis, there are strong arguments for making one of the last Social Democrats who is popular with voters the party leader.

A woman who entered politics relatively late in life. Born in Brandenburg, she was already nearly 30 years old when she joined the SPD in 2003. Prior to that, she had studied public finance and worked as a tax official.

blocks.caption: Schwesig served in Merkel's cabinet before returning to Mecklenburg Western-PomeraniaImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Schwesig: Underestimated by opponents?

Her political rise was rapid: Local politics in the state capital of Schwerin, Social Affairs Minister in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, and finally, in 2013, Federal Family Affairs Minister under former Chancellor Angela Merkel. By then, she had become well-known nationwide.

Her opponents often underestimated her, especially men. A CDU politician once derisively called her the "coastal Barbie." "Young, blonde, East German" was the headline when she became a federal minister.
Perhaps this was also because Schwesig never came across as a classic power-seeking politician. Her strengths, say her supporters, lie in her calm perseverance, fighting spirit, and pragmatism.
Nord Stream 2

This tenacity nearly proved to be her undoing in the dispute over the Nord Stream 2 gas pipeline. In 2017, Schwesig returned to Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania to succeed State Premier Erwin Sellering, who was seriously ill at the time. Sellering had maintained very good relations with Russia, and Schwesig continued his policies.

This included defending the construction of the Baltic Sea pipeline — which was intended to transport even more Russian gas to Germany — in the face of criticism from Eastern Europe, the US, and some in Germany. When the US threatened sanctions in 2021, Schwesig even attempted to secure the completion of Nord Stream 2 by establishing a "climate foundation" funded by Moscow.

blocks.caption: Schwesig's support for the Nord Stream pipeline became a political liabilityImage: Jens Büttner/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: State premier with a 60% approval rating

After the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, her stance became a political liability. Schwesig made a political about-face and admitted to mistakes. To this day, however, she defends the logic behind her decisions at the time.
This has not caused her any lasting damage. Currently, in a direct election, 60% of voters in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania would vote for Schwesig as head of government.
The current state government, made up of the SPD and the socialist Left Party, is also performing well in polls. But it remains to be seen whether this will be enough to secure another term.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: Poa: Defense has ‘strategy’ to address questions on Duterte SALNs
articles.summary: The defense questions whether Ombudsman records division OIC Karen Batu was in a position to testify on alleged irregularities in Duterte's SALNs

blocks.text: ARRAIGNED. Vice President Sara Duterte arrives at the Quezon City RTC on September 11, 2026, to attend arraignment proceedings for her grave threats case.
Jire Carreon/Rappler
The defense questions whether Ombudsman records division OIC Karen Batu was in a position to testify on alleged irregularities in Duterte's SALNs

items: The defense counsel for Vice President Sara Duterte questioned the competence of an Ombudsman official to testify about alleged irregularities in her Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALNs), arguing that the official lacked personal knowledge of the records.

The prosecution countered that the witness was testifying based on the Ombudsman's records, and the Senate impeachment court allowed the presentation of Duterte's SALNs from 2007 to 2025 to establish a baseline for the trial.

The Senate impeachment court is preparing for the presentation of amici curiae, including four retired Supreme Court justices, to provide guidance on the voting threshold for Duterte's trial, with a vote expected on September 23.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines– The defense counsel of Vice President Sara Duterte questioned on Tuesday, September 15, the competence of an official of the Office of the Ombudsman to testify on alleged irregularities in the Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALNs) of the country’s second-highest official.

On Day 25 of the impeachment trial, defense lawyer Justin Nicol Gular underscored that Ombudsman records division officer-in-charge (OIC) Karen Batu has no personal knowledge of the contents of Duterte’s SALNs including her personal properties, liabilities, net worths, and disclosures of business interests and financial connections.
Batu also has no personal knowledge whether or not there were irregularities, unusual entries, or errors in Duterte’s records, he added.
“In testifying in today’s trial, you cannot conclude whether the Vice President has or does not have ill-gotten wealth,” said Gular.
The prosecution swiftly objected, saying “it was clear from the very start that the witness was only testifying based on the [Ombudsman’s] records.”
“We’ve been fair with the witness in our direct [examination] only asking her to that,” private prosecutor James Bryan Ibrahim Alih said.

Duterte’s financial records were scrutinized during the trial, with prosecutors presenting her SALNs from 2007 to 2025. The defense initially objected to the presentation, explaining that she was not an impeachable officer prior to 2022. Senate impeachment court Presiding Officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero, however, allowed the presentation, citing the need to establish a baseline.

“The Chair would like to remind counsel for the respondent of the ruling of the Chair with respect to the issuance of the subpoenas covering the period 2007 up to 2025, that pursuant to OMB, Office of the Ombudsman vs. Bernardo GR No. 181598 dated March 2013, there is a necessity to establish the baseline, not for the prosecution but equally for the respondent, in order to find out what is the base figure for the computation of the SALN during her term,” Escudero said.

Defense spokesperson Michael Poa, in a press briefing, said Batu was not the proper witness to interpret the SALNs, adding she was called to testify to identify Duterte’s SALNs that were in the custody of the Ombudsman. He also said the defense will present a strategy, during their presentation of evidence, to address questions on the SALNs.

“We have our strategy on that matter, actually. Because obviously, I will not, without disclosing the specifics, I will also not deny na siyempre, napag-isipan na ng depensa kung paano natin gagawin yan at ipapaliwanag ang mga bagay-bagay,” Poa said.

(We have our strategy on that matter, actually. Because obviously, I will not, without disclosing the specifics, I will also not deny that we have already formulated ways on how we will explain the SALNs.)

“Meron naman kaming mga naisip na paraan at estratehiya… Asahan niyo na lang po at abangan niyo na lang po ‘pag kami naman ang nag-present ng ebidensya kung sakaling may mga kailangan ipaliwanag doon sa mga nakalagay,” he added.
(We thought of ways and strategies. We will show that to the public during our turn to present evidence.)
In a related development, the Senate impeachment court is now preparing for the presentation of the amici curiae, or “friends of the court” on Wednesday, September 16.

The impeachment court has tapped four retired Supreme Court (SC) justices to provide guidance on the resolution of the voting threshold for Duterte’s trial. They are: retired Chief Justices Artemio V. Panganiban, Reynato S. Puno, Hilario G. Davide Jr., and retired Associate Justice Adolfo S. Azcuna.
Panganiban, Puno, and Azcuna will physically attend the presentation while Davide will submit an advisory to be read before the court.
RELATED STORY: ‘Amici curiae’: Where do invited ex-justices stand on conviction threshold debate?

Each senator-judges will be provided five minutes to pose a question to the retired SC justices. Following their presentation, an oral argument between the defense and prosecution panels on the matter will be held on September 23, with each side given 15 minutes to present its position.
Senator-judges are expected to cast their votes on the voting threshold issue on the same day. – Rappler.com
