articles.title: Communauto says it was hit by data breach initiated by its own employee
articles.summary: The Montreal car-sharing company said it was hit by a potential data breach after one of its employees tried to access customers' personal information.

image.caption: The Montreal car-sharing company Communauto says it has about 50,000 customers in Quebec alone. (Olivia Laperrière-Roy/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Montreal
The Montreal car-sharing company said it was hit by a potential data breach after one of its employees tried to access customers' personal information.
Breach affected 'some thousand members' across the country, says company
The Montreal car-sharing company Communauto said it was hit by a potential data breach after one of its employees tried to access customers' personal information.
In an email sent to affected customers on Monday evening, Communauto said the incident happened during the night of Sept. 3 to 4.
"Our investigation determined that an automated script had been deployed without authorization by an employee in an attempt to access and download customer records," the email reads.
The company says police executed a search warrant the next day at the residence of the employee suspected of carrying out the breach to seize their computer equipment.

Communauto says account passwords and payment information were not affected by the breach, but that personal information, including people's names, addresses and driver's licence numbers, was. If the customer had a photograph of themselves or of their licence attached to their file, then those were downloaded as well.
In a statement to CBC, Communauto's vice-president of strategic development, Marco Viviani, said the breach affected about two per cent of its users, representing "some thousand members" Canada-wide.
"At this stage, we hope that no data was disclosed externally," he said.

"Based on the information available to us, we did not believe it was necessary for anyone to be taken into custody, but we have not received any additional details since law enforcement became involved."
Viviani says the company hired a specialized consulting firm to monitor the web and dark web for any signs of data exposure.

Communauto says those affected by the breach should "remain vigilant regarding unsolicited emails, phone calls, and text messages, particularly those requesting personal information, payment, urgent action, or encouraging you to click on a link or open an attachment."
It says customers should set up multi-factor authentication and make sure their account password is strong and unique.

articles.title: AFP to continue providing VP Sara Duterte with security detail
articles.summary: The Armed Forces of the Philippines on Tuesday said that it has not received a request to withdraw Vice President Sara Duterte"s military security detail, so it will continue guarding her.

blocks.text: Published September 15, 2026 7:06pm
The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) on Tuesday said that it has not received a request to withdraw Vice President Sara Duterte’s military security detail, so it will continue guarding her.
This came after National Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro said that Duterte was free to request the withdrawal of her security detail if she did not feel safe around them.
Asked if there was an official request from the Office of the Vice President, AFP spokesperson Colonel Francel Margareth Padilla said there was not.

“We are not aware of any of that. For the side of the Armed Forces of the Philippines, generic po ito. Not directed to any particular individual or any entity po no. For us in the AFP, duty po natin ‘yan, mandato po natin na kasama sa mission ng Sandatahang Lakas ng Pilipinas to protect our VIPs accordingly,” Padilla

(We are not aware of any of that. For the side of the Armed Forces of the Philippines, this is generic. Not directed to any particular individual or any entity. For us in the AFP, it is our duty, our mandate, it is in the mission of the Armed Forces of the Philippines to protect our VIPs accordingly.)
Padilla said that they will continue with this mandate and secure the Vice President.

After Duterte expressed distrust of the courts and police system, she posted a supposed screenshot of a conversation with former AFP Chief of Staff General Romeo Brawner Jr. reportedly promising Duterte and her family protection in 2024.
“I think that needs to be validated ano. At this point, we don't have information on that,” Padilla said when asked about the arrangement.

Duterte’s statements that she felt unsafe around police were made when she was posting bail for her three counts of grave threats charges. She had publicly said that she had spoken with someone to kill President “Bongbong” Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos and then-House speaker Martin Romualdez if she were killed. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Sara Duterte camp: Strategies in place to explain SALN figures
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte's defense team said Tuesday it has strategies in place should the time come when her counsels need to explain the movement of figures in her Statement of Assets,…

blocks.text: Vice President Sara Duterte's defense team said Tuesday it has strategies in place should the time come when they need to explain the movement of figures in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN).

"We have a strategy on that matter, actually. Obviously, without disclosing the specifics, I will also not deny na siyempre napag-isipan na ng depensa kung paano natin gagawin 'yan," defense team spokesperson Atty. Michael Poa said.
(We actually have a strategy on that matter. Obviously, without disclosing the specifics, I will also not deny that the defense has naturally thought about how we will handle that.)
"Asahan ninyo na lang po at abangan ninyo na lang po pag kami naman ang nagprisinta ng ebidensya, kung sakaling may mga kailangan ipaliwanag du'n sa mga nakalagay," he added.
(You can expect and watch out for that when it is our turn to present evidence, should there be things that need to be explained there.)
When asked if the strategy included calling for Duterte, he replied: "Not necessarily."
On the 25th day of the trial, Article 2 of the impeachment case was discussed, where part of the supporting documents presented was the vice president's SALN.

Article 2 of the Articles of Impeachment alleges that Duterte accumulated unexplained wealth by failing to fully and truthfully disclose all of her and her spouse's assets, liabilities, and net worth in her SALNs for 2022, 2023, and 2024.
Additionally, it claims she failed to divest from—and instead willfully maintained—all of her business interests throughout her tenure as vice president from 2022 through 2025.
Atty. Karen Batu
On Tuesday, the House prosecution panel presented a new witness, Atty. Karen Batu, officer-in-charge of the Records Division of the Office of the Ombudsman.
She testified on matters contained within the SALNs of Duterte and her husband, Manases Carpio.

Recalling her testimony, the defense team stated that Batu was presented solely for the purpose of identifying the SALNs, which are in the custody of the Office of the Ombudsman as the official repository.
Poa said no personal knowledge was expected from Batu, given the limitations of her role as records custodian.

"Kumbaga, custodian lang po talaga siya ng lahat ng SALN na pinapasa sa kanila and therefore hindi siya makakapag-testify on kung mayroong ill-gotten [wealth] or may non-declaration or non-disclosure sa SALN," Poa said.
(In other words, she is really just a custodian of all the SALNs submitted to them, and therefore she cannot testify on whether there is ill-gotten wealth, non-declaration, or non-disclosure.)
"Kasi base lang po talaga sa dokumento, kumbaga parang binabasa lang niya yung dokumento kanina kung napansin ninyo," he added.
(Because it's really just based on the document—in other words, if you noticed earlier, she was simply reading from the document.)
For the defense panel, Batu is not qualified to interpret any guidelines concerning the matter, reminding the public that she was only called to identify and present the SALNs.

"So I think hindi pa ito yung tamang witness para mag-interpret ng ganitong bagay. Just to be fair to both parties and, of course, to the witness—kasi para maintindihan ng ating mga kababayan, 'yung witness talaga hindi siya pinatawag para mag-interpret ng kung anumang nasa loob ng guidelines ng CSC or ng [6713]," Poa explained.

(So I think this is not yet the right witness to interpret these matters. Just to be fair to both parties and, of course, to the witness—so that the public understands—the witness was really not called to interpret whatever is inside the guidelines of the CSC or RA 6713.)
Poa was referring to Civil Service Commission (CSC) guidelines, which govern government appointments, merit systems, and employee discipline.
Meanwhile, Republic Act 6713 refers to the Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees.
Poa noted Batu's caution, pointing out that she even offered a disclaimer stating she could not draw conclusions on certain matters.

"Kasi ngayon talaga yung kay Atty. Batu, if you noticed, she's testifying based on her personal experience, 'di ba, o 'yung napapansin niya sa trabaho niya. But lahat po kasi 'yon ay hindi conclusive, and Atty. Batu was very careful by saying na she cannot conclude on these matters," Poa said.

(Because right now with Atty. Batu, if you noticed, she's testifying based on her personal experience or what she observes in her job. But all of that is not conclusive, and Atty. Batu was very careful by saying that she cannot conclude on these matters.)
"So kung talagang kailangan ipaliwanag 'yung bawat pagtaas, that will either come to the later witnesses or sa mismong ebidensya na mismo ng depensa," he added.
(So if each increase really needs to be explained, that will either come through later witnesses or directly from the defense's own evidence.)
Spokesman Paolo Panelo
Poa clarified that he has not served as Duterte's spokesperson since October 2024.
Instead, he stated that he transitioned to serving as one of her lawyers, and now acts as the spokesperson for her defense team in the impeachment trial.
"Ako naman kasi, since October 2024, hindi na po ako tumayong spokesperson ni Vice President Sara Duterte or ng OVP," Poa said, referring to the Office of the Vice President.
(As for me, since October 2024, I have no longer served as the spokesperson for Vice President Sara Duterte, or the OVP.)

"Ako po ay naging abogado na lamang niya at ako po ay tumatayong tagapagsalita ng defense team—not of the Vice President, not of the OVP—but just the defense team as one of the lawyers in the defense team," he added.
(I became her lawyer strictly, and I am acting as the spokesperson for the defense team—not for the Vice President, not for the OVP—but specifically for the defense team as one of its lawyers.)
Last Wednesday, Atty. Paolo Panelo was appointed as the new spokesperson for Duterte, replacing Ruth Castelo.
Poa said he and Panelo have distinct duties, even though both serve spokesperson functions.

However, he noted that Panelo could still answer questions regarding the impeachment, though he won't be involved in matters of strategy or evidence, as those will remain within the purview of the defense team.
Poa said he has worked with Panelo before, so they maintain open communication.
"Parang lang masigurado na hindi kami nagco-conflict with one another in fairness to Atty. Panelo, he also reaches out to me naman to us to ask questions," Poa added.
(Just to make sure we don't conflict with one another, in fairness to Atty. Panelo, he also reaches out to me and to us to ask questions.) — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Venice best actress winner says she signed on at Danish job centre days before her victory
articles.summary:
Mathilde Arcel, who won the Volpi Cup on Saturday for her role in Golden Lion winner Woman Unknown, said job offers have now begun to arrive

The winner of this year’s best actress prize at…

blocks.text: The winner of this year’s best actress prize at the Venice film festival has revealed that she is on unemployment benefits and had to fly to back to Copenhagen to report to the job centre before receiving her award.

On Saturday night, Danish actor Mathilde Arcel won the prestigious Volpi Cup for her first leading role in a feature film, May el-Toukhy’s post-second world war drama Woman Unknown, which also won the Golden Lion award for best film.
Jury president Maggie Gyllenhaal said the judges had been able to relax Venice rules around not awarding more than one prize per film because the vote for Arcel had been unanimous.

After her triumph, the 30-year-old actor revealed in interviews with Danish media that she had returned to Denmark after her film’s premiere to sign on at the job centre, as she is on unemployment benefits when not working on films. She then returned to the Lido after being told it would be wise to be present at the awards gala.
In the UK, actors’ trade union Equity said in a 2023 report that 63% of its members have been in receipt of social security at some point in their life.
Set in the direct aftermath of the Nazi occupation of Denmark, Woman Unknown tells the story of Marie, a young housemaid and nanny who is about to marry her widowed industrialist employer.

But a chance encounter with an old schoolfriend threatens to reveal a shameful secret, exposing Marie to the retributive hounding of female “horizontal collaborators” who had intimate relations with German soldiers.

At Venice, Arcel drew wide critical praise for the contained inner anguish she brings to the role of Marie. “Mathilde is going to blow our socks off,” Gyllenhaal said in a press conference after the awards ceremony.

The actor said her agent had received several calls with new job offers since she scooped the Volpi Cup, the male version of which went to Hollywood veteran John Malkovich. “There are a lot of calls and a lot of interest from abroad and things like that, and we need to talk about what’s going to happen,” she told Danish broadcaster DR.

Speaking in Venice on Saturday night, Arcel joked that her ultimate dream would be to play a part in one long-running British TV detective drama she was particularly fond of. “I really want to keep on working and meet some new artists”, she said. “I’m looking so much forward to what the future will bring, perhaps even a role in Midsomer Murders”.

articles.title: Poland seeks new defense deals with Philippines
articles.summary: Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Wladyslaw Bartoszewsk says Poland is investing nearly $50 billion for its defense industry and could sell military hardware abroad, including to the Philippines

blocks.text: POLAND FLAG. The flag of Poland.
Darwinek, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons
Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Wladyslaw Bartoszewsk says Poland is investing nearly $50 billion for its defense industry and could sell military hardware abroad, including to the Philippines

MANILA, Philippines – Poland is seeking new defense partnerships with the Philippines, a senior foreign ministry official said on Tuesday, September 15, after completing the delivery of Black Hawk helicopters to Manila last month.

Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Wladyslaw Bartoszewski, who was in Manila for annual political consultations with the Philippines, said Poland is investing nearly $50 billion for its defense industry and could sell military hardware abroad, including to the Philippines.

items: Bartoszewski said Poland could sell both reconnaissance and fighting drones, radar equipment, anti-aircraft missiles and armored personnel carriers. A Philippine military delegation recently visited Poland to look into equipment that Manila can buy, he said.

The Philippines acquired 32 S-70i Black Hawk helicopters from Polish Sikorsky subsidiary PZL Mielec in a deal worth P32 billion ($509.60 million) in 2022. The delivery of the last seven helicopters was completed last month, the Philippine military said.
Bartoszewski said separately talks were ongoing between Ukraine and Poland for the transfer of Warsaw’s MiG-29 fighter jets in exchange for drone technology from Kyiv.
Bartoszewski said the two sides are discussing whether to refurbish the jets before transferring them to Ukraine as well as the kind of technology Warsaw gets in return.
Poland has been one of Ukraine’s strongest backers since Russia began its full-scale invasion in 2022, providing military aid and serving as a ​key logistics hub for Western assistance.

blocks.text: (Reporting by Mikhail Flores; Editing by Martin Petty)

articles.title: Denmark says Russian warship fired flares at military helicopter
articles.summary: The Danish prime minister has accused Russia of "reckless" behaviour, while the Kremlin is yet to comment.

blocks.text: Denmark has accused a Russian warship of firing two emergency flares at one of its helicopters while it was tracking the vessel in the Baltic Sea.
The Danish government has summoned the Russian ambassador over the incident, which it said happened during a "routine" monitoring operation on Monday.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen branded the Russian action "reckless" and said it was designed to "intimidate and divide".
Moscow has not commented on the incident.

It came on the same day Nato forces shot down a drone over Lithuania in the latest security scare on the alliance's eastern flank, where tensions remain high during Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

In a statement detailing the incident in the Baltic Sea, the Danish armed forces said: "One of the air force's Fennec helicopters was today fired at with flares during a routine photographic operation of a Russian frigate, which was located in international waters off Gedser."
Of the two flares fired at the helicopter, one passed close to it, the statement added.
The Danish foreign ministry described the incident as "completely unacceptable".
Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen accused Russia of "gradually shifting the boundary for what they consider acceptable behaviour", adding: "That is something we cannot accept."
Overnight, Nato fighter pilots shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace.
Authorities said the drone likely entered southern Lithuania, near the second-largest city of Kaunas, from neighbouring Belarus shortly after midnight on Tuesday.
The origins of the drone are yet to be determined, the Lithuanian national crisis management centre said, but the country's president pointed to increased Russian aggression in recent months.

President Gitanas Nausėda wrote on X: "With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region. Together with our Nato Allies, Lithuania will defend its airspace."
Lithuania shares a large part of its southern and eastern border with Belarus, a key Russian ally.

Poland also announced there had been "aviation operations" in its airspace on Monday night "due to the activity of Russian Federation's jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles conducting strikes on Ukrainian territory".
It said the overnight operations were of a "preventive nature" and aimed at "securing airspace and its protection, especially in areas adjacent to threatened regions".
Nato jets have been scrambled several times to shoot down stray Ukrainian drones that have crossed into Baltic countries Estonia and Latvia this year.
Ukraine has blamed the stray drones on Russian electronic warfare, technology designed to change the flight paths of Ukrainian drones.

articles.title: NATO fighter jet shoots down drone over Lithuania
articles.summary: An Italian NATO fighter jet shot down a drone over Lithuania ‌shortly after midnight on Tuesday morning, the Lithuanian National Crisis Management Centre said.

image.caption: Debris of what the Lithuanian National Crisis Management Centre says is a drone shot down by a NATO fighter jet lies on the ground near Pratkunai, Lithuania, on Tuesday in this screengrab from a handout video. (Lithuanian Army/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New
An Italian NATO fighter jet shot down a drone over Lithuania ‌shortly after midnight on Tuesday morning, the Lithuanian National Crisis Management Centre said.
It was not immediately clear if the drone was fired by Russian or Ukrainian forces

The drone, which was likely to have entered from Belarus, was shot ​down near Pratkunai village in southern ​Lithuania, near Kaunas, the second-largest city, the centre's spokesperson said. Its origin had yet to be ​determined, he said.
Military drones ​straying into the ⁠airspace of Russia's neighbours have stoked concerns that Russia's war in Ukraine is spilling over NATO's borders.

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said that strikes close to the alliance's territory would drive the trans-Atlantic organization to increase its support for Kyiv. Rutte also pledged to bolster the 32-nation alliance's own defences along its long eastern border with Russia.
Concerns grow over Russia’s incursions into NATO nations

Officials did not say whether ⁠the drone was ⁠believed to be Ukrainian ‌or Russian. In recent months, Ukrainian drones have repeatedly entered NATO airspace in the Baltic region. Kyiv says they were steered off course by ⁠Russian signal jamming.
A drone alert was issued earlier in the capital Vilnius and surrounding region.
The Lithuanian army shared video ‌from the site of the crash, showing debris scattered in grass. Some of the parts appeared to be made from wood and some appeared charred.

Fighters ​with the NATO Baltic Air Defence mission have patrolled the skies of ⁠Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia since the Baltic countries joined ⁠the alliance in 2004. The mission's jets shot down stray ⁠Ukrainian ⁠drones over Estonia ​in May, and over Latvia in June and August.
Denmark reports encounter with Russian ship

Separately, Denmark said a Russian frigate fired two flares towards a Danish military helicopter on Monday. Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen called the incident "unacceptable" and said it could have endangered human lives.

Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the incident was serious but not surprising, calling it part of a ⁠pattern in which an increasingly aggressive Russia has intensified its hybrid warfare against Europe and is testing NATO.
How NATO is tracking airspace threats over eastern Europe
The Russian Embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The Baltic Sea region is on high alert after incidents involving gas pipeline ​outages, airspace violations and drone sightings.
Russia has dismissed accusations over such incidents and repeatedly denied carrying out hybrid attacks in Europe.

In fighting on Tuesday, a Russian drone attack ‌killed one person ​and knocked out ​power in parts ​of the ⁠city ⁠of Zaporizhzhia ‌in southeast Ukraine, the ⁠acting regional governor Mykhailo Semikin said.

As well, the regional governor of Odesa, Oleh Kiper, said that Russia hit port ‌infrastructure in ​Ukraine's southern ​Black Sea region overnight, ‌with residential buildings, ‌logistics facilities and transport infrastructure ​coming under attack.
‌Russian ​forces hit ​a cargo ship ​and ⁠a ⁠ferry ‌carrying ⁠military supplies ‌in ​Ukraine's ⁠port ⁠of Chornomorsk, ⁠the ⁠Russian Defence ​Ministry ⁠said on ⁠Tuesday.

U.S. President Donald Trump on Monday posted on social media that Russia and Ukraine had agreed "not to hit" each other's energy infrastructure. He had earlier called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian diesel infrastructure, saying ​the attacks were causing a shortage of the fuel that is "hurting ​the world."
Trump didn't offer further details on the purported agreement.
Zelenskyy said late Monday that Kyiv was "ready to support de-escalation," but expressed doubts Russia would adhere to such a demand.

articles.title: Democrats say supreme court rejection of Trump mail ballot restrictions will ensure ‘safe, secure and accurate elections’ – US politics live
articles.summary: Comments come after court on Monday rejected the president’s mail ballot restrictions ahead of the November midterm elections

blocks.text: Key events

items: 10m agoTrump facing AI backlash in Congress as push for guardrails intensifies
28m agoSupreme court rejection of Trump mail ballot restrictions will ensure 'safe, secure and accurate elections'

blocks.text: Trump facing AI backlash in Congress as push for guardrails intensifies

blocks.caption: David Smith

blocks.text: David Smith
Donald Trump is facing a rare backlash from the US Congress as Democrats and some Republicans push for guardrails on the world’s most powerful AI companies.
Concerns over the dangerous potential of AI reached fever pitch this week after tech leaders sounded the alarm over the rapid advancement of the technology and its potential threat to humanity.

Trump dismissed the anxieties on Monday, describing them as a “HOAX” and “conspiracy” and insisting on social media: “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!”

But the 80-year-old president, who has sidelined Congress on numerous issues during his second term, looks increasingly isolated as members of both major parties acknowledged the risks and expressed a desire to act before it was too late.

Don Beyer, a Democratic congressman from Virginia, said: “History will look very poorly on that tweet. He’s not paying attention – or he’s paying attention to the wrong people. He’s being really foolish: not the first time he’s been really foolish but perhaps catastrophically foolish in this case.”

Recent surveys by the University of Maryland’s Program for Public Consultation found 85% of Democrats and 79% of Republicans want a new federal agency to monitor and regulate AI; and 82% of Democrats and 78% of Republicans favour government safety tests for AI making critical decisions.
Supreme court rejection of Trump mail ballot restrictions will ensure 'safe, secure and accurate elections'
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Lawmakers have given their support to the supreme court’s rejection of Donald Trump’s bid to restrict mail ballots for the midterm elections.
The decision capped a flurry of last-minute legal action with voting already underway, with states allowed to continue sending out mail ballots under the same processes used for years.

Election officials have said there was simply no way to carry out a complete overhaul in the weeks before the midterms. Alabama, North Carolina and Wisconsin began sending mail ballots to voters over the past week while the new system was still not active.

Washington’s secretary of state Steve Hobbs, a Democrat, said the decision means work “to carry out a safe, secure, and accurate election” can continue ‘without having to upend our election processes to meet unrealistic ballot mail requirements.”

In Arizona, another largely vote-by-mail state, Democratic secretary of state Adrian Fontes said “it is crucial for us to continue rejecting the notion that access and security are mutually exclusive when it comes to running strong elections.”

Utah Lt Gov Deidre Henderson, a Republican serving as the state’s chief election officer, said on social media that the supreme court’s decision means “Utahns can have confidence that the 2026 election will proceed as normal.”
In other developments:

items: Mitch McConnell, the 84-year-old former Senate majority leader from Kentucky, was seen in Washington for the first time in months on Monday, minutes before his office released a statement saying that he was back at work.

With a slip of the tongue reminiscent of Joe Biden, Gavin Newsom, California’s Democratic governor, told CNN that he would not run for president in 2028 if his fellow Californian, former vice-president Kamala Harris, decides to run again, since “I know what that means: I know her base of supporters, I know her friends, the zen diagram on that is just pure crossover.”
Donald Trump claimed there is a “SICK conspiracy” against artificial intelligence and data centers in response to the growing calls for greater checks on AI development.

In a statement posted on social media, Barack Obama, the former US president, called for the pace of AI development to be slowed to allow time for the federal government to develop regulations to address “serious safety concerns”.

articles.title: Russian warship fires flares at Danish helicopter
articles.summary: Denmark has summoned Russia's ambassador over a Baltic Sea encounter that Copenhagen says is part of an increasingly aggressive pattern of Russian behavior.

image.caption: Denmark's military uses the related Fennec helicopter for tasks including surveillance and reconnaissanceImage: gemeinfrei

blocks.text: A Russian warship fired two flares toward a Danish military helicopter in the Baltic Sea, with one passing close to the aircraft, Denmark's armed forces said on Tuesday.
The confrontation comes amid heightened security concerns on NATO's eastern flank during Russia's war in Ukraine.
How has Denmark responded?
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the incident fitted a broader pattern of increasingly aggressive Russian behavior in Europe.
She accused Moscow of intensifying its "hybrid war against Europe" and testing and challenging NATO, and called on European countries to strengthen their defenses.

"Reckless action from Russia towards Danish military during a routine overflight yesterday. Russian actions are meant to intimidate and divide. They will not succeed. We will not waver," Frederiksen said in a statement on X.
Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen condemned the incident as "completely unacceptable" and summoned Russia's ambassador, saying the action could have put lives at risk.
The foreign minister accused Moscow of "gradually shifting the boundary for what they consider acceptable behaviour," adding: "That is something we cannot accept."
What happened in the Baltic Sea?
Denmark's armed forces said one of its Fennec helicopters was carrying out a routine photographic reconnaissance mission when the incident occurred.
The helicopter was observing a Russian frigate in international waters off Gedser, a Danish port on the Baltic Sea.
The Russian vessel fired two flares towards the helicopter, according to the Danish military.
"One of the flares passed at close range to the helicopter," it said. No one on board was injured.

The incident came against a backdrop of growing tensions along NATO's eastern flank. Poland has repeatedly scrambled fighter jets during Russian attacks on neighboring Ukraine and reported incursions by Russian drones into its airspace.

NATO members in the region have stepped up air patrols and other defenses as Moscow's war in Ukraine has increasingly raised fears of spillover and direct confrontations between Russian and alliance forces.

articles.title: Alberta referendum pitches more control over immigration. Here's what you need to know
articles.summary: Alberta's first of five immigration-related questions in the Oct. 19 referendum pitches more provincial control over immigration.

image.caption: People make their way to work in downtown Calgary in this file photo. (Evelyne Asselin/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Albertans will head to the polls on Oct. 19 to cast their votes on 10 questions put forward by the provincial government.
You’ve probably heard of the one related to separation. The other nine have received far less attention.
Five of the questions in the referendum will address immigration policies and could lead to major changes for newcomers to the province.
But both the questions and the process citizens face on voting day are unprecedented in Alberta and, it’s been argued, are also unfamiliar and complex.
CBC News is breaking down the referendum questions and providing some important context so you feel better prepared to vote.

The first immigration-related ballot voters will see is: “Do you support the government of Alberta taking increased control over immigration for the purposes of decreasing immigration to more sustainable levels, prioritizing economic migration and giving Albertans first priority on new employment opportunities?”
Let’s delve deeper into what the question is asking, how we got here, and what the full picture looks like when it comes to immigration to Alberta.

items: Follow all of our Alberta referendum coverage

blocks.text: Breaking down the question
If you come away from reading the 34-word question confused, you’re not alone. There are several aspects to that one sentence, so let’s break it down, bit by bit.
First, there’s the heart of the UCP government’s proposition: It’s asking you, the voter, whether the Government of Alberta should take increased control over immigration.

Immigration is a shared jurisdiction of the federal and provincial governments with federal paramountcy, so what’s implied here is that the province would have more say when it comes to newcomers entering Alberta.
Then, there’s this next bit: "for the purposes of decreasing immigration to more sustainable levels."
So, it seems the province wants to see fewer newcomers move to Alberta. But what exactly are the “sustainable levels” of immigration it’s trying to achieve?

When asked to define the phrase, Sam Blackett, the premier’s director of media relations, said: “Alberta supports balanced and sustainable immigration levels that maintain a strong focus on economic immigration to address skilled-labour shortages. Immigration levels should be responsive to our province’s current and future economic needs.”
The province hasn’t provided exact immigration targets it would consider “sustainable,” and experts tell us it’s a hard term to define. More on that later.
Let’s move on to the next point in the referendum question: “prioritizing economic migration.”

When the province says it wants to prioritize economic migration, it means it wants to attract skilled workers who already have the training and abilities to fill the specific needs of Alberta’s economy.
Those immigrants would take on skilled positions that are not being filled by Albertans or Canadians, the province clarifies in the FAQ section of its official referendum website.
Lastly, the referendum question suggests Alberta wants more control over immigration for the purpose of giving “Albertans first priority on new employment opportunities.”
The critical question here is: who is an "Albertan"?
The definition of "Canadian” is straightforward enough, because having citizenship determines whether someone is legally Canadian.

But the definition of "Albertan" is trickier to spell out. Canadians and permanent residents can move to Alberta from another province at any time and establish residency for health care and driving purposes after living in the province for 90 days.
When asked, the province did not define who it views as the “Albertans” who would be given priority for new employment opportunities, should the question receive a majority.
So, the first referendum question on immigration is a hefty one that comes with a complex history. Let’s get into that next.
How we got here

Over the past decade, Alberta has experienced a period of rapid growth. Its population increased by roughly 600,000 in the five-year period from July 2021 to July 2026, according to Statistics Canada.
Last year, the province crossed a total population of five million.
Two-thirds of that increased population comes from international migration (408,000) and 20 per cent from people coming to Alberta from other provinces (122,000), according to the federal agency.

Compared to the other major provinces (Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia), Alberta reached the highest growth rate over that period, which was in line with a national increase as the country welcomed more immigrants.
Alberta is still growing the fastest among the major provinces, though population growth has slowed down significantly.
In the five-year period of rapid growth, Alberta made efforts to bring more people into the province.

In 2022, the Government of Alberta under former premier Jason Kenney launched its “Alberta is Calling” campaign, initially aimed at attracting skilled workers from Toronto and Vancouver. In March 2023, it rolled out a second round of the ad campaign, this time targeting skilled workers from Ontario and Atlantic Canada.

items: Alberta isn't calling anymore because you're already here
Should Alberta take more control of immigration? This hyper-local rural program has some lessons

blocks.text: And then there’s the provincial nominee program that allows the province to nominate people for permanent residence, including skilled workers, entrepreneurs and others, based on economic priorities. Nominees may also include temporary foreign workers who already work in Alberta, as a way to transition them to permanent residency.
Each year, the allocation target is different. In 2026, it was 6,600 people.

In 2024, the allotment was closer to 10,000. In a letter that year, Smith called on former prime minister Justin Trudeau’s government to double the number of Alberta's federal immigration allotments to 20,000 and add 10,000 on top of that for Ukraine evacuees.
The province now says the current immigration level isn’t sustainable. And as with so many things, there's a mix of politics and policy at play.

The UCP government blames Trudeau’s “open border” immigration policy for bumping the number of newcomers, including “millions of individuals without the skills needed to fill our nation's and province's specific economic needs,” it says on its referendum website.

In 2024, Canada admitted 483,600 immigrants as permanent residents — the highest annual number recorded by Statistics Canada since 1972. The preliminary number of non-permanent residents living in Canada peaked at 3,149,000 on Oct. 1, 2024, according to the agency, which will update the number in September.

It wasn’t just Alberta pointing the finger. Trudeau-era policies have been widely criticized for an immigration increase, especially in the number of temporary foreign workers and international students (who largely make up the non-permanent resident pool) admitted to Canada.

But to say Trudeau had an "open border" policy isn’t accurate in the literal sense. That term typically refers to the free movement of people across international boundaries with minimal restriction — something the Liberal government of the day did not allow.

Another claim Alberta is making is that some employers have relied "far too heavily on temporary foreign workers to fill employment positions without giving Albertans and other Canadians adequate opportunity to secure those jobs first," according to the province's referendum FAQ online.

It’s important to remember here that in order for a Canadian employer to hire a temporary foreign worker to fill a position, they have to fill out a labour market impact assessment first to prove there are no Canadians available to take on that job.
Alberta's referendum website prompts complaints

All in all, the province says Ottawa’s “unsustainable” immigration policies have had a negative impact on Alberta’s ability to fund and deliver social services like health care and education, "directly impacting Albertans' access to these services and costing taxpayers billions of dollars."
For many Albertans grappling with the growing pains of a rising population, that message resonates.
Polls commissioned by CBC News in 2025 found over 60 per cent of Edmontonians and Calgarians felt their city was growing too fast.
Some have pinned the blame more directly on immigrants. At one of the province’s Alberta Next Panel events last year, the Lloydminster crowd cheered at the idea of mass deportations.
A recent poll commissioned by CBC News also found more than half of Albertans want the province to take a more active role in setting the rules for immigration.

Christopher Worswick, a labour economist and professor at Carleton University whose work explores the economics of immigration, said the policies that allowed the surge in temporary residents and immigrants to Canada have turned public sentiment against welcoming newcomers.

“I think that there was a sense that came out of that that the housing implications in particular, but also the health-care implications of providing services to this rapidly growing segment of the population under the immigration/temporary migration categories, sort of led people to think that this was too much,” he said.
“And so you started to see public opinion shifting away from … unconditional support for immigration.”
Immigration levels already on the decline
Data shows immigration is already on the decline, due in large part to the federal government.
That’s the first thing people need to know before answering the first question on the October ballot, according to Ethel Tungohan, an associate professor of politics at York University in Toronto.

“[Canada has] gone down from an expected 500,000 [permanent resident] admissions in 2025 to 395,000 admissions to now in 2026: 380,000 admissions. So already we are cutting back on immigration,” said Tungohan, the Canada Research Chair in Canadian migration policy, impacts and activism.

items: Alberta’s population is still growing despite Ottawa’s immigration crackdown: StatsCan

blocks.text: While Alberta is still growing the fastest amongst the major provinces, fewer immigrants are moving to Alberta. The number of immigrants who moved to the province in the first quarter of 2026 (11,100) fell by about 18 per cent from the same time last year, according to Statistics Canada.
Temporary resident targets reduced
Preliminary Statistics Canada data shows more temporary residents left the province than arrived over the past year, contributing to Alberta’s population growth slowdown.
Temporary residents are non-permanent residents, including international students and temporary foreign workers.
This past year, the province saw its lowest increase in population since 2021, at 0.94 per cent, according to Statistics Canada.

As of June, Alberta has about 260,000 temporary residents. Of those, 66 per cent were work permit holders (including some who also have a study permit). A little more than 14 per cent of Alberta’s non-permanent residents only hold a study permit, down from 27 per cent about five years ago.

items: Some Alberta international students speak out after being denied post-graduate work permits

blocks.text: Ottawa’s 2026-28 Immigration Levels Plan reduces the temporary resident target by almost half, from 673,650 in 2025 to 385,000 in 2026, and 370,000 in 2027 and 2028.
What exactly are 'sustainable' immigration levels?
Back to that question about "sustainable" immigration.
Kevin McQuillan, a research fellow at the University of Calgary’s School of Public Policy, says it’s a concept that’s not easy to define.

As Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government has made a “jarring cutback” to immigration through its policy changes, McQuillan reminds us that not everyone wants or benefits from lower immigration numbers.
Take universities and colleges, for example.
Last November, the University of Calgary told CBC News it was losing an estimated $34.7 million in 2025 due to the decline in international student enrolment.
Many post-secondary institutions built new residences or expanded programs, in part, for the large influx of international students who pay higher tuition than domestic students, McQuillan said.
Now, those institutions are "feeling a pinch," he said.
“The idea of ‘sustainable,’ I think in principle is a good one, but to translate that into exact targets I think is difficult."

items: Post-secondary institutions in Alberta cutting staff to deal with strained financial situations
University of Calgary faces $34.7 million shortfall amid more international student cuts

blocks.text: According to Worswick, “sustainable” is a fairly new term being used in immigration policy discourse to describe provincial and federal immigration targets.
“In the past, people would talk about absorptive capacity with respect to immigration,” he says.

An example of absorptive capacity is if Canada identified highly skilled immigrants who it thinks would likely find success in the labour market, the country may consider whether it can build new homes fast enough to house the new migrants, or if the health care system can be expanded quickly enough to absorb the additional load, Worswick explained.

A spokesperson for Lena Metlege Diab, the federal Minister of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship, says, “Our government and that of Alberta both agree on the need to restore sustainability to our immigration system and that’s exactly what Canada’s new government has been doing,” citing slowing population growth.

“We recently expanded the Provincial Nominee Program, giving provinces more control over the selection of immigrants. And, using existing powers, Alberta has already launched pathways for health-care workers, rural communities, law enforcement professionals, and entrepreneurs.”
LISTEN | Part one of a two-part documentary on Canada's political 180 on immigration:
Front Burner21:48Canada's immigration 180: Part 1
What your 'yes' or 'no' vote could mean
At the heart of this question is a tug of war between federal and provincial control over immigration.
Voting "yes" to the first referendum question means supporting Alberta's pitch to exert more power over how many newcomers — and which kind — are welcome to the province.

items: What some immigrants could lose if Alberta votes yes to Danielle Smith's questions

blocks.text: For Worswick, the question signals that Alberta could be looking to develop a more independent economic immigration program, akin to Quebec.

That province has a special agreement with the federal government that asks skilled workers who want to become permanent residents to apply to the Quebec government first, allowing the province to set immigration targets.

But Tungohan said a "yes" vote could have enormous implications, creating a "chilling effect" that drives residents, and subsequently businesses, away from the province if they view Alberta's heightened immigration control as creating a "hostile" environment.
"It is going to turn our backs away from Alberta's long and storied history of being a place ... of settlement and immigrant innovation."

items: Pollster says this demographic is one to watch in Alberta's independence debate

blocks.text: Already, the question has raised concerns among established immigrants in Alberta about whether they are welcome in the province they’ve called home for years.
Alberta’s Filipino community raising questions about its future ahead of referendum
Worswick said a “yes” vote could mean the public sentiment that has turned against newcomers could eventually turn again with a “stable, steady inflow” of immigrants and temporary residents.
But, he cautions that it largely depends on how the provincial government develops that policy if the referendum receives a majority.

In an online analysis of the referendum questions, the Alberta branch of the Canadian Bar Association notes that, "Giving Albertans first priority on new employment opportunities is legally problematic. All individuals (not only citizens) have equality rights under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms that prevent discrimination in hiring."
A “no” vote on the first referendum question means the voter would prefer to keep decision making on immigration primarily at the federal level, Worswick said.

“For example, if you're a resident of Alberta and you're not confident that the [provincial] governments that you see elected are going to do a good job of this, you might vote ‘no’ to say ‘I'm comfortable leaving this as a predominantly federal jurisdiction.’”
But he reminds voters that “the province deals with the problems” related to an increased population, not Ottawa.
“The province … should provide social housing and social assistance [and health care], and the federal government may or may not transfer funds,” Worswick said.
“A lot of these issues and housing all fall within either provincial or municipal levels. They're not really federal jurisdictions.”

blocks.text: These six leading candidates for sectoral representatives were chosen through the direct plurality of valid votes cast for nominees in their representative sectors. In every election cycle, the chosen representatives will rotate among the region’s six major non-Moro indigenous groups: the Teduray, Lambangian, Erumanen ne Menuvu, Dulangan Manobo, Blaan, and Limbubungan Higaonon.

articles.title: One of Sydney’s largest councils joins ban on ‘pervert’ glasses at local swimming pools
articles.summary:
Councillors say locals have been raising concerns about people secretly filming in change rooms, swimming pools and around schools

  • Get our

blocks.text: One of Sydney’s largest councils has joined the City of Brisbane and the City of Yarra to issue a ban on AI smart glasses at public pools as concerns mount over the potential for predators to exploit the new technology.
On Tuesday evening, Canterbury-Bankstown voted overwhelmingly in favour of banning the tech at its local pools, with its mayor, Bilal El-Hayek, describing them as “pervert glasses”.
Since their release, there have been reports of women being filmed without their consent and their interactions with a glasses-wearing influencer posted on social media.

“Chat groups, Facebook, local community forums and Tik Tok are just some of the online platforms where women are venting their concerns over the smart technology that threatens both safety and privacy,” El-Hayek told councillors at the meeting.
“Their biggest concerns are around ‘perverts and paedophiles’ secretly filming in change rooms, swimming pools and around schools.

“The latest AI smart glasses are wearable devices with high resolution cameras … and AI powered features like real time translation, object recognition and open-ear audio … these glasses can not only film, record and share footage, they can also scan your face and potentially access and retrieve information about you.”
Last month, Brisbane became the first council in Australia to publicly announce a ban on covert filming at its 21 public pools amid growing fears to protect child safety.

The head of policy at Digital Rights Watch, Tom Sulston, praised the decision. He said it was “vital that councils across Australia ensure that public spaces like swimming pools are safe for families to enjoy without the threat of unwanted video surveillance”.

“We all need to be able to go out in public without fear of being covertly recorded and having the images uploaded to the internet without our consent,” he said. “We look forward to seeing not just councils following Brisbane’s lead, but also state and federal governments.”

Yarra in inner Melbourne followed suit, voting last week to ban smart glasses from its leisure and aquatic facilities, childcare centres and playgrounds. It also confirmed it would call on the federal government to bring in stronger privacy laws to protect people from new technologies.

Randwick council in Sydney’s eastern suburbs has also banned the new technology at the Des Renford leisure centre. In a statement to Guardian Australia, it said “growing community concerns” about their potential misuse were behind the decision.

“Signage has been installed at the entrance and anyone wearing smart glasses in the centre will be asked to remove them or leave,” it said. “This precautionary measure will help ensure the centre remains a safe, welcoming and family-friendly place for all visitors.”
The bans will not apply to people with accessibility concerns, including vision impairment.
The federal attorney general, Michelle Rowland, has not ruled out banning the glasses but has indicated how complex the laws are governing the new technology.
In August, she wrote to the privacy commissioner, Carly Kind, raising concerns she’d received from the community about their growing uptake and requesting it be given priority consideration.
“Privacy is an essential part of all our lives; it allows us to be who we are with dignity and without fear,” she said at the time.
“Unlike other forms of technology, smart glasses may be used more discreetly, making it harder to know when you are being recorded.
“The government is continuing to work on the next phase of privacy reforms to ensure our privacy laws are fit for purpose in the digital age.”
Australia’s online safety regulator has urged smartglasses companies to automatically blur people’s faces filmed on the devices, and make it clearer when someone is filming.

In advice to industry published at the end of August, the office of the eSafety commissioner warned that while smartglasses with cameras, such as Meta’s Ray-Ban, can offer accessibility benefits to low vision or blind people, companies might pit “accessibility benefits against safety and privacy considerations”, and noted there was already a backlash to the technology.

blocks.text: Parts of the Netherlands, including Amsterdam, have been hit by major rail disruption after suspected sabotage to the tracks, the country's railway operator has said.
ProRail warned that passengers in the country's centre and north should expect cancellations and delays on Tuesday, while several level crossings were also malfunctioning.
Pipes were attached to the tracks in multiple locations, according to local media. In a statement, ProRail said the incident appeared to be "an intentional disruption... caused by human action".
It added that no suspects or motives had been identified, but the national police unit was investigating. The BBC has contacted police for comment.
The network's website showed that 15 disruptions had been recorded across the country on Tuesday, with routes to the main international airport, Schiphol, and Utrecht also affected.
ProRail said in a statement: "Materials were found at multiple locations in the track that were deliberately placed there. This causes section malfunctions. Sabotage appears to be involved".

Footage published by Dutch public broadcaster NOS on Tuesday showed police carrying what appeared to be metal pipes - about 1.5 metres (5ft) - away from railway tracks at Veenendaal in the central Netherlands.

articles.title: Australia’s Indigenous population estimated at 2.2m before ‘demographic catastrophe’ of colonisation
articles.summary:
Study finds earlier numbers were underestimated, suggesting impact of diseases and massacres were much greater than previously thought

  • Get our

blocks.text: The number of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in Australia before colonisation was dramatically underestimated, according to new research that suggests many more of them were killed.
Modelling by a national research group puts the population levels before the 1788 first fleet arrived at 2.2 million, compared with early estimates of 250,000 people.
The research, by the Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence for Indigenous and Environmental Histories and Futures (CIEHF), has been published in the peer-reviewed Nature Human Behaviour.

The authors wrote that, historically, population estimates have been poor “due to lethal diseases, frontier and structural violence, and absence of systematic censuses” and that it’s “invaluable to truth-telling and reconciliation” to try to rectify that.
They warn readers that the content of the study is confronting and possibly distressing.

The modelling showed there had to be millions of excess deaths from smallpox and other diseases, massacres, and the other results of colonisation such as dispossession and malnutrition, according to co-author Prof Corey Bradshaw, a global ecology professor at Flinders University.

His previous research found that an 1789 smallpox outbreak alone killed as many as 220,000 Aboriginal people. There were also other smallpox epidemics, as well as outbreaks of measles, influenza, tuberculosis, typhoid and other diseases.
Bradshaw said he would bet his career that massacre databases were underestimated by an “order of magnitude”.

“If you’re a frontier farmer, a colonialist that came out to a new area, and you were trying to remove people from ‘your’ land, you’re not going to write extensively about how many people you killed to do that,” he said.

“There’s another component here that’s essentially greed and racism – the entire concept of terra nullius was based on not many people being here. If there’s a systematic desire to take land [fewer people means a] better justification for imperialism.”

Australia was colonised on the basis of terra nullius, that it belonged to no one. That concept was overthrown with the high court’s Mabo decision, when it was recognised that First Nations people had been here for tens of thousands of years.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people were not properly counted in the census until 1971, after the 1967 referendum. A that point, 115,953 people identified as Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander.
In 2021, 812,728 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people were counted in the census, a figure revised upwards to 983,257 with post-census recounts.
The 2.2 million figure, as well as a new estimate of 2.06 million excess deaths between 1788 and 1861, means the population was reduced to about 7% of its original size.

“We are not talking about a marginal consequence of colonisation but a demographic catastrophe at the heart of the Australian story,” distinguished professor Larissa Behrendt said. A Euahleyai/Gamillaroi woman, she is also the chair of the CIEHF’s advisory committee.

Early on after colonisation, various people estimated how many Aboriginal people were in their region. For example, governor Arthur Phillip estimated Gadigal people of the Eora nation came to about 1,500.

The first continent-wide estimate by social anthropologist Alfred Radcliffe-Brown put the number between 250,000 and 300,000, but mainly used observations from after the impacts of colonisation had been felt.
after newsletter promotion

Radcliffe-Brown was aware that was an underestimate, but many researchers since have relied on that count as a baseline. Again, often recognising that it would be an undercount because of historical reasons and because changes in who identified/was identified as Aboriginal.

In 1983, economic historian Noel Butlin estimated the population at about 900,000. Later he increased that to between 1.1 million and 1.3 million. In 1987, archaeologists John Mulvaney and J. Peter White argued it was more likely 750,000.
There have been many and varied estimates since, usually based on historical and ethnographic information.

The Australian team used different approaches to model the population. They looked at archaeological items to reconstruct how many people would have been there at a particular time, reconstructed the climate and the productivity of the land to infer how many people it could sustain, and looked at genetic data to work back in time based on known DNA mutation rates.
They also reviewed, but did not rely on, ethnographic estimates.

“The findings highlight the scale of demographic catastrophe experienced by Indigenous Australians due to colonisation, with the implications being a heightened understanding of intergenerational trauma and to inform future policy that assists Indigenous people,” said co-author and distinguished professor Lynette Russell of the Monash University Indigenous Studies Centre and CIEHF.

The authors wrote that Australia must prioritise reconciliation, engagement and policymaking with Indigenous people who still suffer intergenerational trauma and that the broader community should embrace the rich culture that survived these events.

The lead author, James Cook University associate professor Alan Williams, said the “devastating findings” highlight the impacts of invasion. But they also demonstrate the “remarkable survival, resilience and recovery over the past century of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Island people”.
Behrendt said the research “tells us something extraordinary”.
“Our survival is one of Australian history’s most remarkable stories,” she said.

articles.title: N.S. families thought they buried their loved ones. Officials are now investigating
articles.summary: Nova Scotia officials are investigating after the new owners of a funeral home in the Annapolis Valley discovered the cremated remains of a “significant number” of people in storage, CBC News has…

image.caption: Kristina Sweeney says she was shocked to learn an urn was discovered with what's believed to be her mother's cremated remains. Sweeney's mother, Elizabeth Pelton, died in 2024 and a funeral was held at that time. (David Laughlin/CBC)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia·Exclusive

Nova Scotia officials are investigating after the new owners of a funeral home in the Annapolis Valley discovered the cremated remains of a “significant number” of people in storage, CBC News has learned. Several families were recently told ashes belonging to their dead loved ones had been found.
New funeral home owner discovers ‘significant number’ of human ashes in storage
· CBC News
· Posted: Sep 15, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago

The province and the Nova Scotia regulator of funeral directors are investigating after the new owners of an Annapolis Valley funeral home discovered the cremated remains of a “significant number” of people in storage, CBC News has learned.

It comes as several Nova Scotia families who used the services of Serenity Funeral Home say they were shocked and horrified to receive calls letting them know that ashes belonging to their dead loved ones had been found.
“I kind of started internally freaking out because I buried my mom in 2024,” said Kristina Sweeney.
“I don't even think the shock has worn off yet … I thought I buried my mom, all of her. I put her in the ground by myself.”

Sweeney wasn't the only one contacted by East Coast Memorial, which recently purchased the buildings from Serenity Funeral Home. Serenity’s head office and crematorium was located in the small community of Coldbrook. The company also had other locations in the Annapolis Valley.

Michelle Carey and her sister Amanda Sabean used Serenity when they buried what they believed were the cremated remains of their father, Hendrik (Hank) Sabean, in the spring of 2018. On Sept. 8, Carey was informed by East Coast Memorial that her father’s full remains were found in storage.
“Having to, you know, bury him and to do this all over again. It's really hard,” said Carey.
The sisters are also left wondering whose remains they buried.
“There’s a family out there that's missing remains of their family member,” said Sabean.

In an email, Andrew George, the owner of the new business East Coast Memorial, explained that his company discovered “a significant number of cremated remains that had been left in storage, some for many, many years.”

George said he and his staff are carefully reviewing the home’s information to “make every reasonable effort to locate and contact families so that these loved ones could be returned to their families or otherwise laid to rest appropriately.”
‘Dozens’ of other urns found, daughter told
Sweeney said when her mother, Elizabeth Pelton, died in 2024 at the age of 60, her body was cremated. Sweeney chose a green urn, which she received and buried.

This month, the employee of East Coast Memorial who returned what’s believed to be the rest of her mother’s ashes gave her a green urn with a different pattern. It had been identified with a sticky note label as her mother’s. Sweeney said the employee told her that there were “dozens” of other urns found.
Another family told CBC their loved one’s remains were delivered to them in a cardboard box.

Sweeney wrote a post on Facebook about her experience and started receiving responses from other families. They recounted similar experiences, believing that they had received and buried their loved ones. Then they were contacted by East Coast Memorial years later suggesting otherwise.
“Every single person I've spoken to was under the impression that they had taken care of all the remains,” Sweeney said. “They were either buried or they took the urn home.”

George said his company is still assessing all the cases and doing its due diligence “as thoroughly as possible for each family,” and so he isn’t able to say exactly how many persons’ remains were found.
Former owner responds

When CBC reached Tony Facey, a former owner of Serenity Funeral Home for 12 years until December 2025, he confirmed there was a “whole stack” of cremated remains dating back as far as 25 years that had never been claimed by families. He said unclaimed remains is a wider issue all funeral homes are dealing with, and this has been an ongoing discussion at the regulatory board. Facey declined an interview.
The president of the Funeral Service Association of Nova Scotia, Kollin Weatherbee, said he’s never heard of a funeral home keeping decades of unclaimed remains.
“It is unusual that a funeral home would hold a portion of someone's ashes without the family knowing,” he said.
Weatherbee added that if a funeral home held ashes for a family, it would only be for a matter of weeks.
And in situations where a next of kin can’t be identified or reached, he said the public trustee usually gets involved within the first 12 days of a death.
Provincial inspectors visit
The province licenses and regulates funeral homes through Service Nova Scotia, while an arm’s-length board licenses and regulates funeral home directors.

The province learned of the stored ashes on Sept. 9 when it was contacted by that board and George, the owner of East Coast Memorial. It assigned two provincial inspectors to visit the crematorium the next day to learn more.

Adam Tipert, the chair of the Nova Scotia Board of Registration of Embalmers and Funeral Directors, told CBC in an email the board is taking the concerns “very seriously” and will collaborate with Service Nova Scotia in its investigation as more information emerges.
The province and the board also conducted an investigation at Serenity Funeral Home in 2018, when the location in Berwick mixed up the bodies of two women. A funeral director had his licence revoked.
That case eventually led to a change in the legislation surrounding funeral homes in 2025.

items: Family horrified after funeral home mixes up bodies, cremates wrong one
New law coming aimed at preventing body mix-ups at funeral homes

blocks.text: A provincial spokesperson said Serenity was routinely inspected in 2022, and some non-compliant administrative matters were resolved.
Following the sale to East Coast Memorial, Serenity is no longer licensed to operate funeral homes in Nova Scotia.
George said right now he is keeping focused on doing what is right for the families.

“We do not want to speculate about decisions or practices that occurred before our involvement,” he said, adding that his company will treat the remains with respect and dignity, as they were “received into our care when we acquired Serenity.”
George said his company is making plans for a community burial ceremony for any remains that can’t be reunited with a family, or if the families direct his company to do so.
Hank Sabean’s daughters still have many unanswered questions, especially since their father had been so clear about his own funeral arrangements and being laid to rest with his family.
“He had strong morals and values, and I know that he would think that this is so wrong that this could happen,” said Carey.
Kristina Sweeney said her mother would also be “really, really disgusted.”
“I felt like my mom and I had been violated,” she said. “I expect when someone passes away that, and I'm sure most people do, they're treated with dignity and respect.”

articles.title: China tightens travel rules over tech security
articles.summary: Beijing says the new rules, which could also apply to foreign and Taiwanese nationals, are aimed at safeguarding "national security."

image.caption: The restrictions come amid a technological arms race between China and the USImage: Wang Yu/Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: Sweeping travel restrictions on Chinese citizens came into effect on Tuesday, including exit bans for people considered to have endangered China's "industrial or technological security."
The new exit-and-entry rules, which were passed in July, apply to citizens deemed to have violated technology import and export regulations, particularly in the field of artificial intelligence.
The State Council in Beijing said the new rules were formulated to "safeguard national sovereignty, security, and development interests."
The regulations apply not only to people within China but also to Chinese citizens deemed to have committed criminal acts abroad.
In such cases, citizens could be "prohibited from leaving the country for a period of six months to three years from the date of their return to China," said the State Council.
Travel bans give Beijing 'wide remit'
The restrictions come as China remains locked in a technological arms race with the United States, with both countries accusing each other of stealing locally developed AI models in recent months.
And analysts warn that the full scope of the new rules will only become clear once they start being implemented.

Security and criminal activities "can be vaguely defined and easily adjusted," said Chong Ja Ian, an analyst from the National University of Singapore, telling the AFP news agency that Beijing has given itself a "wide remit."
Hong Kong activist pleads guilty to foreign collusion
Will China's new travel bans affect foreigners?
Under the new regulations, foreign nationals could also be denied entry to China for up to five years if found to have made false statements in ​visa applications.
Foreign governments have often reported instances of citizens being denied permission to leave China due ⁠to security-related ​investigations.
Analyst Chong highlighted the recent case of US citizen Min Zin who the US government said was detained improperly in Yunnan province in June.
"The case of Min Zin is a reminder that the range of people [that Beijing] could restrict from exiting could be quite wide – and potentially arbitrary," he said.

blocks.caption: Analysts warn it could take some time before the full scope of the new rules becomes clearImage: Tetiana Chernykova/Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: Chinese travel bans: Taiwan warns citizens
The new rules could have particular implications for Taiwanese nationals who work in the tech sector and who travel between Taiwan and China.
Authorities in Taipei have warned citizens to take extra care on visits to China, which considers people from Taiwan to be Chinese citizens.
Beijing has dismissed any such concerns, claiming the rules provide better legal protection for Taiwanese.

Dylan Loh, an associate professor at Singapore's Nanyang Technological University, told AFP the travel restrictions "send a message" that China will take action to prevent "leaks in security or national interest-sensitive areas."

articles.title: Netherlands: Suspected sabotage disrupts train services
articles.summary: A major outage has hit parts of the Dutch railway system after objects were found placed across lines, authorities say. The company responsible for rail infrastructure says it suspects deliberate…

image.caption: The disruption began during Tuesday's morning rush hourImage: Vincent Jannink/ANP/IMAGO

blocks.text: Train services in various parts of the Netherlands have been severely disrupted, with ProRail, the company that maintains the nation's rail infrastructure, saying that sabotage was possibly at play.
National railway company NS said that train services around the central cities of Zwolle, Deventer and Amersfoort have been affected since the morning rush hour.

blocks.caption: The national railway company said it is not clear when services can resumeImage: Vincent Jannink/ANP/IMAGO

blocks.text: What do we know about the causes of the disruption?

In a statement, rail authority ProRail said that "[m]aterials deliberately placed on the tracks have been found at several locations. This is causing track-circuit failures. It appears to be a case of sabotage."
The ‌objects caused failures ‌across ​the network, affecting several level crossings, which disrupted ​road traffic, Pro Rail said.
ProRail ​workers ​were clearing the ​objects and ‌working to restore safe conditions, it ​added.
Though the company itself did not say what the "materials" were, a ProRail spokesperson told the daily de Volkskrant that "pipes had been found attached to the line" in several places.
This caused the disruptions, as the railway security systems can register a train's presence on a line because of an object placed on it and thus block access for other trains.
The spokesperson told the paper that one train had even collided with one of the pipes laid on the tracks, but that no accident or injuries had occurred.

blocks.caption: The disruption originated at 13 locations on tracks in the central NetherlandsImage: Vincent Jannink/ANP/IMAGO

blocks.text: Important event in The Hague
It remains unknown whether the incident has to do with so-called Prinsjesdag, the day the Dutch government presents its annual budget to parliament, where the reigning monarch gives a speech.
On the day, thousands of people go to The Hague to watch the royal family ride through the city in horse-drawn carriages.
