articles.title: Why AI researchers warn humanity could face extinction
articles.summary: Could artificial intelligence pose an existential threat to humanity? Some leading researchers are warning against an unregulated race toward AI superintelligence.

image.caption: Some researchers argue that artificial general intelligence could pose unforeseeable risksImage: Marc Asensio/NurPhoto/IMAGO

blocks.text: Dramatic warnings about the existential risks posed by artificial intelligence to humanity are nothing new.
As early as the 1940s, the renowned scientist and science fiction author Isaac Asimov explored potential risks and unintended consequences of intelligent machines.
In 1991, Hollywood blockbuster "Terminator 2" imagined a dystopian 2029 in which an out-of-control military AI called Skynet directs killer robots in a war against humanity.
If the warnings of several of the biggest names in AI are to be believed, a similar scenario could become a reality — even before 2029.

blocks.caption: The opening sequence of 'Terminator 2' depicts a dystopian future where AI has spiraled out of control and turned against humanityImage: Columbia/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Growing calls for strict regulation
"The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade," AI researcher Jacob Coxon posted on X last week, without exactly explaining how it might happen.
"No other human activity poses this level of danger," he added.

Coxon also revealed that he had quit his job at Anthropic, a US-based AI company, in protest against what he saw as an irresponsible race among AI companies to develop an ever better, self-improving superintelligence.

He warned that algorithms could begin to analyze and improve their own source code independently, which could shrink development cycles from several months to just a few minutes and thus make them uncontrollable.

Coxon is not an isolated voice. Nobel Prize-winning physicist Geoffrey Hinton, often called the "Godfather of AI," has been warning for years about the serious consequences of artificial superintelligence.

In 2023, he left his job at Google to publicly warn of the dangers of AI technologies he helped pioneer. Yoshua Bengio, a pioneer of artificial neural networks and deep learning, has also expressed concern about current developments and called for government regulation.

As recently as July 2026, more than 1,000 employees of leading AI companies warned in an open letter of an imminent loss of control if the race for "superintelligence" were not subject to significantly stricter regulations.
Caught in an unregulated race?
Despite the growing warnings, US President Donald Trump's administration has clearly shifted its AI policy toward minimizing regulatory hurdles and accelerating AI development.

In his X post, Jacob Coxon indirectly criticized the consequences of this policy: "At OpenAI, many have not deeply internalized the civilizational stakes. At Anthropic, the stakes are well-understood, but they are locked in a race to get there first — they believe no one else will act responsibly, so they must do it themselves, despite the risk."
Coxon, who had moved from OpenAI to Anthropic in early 2026, is familiar with both corporate cultures.
In an interview with The Wall Street Journal, he said that under the "most aggressive scenarios," things could spiral out of control as early as the end of 2027.
America's AI boom: Who pays the price?
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, for his part, is currently calling for a coordinated, industry-wide slowdown in development to buy time to address the risks and prevent any misuse of AI.

In a lengthy essay shared on X over the weekend, he wrote that in six to 12 months, AI agents "could be capable ​of taking over the entire internet" and potentially cause "hundreds of billions of dollars in damage" without proper guardrails.
Both Elon Musk, who runs xAI, and Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, said they agree with Amodei.
The alignment problem

In recent years, numerous experts have voiced concern about the rapid AI advances, particularly the development of artificial general intelligence, which refers to systems that not only solve individual tasks but also match or exceed human intellectual capabilities in nearly all areas.
Sophisticated AI models, for instance, may pursue goals in ways that diverge from human intentions, something AI security researchers refer to as the "alignment problem."
On top of that, even developers can't always fully understand how AI makes certain decisions.
And so, it's no surprise that Coxon's former colleague Evan Hubinger came to his defense.

"Jacob is correct here — we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," Hubinger, who himself is the team lead for alignment stress tests at Anthropic, wrote on X.

In his post, Hubinger made clear that Anthropic hasn't yet found a solution to the alignment problem and warned that an AI model might begin to resist being shut down, because that would limit its ability to achieve its programmed goal.
Exaggerated hysteria?
Other AI experts, however, consider such doomsday scenarios to be extremely unlikely.
Among the most prominent critics of the so-called AI doomers is Meta's chief scientist, Yann LeCun. In October 2024, he dismissed such concerns as "complete nonsense."
Still, other experts note that developing AI systems requires enormous amounts of computing power, energy, data and infrastructure.
They argue that an AI model cannot simply take over the world because it would need to rely on servers, power grids, communication systems and physical resources that are controlled by humans.
China's humanoid robots put to the test
Does the real danger lie elsewhere?
In fact, many experts see the short-term risks not so much in the extinction of humanity as in the numerous indirect consequences of AI systems that already exist even without superintelligence.
These include disinformation campaigns on an unprecedented scale and the related manipulation of democratic processes, an expansion of mass surveillance, and job losses across numerous industries.

Just last week, Anthropic revealed that there had been several attempts by users to misuse its Claude AI models for research that could support biological weapons development. The company said it had banned the accounts involved.
In August, Meta, Anthropic and OpenAI caused a stir when they announced that their AI systems had unintentionally carried out autonomous hacking activities.
Following reports of further AI hacking attacks during testing, even top US AI frontier labs are now expressing a willingness to slow down the development of the technology.
This piece was originally published in German.

articles.title: COVID-19 benefit repayment is hurting low-income Canadians, report says

image.caption: The Canada Revenue Agency reported that as of last November, it was owed more than $10 billion in COVID-19 benefits paid out to those who were ineligible. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Over six years after the COVID-19 pandemic began, the federal government is still trying to track down billions of dollars sent to Canadians who were later found to be ineligible for benefits. According to a new report, much of that burden still rests on low-income Canadians.
Think-tank says collecting debts from ineligible recipients is costly, ineffective
Over six years after the COVID-19 pandemic started, the federal government is still trying to track down billions of dollars sent to Canadians who were later found to be ineligible for benefits.

According to a report from Maytree, a think-tank and advocacy group that studies poverty, those recollection efforts disproportionately affect low-income Canadians who can't pay, and ultimately cost more than they recover.
It calls for an end to the government's efforts to recover pandemic benefits.

In total, Ottawa distributed about $14 billion in COVID-related benefits to individuals who didn't meet the Canada Revenue Agency's income requirements. Most of that sum was provided under the Canada emergency response benefit (CERB) and later the Canada recovery benefit (CRB).

By the end of last November, the CRA reported that $10 billion was outstanding, over $8 billion of which was owed on CERB and CRB payouts. CBC News reached out to the CRA for updated figures, but the agency was unable to provide them after more than two weeks of requests.

items: CRA says it's owed $10 billion in COVID-related benefits sent to ineligible recipients

blocks.text: "This is not a story about fraud," the report says. "It is a story about what happens when a government moves fast, makes mistakes and then hands the bill to the people least able to pay it."
John Stapleton, co-author of the Maytree report and a social policy expert, says his group acknowledges some people knowingly applied for benefits they shouldn't have received.
"We're not asking them to absolve those people," he said. "[But] there's some people out there that got caught in this net who are really suffering as a result."
In Budget 2025, Ottawa provided $123 million to support the government's collection of its pandemic response benefits over two years, starting in 2026-27.
According to Stapleton and Tyler Meredith, a senior fellow at the Munk School of Public Policy and a fellow at Maytree, many Canadians who still owe a debt on pandemic benefits are low-income.
"By the time you asked them to repay that benefit, they would have already, frankly, used that money," Meredith said.
Meredith was the head of economic and fiscal policy under former prime minister Justin Trudeau and a main architect of the federal government's economic response to the COVID-19 pandemic.
"It was always clear, I would argue, that the intent of the program was to be for people who had lost income," Meredith said.
While he said the government needed to provide certainty to Canadians that support was there if they needed it, the program was misunderstood as a form of universal income.

items: CRA reversed $246M in pandemic benefit debts after thousands contested eligibility status
Canadians told to pay back CERB say eligibility requirements were unclear

blocks.text: "Most people don't check the fine print," Meredith said.

CERB was in place from March to October 2020. Applicants had to have earned at least $5,000 in income in the last 12 months, lost income as a result of the pandemic and not been receiving EI in order to be eligible. They received $2,000 every four weeks.
CERB 'didn't have a plan for recovery'
Meredith said the government didn't have a plan to recover ineligible benefit payouts when it was initially launching its pandemic relief programs.
"Our goal, in all of the programs we were designing, was to have something that was like 80 to 85 per cent ready, knowing that we would amend and adjust the program as we went," Meredith said.
"We just didn't have time to wait."

According to Meredith, the government's initial plan was to deliver benefits by traditional means like through the quarterly GST tax credit — now the groceries and essentials benefit — or Canada's employment insurance system. But Meredith said the EI system would have been overwhelmed as millions of Canadians were set to lose work during the pandemic.
Because of this, the government drafted the Canada Emergency Response Benefit Act to create a new system, legislation Meredith said was put together in "a matter of a couple days."

items: Federal COVID-19 vaccine, benefits rollout swift but wasteful: AG
More than 1,000 Canadians take CRA to court over pandemic payments — and some win

blocks.text: The government allows for interest-free repayment over time.

But CERB's legislation "doesn't have a mechanism inside it to say the government is permitted, or CRA's officials are permitted, to entertain some form of settlement," Meredith said. "From their point of view, their hands are tied."

"The Federal Court has confirmed that the CRA is required to apply the eligibility criteria established by legislation and does not have discretion to depart from those requirements," the CRA told CBC News in a written statement.

The CRA said it is not legally obligated to pursue all ineligible CERB payments. According to Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC), the CRA can allow payment deferrals if a client is facing financial hardship. If it determines that hardship is permanent, the CRA can recommend a debt for writeoff to ESDC.
Can Ottawa dissolve the debt?

But Meredith says simply writing off the remaining debt owed by those ineligible for benefits is "not a realistic option" and "probably politically unpalatable for any government, at any point in time."

He pointed to the government's use of partial forgiveness on loans from the Canada emergency business account program (CEBA) as a possible guide, and suggested it develop an option to "spread out repayment costs over a much longer period of time."

items: Businesses need to pay CEBA loans or lose free money — because the deadline isn't changing

blocks.text: In its report, Maytree outlined a plan to wind down the collection of pandemic benefits along a suggested timeline. It also recommended the Office of the Parliamentary Budget Officer examine the cost of the government's collection efforts.
Other recommendations include amending the Income Tax Act to give the CRA discretion to make deals on the remaining debt and for the CRA to resolve over 1,200 outstanding cases by the end of 2026.
"I think it's incumbent upon government to set out a framework," Meredith said.

"Up to now, they've largely avoided making or entertaining any of that, both because there will eventually be some fiscal costs associated with doing so, but also because, I think the reality is people have harsh attitudes towards this.… If you used a program that you shouldn't have, they don't think that you're deserving usually of amnesty."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
David Cummings is a reporter for CBC News.

articles.title: Denmark summons Russia’s ambassador after warship fires flares at Danish army helicopter – Europe live
articles.summary:
Danish PM says action was ‘reckless’ as Moscow-attributed security incidents continue to intensify across Europe

Separately, Dutch authorities are investigating a major outage that…

blocks.text: Morning opening: Russia-attributed security incidents intensify across Europe

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa
Denmark has summoned Russia’s ambassador after a Russian warship fired two emergency flares at a Danish army’s helicopter in the Baltic Sea in the latest of incidents attributed to Moscow.
The incident took place during what Denmark said was “a routine” monitoring of the frigate.

“Reckless action from Russia towards Danish military during a routine overflight yesterday. Russian actions are meant to intimidate and divide. They will not succeed. We will not waver,” prime minister Mette Frederiksen said.

blocks.caption: Denmark's prime minister Mette Frederiksen, leader of Denmark's Social Democrats. Photograph: Henning Bagger/Ritzau Scanpix/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Denmark’s foreign minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said the frigate’s behaviour was “completely unacceptable.”
The incident took place amid worsening security situation in Europe.
Separately, Nato fighter jets stationed on the alliance’s eastern flank shot down a drone – believed to be flying from Belarus – over Lithuania last night.
“With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region,” Lithuania’s president Gitanas Nausėda said.
Meanwhile, Poland discovered remains of a suspected Russian drone near its Baltic Sea coast, just a day after a Russian drone hit a train on Ukraine’s border with Poland on Sunday.
It’s Tuesday, 15 September 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.
Key events

items: 4m agoLithuania briefs EU, Nato allies about drone incident, minister says
27m agoSuspected sabotage disrupts Dutch trains
30m agoDanish incident further proof of Russia's 'aggressive' behaviour, former Danish defence minister warns
32m agoMorning opening: Russia-attributed security incidents intensify across Europe

blocks.text: Lithuania briefs EU, Nato allies about drone incident, minister says
Meanwhile, Lithuanian defence minister Kęstutis Budrys said he informed Nato allies about last night’s drone incident, with discussions now ongoing on how to strengthen the alliance’s eastern flank.

blocks.caption: Military police and response vehicles stand parked near the site where a NATO fighter jet shot down a drone near Pratkunai village, Lithuania. Photograph: Lithuanian Army/Reuters

blocks.text: He said Lithuania will be “requesting discussions on these topics both in the EU and Nato, because it is obvious that we all still have a lot of homework to do,” Lithuanian public broadcaster LRT reported.
The drone was shot down by Italian fighter jets taking part in a Nato mission, Italy’s defence ministry confirmed.
Suspected sabotage disrupts Dutch trains
Separately, Dutch authorities are investigating a major outage that affected parts of the country’s railway system, suspecting a possible sabotage after objects were placed on tracks.

blocks.caption: Passenger information at Zwolle station. No trains are running in parts of the country due to a disruption that originated at 13 locations on the tracks in the central Netherlands. Photograph: ANP/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The objects caused failures across the network, affecting several level crossings which ‌disrupted road traffic, Dutch rail infrastructure operator Pro Rail said ​in a statement.
It explained that as a result, “our computer system identifies a section of track as occupied, even though there is no train present.”
“Because safety always comes first, signals automatically turn red. As a result, trains must stop or slow down. Level crossings can also malfunction,” it said.
It did not comment on who could be behind the incident.
Danish incident further proof of Russia's 'aggressive' behaviour, former Danish defence minister warns
Former Danish defence minister Troels Lund Poulsen warned that the frigate incident was a further proof of Russia’s “extremely aggressive” behaviour seeking to “provoke potential conflicts.”
“We should be very aware of that,” he said in comments reported by Danish broadcaster DR.
Defence minister Jeppe Bruus called an all-party meeting on the incident this morning to give political leaders a more detailed read on what happened, DR said.

articles.title: Chocolate faces more climate shocks as study highlights risk of extreme rainfall
articles.summary: As West African cocoa farmers feel the pain of drought, aging trees and competition for farmland, new research out of Harvard says extreme rain is an under-appreciated danger — often hammering…

image.caption: The road to chocolate starts with these beans, and they face many threats including too much rain during the wet season, says a new study. (Francis Kokoroko/Reuters)

blocks.text: As stores around the country trot out hyper-bright boxes of bite-sized chocolate for Halloween, a new peer-reviewed study says there's an underappreciated threat that cocoa production faces.
"People have tended to focus on heat and drought as the main climate risks, and those do matter," said Anna Lea Albright, who led this research as an environmental fellow at Harvard University.
"But what we found is that the strongest weather risk to cocoa is actually heavy rainfall."

Cocoa prices have shot up in recent years and consumers have felt it. Today, a tonne of cocoa hovers around $6,000 US, from a relatively long period of trading around $2,000 to $3,000 US per tonne since 2014. In 2024, the price shot up to over $12,000 US. That was triggered by multiple factors including heavy flooding in West Africa, where more than two million farmers help make it the world's biggest cocoa-growing region.
Boo! Chocolate prices are haunting Halloween shoppers
Leslie Agyare, founder of Three Mountains Cocoa, which works with thousands of farmers in a mountainous region of Ghana, says the rainfall has been a real challenge this year.
"Just imagine, you manage your whole crop, then it's raining so much and you can't harvest because the rains are just too much," Agyare told CBC News from London, England.

But even as climate change, driven by humanity's burning of fossil fuels, is expected to make extreme rainfall events worse, the authors say there are ways to mitigate the impact on this crop that billions of people enjoy.
The risks of rain

The study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, focused on Ghana, the world's second largest producer of cocoa. Using newly available district-level data on production, the authors compared that to rainfall and temperature data.

"When we did that pairing, extreme rainfall during flowering stood out as limiting yields, much more so than temperature during those months," Albright told CBC News from Paris. While cocoa trees need this moisture during the wet season, too much of it can damage the sensitive flowers and young pods.

Wet conditions, Albright says, can also lead to more fungal infections — such as black pod disease — that are spread by splashing rain. The connection between extreme rain and lower yields was also found when the team looked at other cocoa-producing countries, Ecuador and Indonesia.
The research also found a clear climate signal, as warmer air holds more moisture.
"In the satellite record, in rain gauges, we see [evidence] over the past few decades that the heaviest rain events during the wet season are indeed becoming more intense," Albright said.
It's worth noting that in West Africa, El Niño typically reduces the risk of extreme rain but raises the chance of drought, which the region is expecting.
"Now there is a dry period — when they need the rain, there is no rain," Agyare said.
Losing ground

While underappreciated, extreme rainfall's impact on crops isn't a new danger. The study also points out non-climactic risks like aging trees and illegal gold mining, which the UN Food and Agriculture Organization says is part of multiple threats to cocoa production.

Still, Sophia Carodenuto, environmental governance expert and associate professor at the University of Victoria, appreciates the study's findings, but says the key question remains about what farmers can do about it.

"You cannot stop rain, especially extreme rainfall," Carodenuto said, acknowledging the authors hinted at potential interventions involving fungicide and better drainage to mitigate spread of fungal diseases.
For Agyare, the solution requires serious infrastructure investment.
"For some areas that we work with, once it rains, the farmers are trapped in that area," he said. "These are kids that can't go to school. These are families that are stuck."
Many farmers also don't have reservoirs to save some of that rainwater for later use. But a major issue, Agyare says, is a system that puts too much work on the farmer.

"In Ghana, they have two issues. The farmers farm, then they do all the post-harvest themselves," he said, suggesting that splitting the post-harvest duties with other labourers would allow farmers to focus on growing only.
This would allow for collection and processing to be done in a centralized area, avoiding the losses that come from farmers drying their beans on the land and losing them during torrential rains.
A cocoa-free future?
These climate shocks, experts say, are making the job of cocoa farming unattractive in West Africa, and a lot harder.

"I think smallholder farmers are going to be a thing of the past," Agyare said, adding that children don't want to get into what their parents are doing and prefer to find opportunities in the cities.

Carodenuto questions whether adapting to the changing climate will eventually be too much, forcing people out of the job. That will add to the price volatility, which won't just edge out farmers, but push chocolate producers to ditch cocoa in chocolate altogether.

"It's been [a] completely crazy spike in price that I think was a major instigator for a lot of the innovation around cocoa-free chocolate," she told CBC News from Graz, Austria, adding that alternative chocolate is being promoted as less vulnerable, with a more resilient supply chain.

Earlier this year, the world's largest food company, Nestlé, entered the space, partnering with a German cocoa-free chocolate startup. That company makes ChoViva, an alternative that uses sunflower seeds, which Carodenuto says is attractive in terms of supply chain control because it's grown in Europe.
Even a significant rise in price, she says, won't result in a better future for the people who grow and harvest cocoa.
"Chocolate, especially the type of chocolate that you give out for trick-or-treating at Halloween, it's been so historically underpriced," Carodenuto said.
"And who's been footing that bill? It has been smallholder farmers in West Africa."

articles.title: Iran and US: Two countries and the pistachio between them
articles.summary: The pistachios sold across the United States have a surprising history: California's trees trace their roots to Iran. Now, both regions face the same threat — their farmland is sinking as groundwater…

image.caption: Pistachios like these sold across the US trace their roots back to IranImage: Svetlanasf/Pond5 Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: Hand-width cracks crisscross Armin's pistachio orchard in southeastern Iran, damaging irrigation pipes and swallowing precious water as the ground beneath him sinks.

"You look, and the earth has opened its mouth, and the water just pours in," Armin says. He has seen the cracks spread rapidly over the past five years, and worries that his children may not be able to work the land as his father and grandfather did before him.

Armin, whose real name DW has chosen not to reveal for security reasons, lives in the arid region of Rafsanjan. For generations, farmers there have cultivated the pistachio tree for its small green edible seed used in everything from ice cream to the viral Dubai chocolate.

The region has long covered much of the world's demand for pistachios, but a combination of drought and groundwater extraction for irrigation has made Rafsanjan one of the fastest-sinking areas in Iran. One study found parts of the ground are dropping by up to 37 centimeters (14 inches) annually. And that is impacting production.

It's a similar picture in California, where some pistachio farmers are also seeing their ground sink. Joe Coelho's family has cultivated the crop since 2000, and he says while his farm in Fresno is not directly affected, "growers are very aware of the risk."

Some areas nearby are facing serious water problems, says Coelho, who is the director of sustainability at American Pistachio Growers. "Subsidence is absolutely a serious issue in parts of the San Joaquin Valley."

blocks.caption: A pistachio orchard in California's Central Valley, now the world's largest producing regionImage: Photosoundsplanet/Pond5 Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: The same pistachio and the same problems

The link between growers in the two countries goes back to the 1960s when US famers started building a pistachio industry. They did it using an Iranian variety — the pistachio that now dominates most Californian orchards is called Kerman, named after a city near Armin's farm.

California has recently overtaken Iran as the world's largest pistachio producer, with most of the crop grown in the Central Valley, where Coelho has his orchard. And though it is one of the world's most productive farming regions, there are places where the ground is sinking by as much as 20 centimeters a year.
Like in Iran, the problem is that more water is being pumped from underground aquifers for crop irrigation than is flowing back in.

"As surface water reliability has declined, growers have relied more heavily on groundwater," Coelho told DW, adding that he has witnessed the land change. "In certain areas, the soil does not have the same structure or water movement it once had."
Pistachio orchards in the Central Valley use around 4% of the valley's crop water. In Rafsanjan, more than nine in 10 liters of groundwater go to pistachio orchards.
As groundwater levels drop from overpumping, spaces within the aquifer collapse, and the earth above begins to sink in a process called land subsidence.

"Land subsidence in Iran is a man-made hazard, not a natural one like an earthquake," says Ali Beitollahi, who leads subsidence research at Iran's Road, Housing and Urban Development Research Center. "Much of the damage cannot be undone. When an aquifer collapses, it can never hold as much water again as before."

Older farmers in Rafsanjan remember reaching water at depths of just 20 meters (66 feet), says Armin. Today, many have to drill down to 300 meters. Some farmlands near Armin's are dead or dying, he says, while other orchards have been abandoned as wells dried up.

It's another blow to the struggling farmers, who says the boom driven by food trends like Dubai chocolate never reaches them because international sanctions and global competition have stripped Iran of the markets it once held as the world's biggest pistachio producer.
"We used to be known for quality," he says. "Now we are known for the low price."

blocks.caption: Ripening pistachios in Wasco, California, where growers, like farmers in Rafsanjan, are pumping more groundwater than flows back in and watching their land sinkImage: Ashley Cooper/Pond5 Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: Two pistachio regions, two different responses
The biggest difference between the two regions is how they are responding to the crisis.
In California, the Sustainable Groundwater Management Act (SGMA), passed in 2014, requires water agencies to balance pumping and recharge in groundwater basins by 2040.

Managed aquifer recharge is one method the state is using to do so. It entails allowing water to recharge aquifers in rainy years, by flooding farmlands for instance, as a store for drought. Coelho is taking part in a pilot project that does just that.

SGMA has seen some progress. According to California's Department of Water Resources, groundwater levels have risen in four out of 10 monitored wells. But large parts of the Central Valley are still sinking.
Helen Dahlke, professor of integrated hydrologic sciences at the University of California, Davis, says recharge alone is not likely to offset decades of overexploitation of groundwater.

"Agriculture is by far the largest consumptive use of water in the Central Valley, so bringing groundwater basins into balance will likely require aligning crop water demand with the long-term water available under a warmer and more variable climate."

In Iran, awareness of groundwater management and subsidence has grown over the past decade among scientists but remains limited, says Ali Beitollahi. He worked on draft subsidence regulations that are currently awaiting government approval.

Pointing to the example of Japan's capital Tokyo where subsidence rates fell dramatically after authorities restricted groundwater pumping, he believes the problem could be managed if the state were to act quickly. Though given the current political situation in Iran, swift action is unlikely.
Another urgent step, he says, "is changing how farmers water their fields immediately, and teaching them why it matters."
Most of Rafsanjan's orchards are still flood-irrigated, meaning large amounts of water are lost to evaporation before it reaches plant roots.
Armin says he is trying to learn from US growers, but that many older farmers are set in their ways.

blocks.caption: Rows of pistachio trees in California's Central Valley, where in some areas the ground is sinking by as much as 20 centimeters a yearImage: Photosoundsplanet/Pond5 Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: The meaning of a pistachio
Across California's Central Valley, the pressures of a warming climate, drought and diminishing groundwater are hard to ignore.
"We live with it every day," Coelho says, adding that California's pistachio farmers also need better water policy as well as better infrastructure and protection of water rights.
"Financial sustainability, water sustainability and environmental sustainability are connected," he told DW.

Armin doesn't see a future in pistachio farming. But when he looks at a single pistachio, he sees more than a crop competing for water or a snack on a shelf half a world away. He sees the history and the present of his family and his region.
"This pistachio sometimes comes from a tree 100 years old," he says. "It has paid for a wedding, for a child's education, for someone's happiness. Its money comes, and it creates a life."
How a Swiss farmer reshapes his fields to fight drought

articles.title: Jaguar Land Rover in talks to sell Defender to Nato countries
articles.summary: Carmaker builds on relationship with British armed forces by seeking to cash in on Europe’s rearmament drive

blocks.text: Jaguar Land Rover is in talks with Nato countries about selling them the newly revamped Defender military vehicle, as the UK-based carmaker seeks to tap into Europe’s defence spending boom.

It is also among carmakers bidding for a UK defence ministry contract worth £900m to replace an ageing fleet of Land Rovers that have been out of production since 2016, competing with General Motors and the UK’s Ineos.

JLR, owned by India’s Tata Motors, has set up a new Defender defence division to explore new partnerships to supply vehicles for people and equipment transportation to defence sectors around the world.

The carmaker is trying to expand beyond its relationship with the British armed forces to exploit a spending boom by Nato countries racing to rearm, as it faces weaker demand elsewhere coupled with higher costs.

JLR insisted that the move, which was first reported by the Financial Times, was not related to its planned 4,000 job cuts globally, as part of an effort to save £1.7bn. It is slashing costs as it struggles with tough trading conditions, Donald Trump’s tariff wars and the fallout from a damaging cyber-attack last year.

As he unveiled three new variants of the Defender Wolf Series II, the next-generation military vehicle, Patrick McGillycuddy, the Defender managing director, said: “Through our newly established Defender defence division, we will offer Defender Wolf Series II to defence organisations worldwide, while also bidding for the UK Ministry of Defence light mobility vehicle tender.”

He said the new 4x4s were “exceptionally robust and versatile,” and added that their lightweight aluminium monocoque construction, with a stiffer body structure, means they can be adapted to the “wide range of roles and operational requirements demanded by military organisations”.

“It is a modern successor to the world-famous Defender Wolf and Land Rovers that have served the British armed forces for more than 70 years,” he said. The new Defender series is designed and engineered in the UK, with an engine built in Wolverhampton.

JLR also wants to break into the $80bn (£59bn) US pickup truck market with a local version of its Defender vehicle. The Defender pickup will be built in the US through a joint venture with Chrysler carmaker Stellantis, the Sunday Times reported at the weekend.
It is the most high-profile UK carmaker to pivot the newly booming defence sector as manufacturers grapple with a transition to electric vehicles and rising competition from Chinese rivals.
after newsletter promotion

Last week, Volkswagen struck a deal to sell its Osnabrück factory to Israel’s Aurelius Capital and VW’s ⁠second-biggest shareholder, its home state of Lower Saxony, in a move labour officials said could save about 1,400 of the site’s 1,800 jobs. The site would switch production from cars to heavy-duty trucks that carry anti-missile systems for the maker of Israel’s Iron Dome, Arrow ‌and David’s ⁠Sling air and missile defence systems.

“These plans involve the potential manufacture of systems and components for air defence systems for Germany and Europe,” Volkswagen said, adding the cooperation could pave the way for further such deals.
Renault is repurposing part of its Le Mans chassis plant in western France to make up to 600 drones a month for the French ministry of defence.

articles.title: Europe launches two climate observation satellites
articles.summary: The European Space Agency has put two satellites into orbit to take a closer look at the impact of climate change. One of them will focus particularly on plant life.

image.caption: The two satellites were carried by a Vega-C rocket, seen here lifting off in French GuianaImage: Ronan Lietar/AFP

blocks.text: Two satellites designed to enhance the monitoring of extreme weather events linked to climate change have been successfully sent into orbit by the European Space Agency (ESA).

The Vega-C rocket carrying the Sentinel-3C and Flex satellites lifted off from the Kourou space center in French Guiana at 10:21 p.m. Monday (0121 GMT Tuesday), with the two spacecraft entering sun-synchronous orbit within two hours of lift-off.
What will the Flex satellite do?

The Flex (Fluorescence Explorer) satellite aims to provide data on the impact of heat waves on plant matter by monitoring the very faint fluorescence emitted by plants when they carry out photosynthesis.
That fluorescence gives an indication of how efficiently vegetation is converting sunlight and carbon dioxide into energy.
The measurements provided by the satellite will thus "help scientists assess plant health, ecosystem productivity and the effects of environmental stress and climate change," according to ESA.
The €350 million ($403.5 million) mission is planned to last three years.
The satellite will orbit the Earth 14 times a day, revisiting particular locations every 27 days.
What is the role of the Sentinel-3C satellite?
The Sentinel-3C satellite is to collect data from the marine environment, including temperature, wave height and ocean currents.
It will also monitor land use and land cover with the aim of optimizing yields to prevent food crises.
Sentinel-3C is part of Copernicus, the Earth observation component of the EU’s space program.
Simonetta Cheli, the director of Earth Observation Programmes at the ESA, described the missions as "essential" in helping with the "climate change we are experiencing."
Edited by Richard Connor

articles.title: US confirms it has weapons in space
articles.summary: The US Space Force justified the weapons deployment by citing its two biggest geopolitical rivals — Russia and China.

image.caption: The Space Force, a relatively new branch of the US military, was created by US President Donald Trump in 2019Image: Cover-Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: The United States has weapons deployed in spatial orbit, the US Space Force said, confirming the existence of such capabilities for the first time.

"The US has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action," a US Space Force spokesperson said in a press release. The statement did not provide specifics on the weapons in question.

"Space control encapsulates the mission areas required to contest and control the space domain — employing kinetic and non-kinetic means to affect adversary capabilities," it said, adding that "these capabilities can be employed for offensive and defensive purposes."
US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink also confirmed the existence of US weapons in space, while speaking at the Air, Space and Cyber Conference on Monday.

The Space Force, the US military's arm dedicated to space, justified the weapons deployment by citing its two biggest geopolitical rivals — Russia and China. It said both countries pose a threat to American interests in space.

China "develops and operates space and counterspace capabilities as part of a military modernization strategy," while Russia "views space as a warfighting domain and believes space supremacy will be a decisive factor in future conflicts," the statement read.
AI and satellites: The new nuclear watchdogs?
The final frontier
The militarization of space is an issue as old as the race to space itself.
In 1967, the world's biggest superpowers and other nations signed the Outer Space Treaty addressing the single biggest concern — deployment of nuclear weapons in space.

Since then, Russia, US, India and China have been exploring ways to fight in space outside of that treaty. That includes targeting each other's satellites critical for military communication, navigation and surveillance.

articles.title: What would it take to make India’s cities better – and safer?
articles.summary:
After a five-storey building collapsed in Delhi, focus is on how urban areas can adapt to growing populations. Plus, Ahmedabad’s ace newspaper delivery driver goes viral

Recently, I may have…

blocks.text: Recently, I may have saved a woman’s life on the road. Somehow, this was something I had expected to happen.

On that day, I saw a truck leave a construction site with a tangled wire trailing behind. I frantically looked to see what the wire was attached to and spotted the scaffolding a few meters ahead. I shrieked and grabbed the hand of the woman walking in front of me just as the metal pipes came crashing down. We hugged for a brief second, and then walked our separate ways.

Mumbai (pictured top) is a city that is being made every day, and so much of the Bandra-Khar area that I inhabit is never not under construction. Since I moved here from Seoul earlier this year, I have learned to be hypervigilant every time I walk the streets.

I was reminded of that moment last week as news broke about the collapse of a five-storey building in Delhi, which killed seven people. Authorities had flagged safety concerns in the neighbourhood months earlier, the Hindustan Times reported, after 23 people died in a fire at another building.

As the world’s most populous country, India can feel like a place where life can be startlingly cheap, and people die every day in tragedies that could have been prevented. According to analysis of government data by the Times of India, between 2020 and 2004 nearly 33,000 deaths occurred due to building collapses, fires or people falling into pits and maintenance holes.

The collapse in Delhi has prompted questions, once again, about the state of urban infrastructure in India’s biggest cities. At a time when the country is undertaking a rapid infrastructure boom – new airports, high-speed expressways, luxury residential towers– daily life in cities like Delhi, Mumbai or Bengaluru appears to be deteriorating.

Indian cities are not walkable, they rank among the worst for air quality, construction is poorly regulated, seasonal flooding is common and waste management remains under pressure. These challenges are only going to increase; the World Bank expects India’s urban population to double, going up to 951 million, by 2050. More than half of the urban infrastructure the country will need by then has yet to be built, it said.

blocks.caption: The problem with India’s roads begins with on-street parking, believe some experts. Photograph: DB Pictures/Alamy

blocks.text: So, what would it take to make our cities better and safer? The experts I spoke to broadly agreed that Indian cities don’t lack rules as much as the political will and institutional machinery to enforce them.

For infrastructure veteran Vinayak Chatterjee, one solution lies in giving urban local bodies more power. He points to a constitutional amendment from 1992 that was meant to strengthen municipalities and give them greater responsibility over urban planning. “But it remains largely unimplemented – in spirit and will. It is a serious matter that affects the very fabric of our urban existence,” said Chatterjee, founder of the Infravision Foundation.

Rahul Goel, an expert on transportation safety and a professor at the Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi, believes the problem with India’s roads begins with on-street parking. “People are using public space for personal use. Everything becomes better when you remove on-street parking,” he said, arguing that freeing up roads would make pedestrians and cyclists safer, reduce traffic jams and make walking easier.

In other cities in the global south, from Bangkok to Manila to Cape Town, one cannot just park their car on the road to run errands, Goel said. He described it as a governance failure, saying there is a need to create more parking spaces and perhaps have civil defense personnel or municipal workers enforce fines.

“Our streets are self-run,” Goel said. “That’s why they are in complete disarray.” He pointed to the Delhi Metro as an example of a space where people follow rules and things are orderly. “When rules are enforced, people follow them.”

blocks.caption: People vacate buildings marked for demolition in Satya Niketan after the collapse of a five-storey building. Photograph: Vishal Kapoor/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The same gap between rules and enforcement is evident at construction sites.

India has detailed guidelines for construction approvals, including how traffic must be managed, what signage must be put up, and creating paths for pedestrians. But compliance remains a significant problem, says Geetam Tiwari, emeritus professor at Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi. In an audit of construction sites on highways, including bridges, Tiwari and her colleagues found widespread violations. Contractors had a financial incentive to complete projects quickly with payments being tied to the pace of construction, she said, adding that penalties for violations were low enough that it was cheaper to simply pay the fine than make fixes.

For unsafe buildings and unauthorised renovations, Tiwari said, the solution also requires bringing stakeholders together: resident associations, landlords, lessees and local authorities to conduct audits, raise awareness and penalise contractors who violate safety requirements. Actions, she said, that should not wait for the next tragedy.

In the aftermath of the Delhi case, the high court has directed authorities to inspect student accommodations for safety. Building owners have been arrested and several municipal officials in charge of the area have been suspended.

A similar governance deficit shows up when it comes to air pollution, another long-time challenge for Indian cities. Ronak Sutaria, founder and CEO of Respirer Living Sciences, has been working on one aspect of this issue: by developing affordable air-quality monitors for construction sites. Respirer’s air-quality monitors are now installed in 5,000 locations across 10 cities in India, helping authorities identify pollution hotspots. (Some cities, including Mumbai, require construction sites to monitor pollution levels.)

“A number of sites are getting alerts [from authorities] and are taking dust-suppression measures, for instance, to bring down [pollution] levels. So, the entire loop is sort of working,” Sutaria said.

Indian cities continue to grow, but the question is whether governance can keep pace. On that afternoon in Bandra, I recall thinking how lucky the woman and I were not to be grievously injured. But we shouldn’t have to rely on luck to survive.
What else we’re reading about

blocks.caption: Xi Jinping, far right, with Russia’s Vladimir Putin and India’s Narendra Modi at this year’s Brics summit. Photograph: Alexander Kazakov/Sputnik/Kremlin Pool/EPA

blocks.text: New Delhi declaration | The Brics summit held in New Delhi over the weekend adopted a declaration with Iran and the United Arab Emirates agreeing to a late-stage compromise on the language about the war in the Middle East. Chinese president, Xi Jinping, who visited India for the first time in almost seven years, announced that China would helm the group’s presidency for the next year.

Political donations | An investigation by the BBC’s Shubhangi Misra claimed that six unrecognised political parties registered in Gujarat received donations of £132m (Rs 1,700 crore) in 2023-24, higher than the income of national parties excluding the BJP. Despite fielding few candidates and evidence of little political activity, the high amounts expose glaring gaps in oversight of political finances.

Women’s health support | Two south Indian states, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, have recently announced policies aimed at supporting women through perimenopause and menopause. Karnataka plans to introduce a women’s health programme that will integrate menopause into the public health system. Tamil Nadu will assess the physical and mental health needs of perimenopausal women.
after newsletter promotion

Calling all emerging writers | Applications are open for South Asia Speaks, a wonderful platform for emerging writers from the region offering free, year-long mentorship and resources to develop a book-length project. The deadline is 30 September – find out more and apply here.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste

blocks.caption: Poet Parag Pawan’s book.

blocks.text: This week, write and professor Amitava Kumar (@amitavawriter), whose latest book, The Social Life of Trains, explores how railways helped shape India’s national identity, suggests the work of a poet he discovered on Instagram:

“Can I begin with a confession? I have been a professor of literature for more than three decades, but I don’t often understand poems. How lovely it is, then, to discover a poet whose lines are as clear and beautiful as the dawn! Recently, I came across the poems of a young Hindi poet named Parag Pawan. They spoke to me and, more importantly, they spoke to our moment. I immediately sat down to translate them into English.

A series of his poems could be translated as Poems for the Unemployed. One of the poems, sharp and precise, begins with the funny, acerbic lines: ‘On the topic of our unemployment / the prime minister gives speeches / but he doesn’t give us jobs. / He works for eighteen hours / while we believe that asking anyone to work / for more than eight hours / is exploitation.’”
Count it
A number worth knowing

blocks.caption: Umar Khalid, who has spent six years in an Indian jail without trial.

blocks.text: That’s the number of days Umar Khalid has spent in jail since his arrest on 13 September 2020 – without trial. Last week, the student activist wrote a searing account describing the daily drudgery of life in prison, published in The Quint. Earlier this year, in his first interview since being jailed, Khalid told the Guardian’s Hannah Ellis-Peterson: “Humanity is a privilege that is not granted to people like me.”
Vibe check

blocks.caption: World’s fastest paper delivery service? Ayan Shaikh at work in Ahmedabad. Photograph: Instagram

blocks.text: As more people read news online, watching Ayan Shaikh (@paperboy_ayan) delivering newspapers with serious swag gave me great joy and some hope. The 22-year-old from Ahmedabad posts videos of it on Instagram, and it’s a feat to watch. Watch his papers swerve, reach gravity-defying heights and land with pinpoint accuracy and tell me his deliveries don’t rival Jasprit Bumrah.

Delivering papers was Shaikh’s first job after he dropped out of school. He spent four years mastering the techniques that would allow him to make faster deliveries to earn more money. The first video, filmed by his friend, had 20m views and a recent one has crossed 128m, more views than many Bollywood stars might command. He starts his day at 4:30am, making 300 deliveries in two hours, before he begins a second shift as a gig worker for quick commerce apps.

“I think people love [the videos] because I do it passionately … from my heart,” he said. “If you do things dedicatedly, anything is possible. It won’t work out once, twice, thrice, but it might on the fourth attempt.”
Get in touch

Do you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us at thisisindia@theguardian.com and we may include your response in a future issue.

articles.title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire
articles.summary: The state post service delivers pensions, medicine and letters to people just miles from the front.

blocks.text: Watch: Ukraine's post office innovation helps isolated communities
By
Reporting fromZaporizhzhia oblast
Every morning Igor Smelyansky looks at a vast map of Ukraine on his office wall and decides where he should put his people in harm's way.
His aides provide him with live intelligence about Russian attacks and he deploys his teams, balancing their potential operational success against risk to life or limb.
But Smelyansky is no military commander. He is the head of Ukraine's state postal service, Ukrposhta.
And every day he must decide how far to send his postmen and women into the deadly "kill zone" along the front lines where the threat of drone attack is ever present.
"If it's too dangerous to go today, we won't go," Smelyansky told us. "We'll go tomorrow, or we'll go somewhere else. The key is to be as agile as you can."

Ukrposhta does more than just collect letters and parcels. It pays out pensions in hard cash, it takes payment for utility bills. And it delivers vital food and medicine to people on the margins of society.

As such, it offers a lifeline to millions of poor and elderly Ukrainians living in remote villages where shops are rare and trips to the city are expensive and dangerous. In a vast rural nation wracked by war, Ukrposhta is part of the glue that holds the country together.

blocks.caption: Map of Ukraine showing areas under Russian military control. Territories under Russian control are shaded pink, including Crimea, most of the occupied areas of Donetsk, large parts of Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions, and a continuous belt of territory along the Sea of Azov connecting Crimea to e…

blocks.text: That has made the service a target for Russia - which in recent months has stepped up not only its attacks on postmen and women but also sorting offices and logistical hubs. The Kremlin has claimed strikes like this are retaliation for Ukrainian attacks on Russian online retailers like Wildberries.

Speaking in his imposing Soviet-era office building that overlooks Kyiv's famous Maidan square, Smelyansky said: "If we don't go [to a village], we don't have basic supply. We don't have food. We don't have medicine. People will struggle. If we do go, they may delay a decision to evacuate from the areas they probably should have evacuated."
There are many risks. If a post van turns up unannounced, a crowd can form, creating a target for an opportunistic Russian drone operator. But if they call ahead, information could leak.
"Is it a danger?" Smelyansky said. "Absolutely. Because there are Russian sympathisers who can give them the location of the truck that's coming."

blocks.caption: Igor Smelyansky stands in his blue Ukrposhta shirt and smiles at the camera. He has greying dark hair, and wears stubble with a smile

blocks.text: BBC
By attacking Ukrposhta, you put pressure on people… who are depending on the truck coming in

blocks.caption: "By attacking Ukrposhta, you put pressure on people… who are depending on the truck coming in", Source: Igor Smelyansky, Source description: Head of Ukrposhta, Image: Igor Smelyansky stands in his blue Ukrposhta shirt and smiles at the camera. He has greying dark hair, and wears stubble with a smile

blocks.text: If Smelyansky chooses not to send a van in, he faces criticism. "You get messages from people from those villages: 'You betrayed us. You didn't come...' But if I go, I may risk the life of the driver."

Smelyansky says Russia is deliberately targeting his staff because of the vital role they play shoring up Ukraine's resilience, helping people stay alive in their homes through the fighting and bitter winters.
"It's not an accident, it's deliberate," he said. "By attacking Ukrposhta, you put pressure on people… who are depending on the truck coming in." Russia denies targeting civilians.
Since 2022, hundreds of Ukrposhta branches and vehicles have been hit, and more than 50 staff have lost their lives, either on the frontline or on their rounds, according to Ukrposhta.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A file photo of a Ukrposhta post office damaged during strikes in Kyiv in April

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
A file photo of a Ukrposhta post office damaged during strikes in Kyiv in April
We travelled with Kateryna Marynych, a 38-year-old postmistress, near Zaporizhzhia - a city not too far from the southern frontlines.

She lost her home and her husband during the full-scale invasion, and came to the area to rebuild her life. She ran the post office in the village of Lukasheve for two years until it was destroyed in March by a Russian drone, targeting soldiers working nearby.
After her van drew up, a steady queue of elderly folk formed. She sat in the front passenger seat, window open, handing out cash, taking payments.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ukraine's post office provides a vital lifeline for people near the front, delivering pensions and medicine

blocks.text: Ukraine's post office provides a vital lifeline for people near the front, delivering pensions and medicine

One customer, Nadiia, said she was grateful: "It's a long way for us to travel to Zaporizhzhia. Especially now, at a time when there are attacks all around us. The fact that they come here is really nice."

Oleksandrivna, 77, arrived wearing a purple dressing gown, walking with a crutch. When I asked her where she would be without Kateryna, she replied: "We would be stuffed! I am just out of hospital after a stroke. Where could I go for my medicine?"

But Mykola, 64, pointed to another service the post office provides to a largely elderly population. "It is very important," he said. "It's one of the few joys of the month: you come out, have a chat with people, collect your pension, and go home."
For many people in remote communities, Kateryna can be their last link with the Ukrainian state.

She says she hopes her customers are proud of her. "They love me, they need me," she said. "They are waiting for me. Sometimes they call me, especially after attacks on Zaporizhzhia and ask me how I am. We are like a big family. My attitude towards them is like a grandmother or grandfather."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Kateryna Marynych has lost her home and her husband in this war - now, she's also lost her post office

blocks.text: Kateryna Marynych has lost her home and her husband in this war - now, she's also lost her post office

The attacks on Ukrposhta form part of Russia's wider escalation of its war on Ukraine, stepping up fast drone attacks on civilian infrastructure including business infrastructure, energy facilities, transport networks and border posts. Analysts say that as Russia's invasion stagnates on the battlefield in the east, it is looking for other ways of putting pressure on Kyiv.

For safety, Kateryna always travels with her partner, Slava, who drives. While she sorts the cash, he works from the back of the van, taking and receiving parcels, delivering food and water. He also carries a side-arm in a holster, for personal protection; these vans carry a lot of cash.

Both wear body armour when close to the front line. And they have an antenna in the van that shows them the location of the small first-person-view drones that render the frontline so deadly. They have seen drones from the car but luckily have not yet been hit.
She accepted her job was dangerous but would never change it. "It is my work," she said. "If I can't, who will do my job?"
Ukraine's defence comes in many forms - and it's not always delivered at the barrel of a gun.
Additional reporting by Mariana Matveichuk

articles.title: Houthis seize strategic Red Sea islands as analysts warn of impending oil crunch
articles.summary:
The militant group in Yemen captured the islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish, near the chokepoint of the Bab al-Mandab strait

Yemen’s Houthi rebels have seized two strategic islands in the…

blocks.text: Yemen’s Houthi rebels have seized two strategic islands in the Red Sea, reinforcing the Iran-backed group’s ability to control a key shipping route, as concerns mount that the world is facing a new oil supply crisis.

The seizure of the islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish is the latest in the militant group’s swift advance across Yemen’s Red Sea coast, after the capture of the port of Mokha and Perim island in the Bab al-Mandab strait.
The islands lie 160km north of the strait which is a chokepoint that connects the Red Sea to the open ocean and Saudi Arabia’s key Asian markets.

The speed of the Houthis’ advance has left Yemen’s Saudi-backed government trying to claw back territory captured by the militants in recent days, while Riyadh grapples with attacks on a critical oil pipeline by Iran-allied militants in Iraq.

Threats from Houthis have left Saudi Arabia on high alert, with air alerts flashing across the country daily, while a series of attacks carried out by the militant group using ballistic missiles and drones wounded 13 civilians on Monday.

Nearly 94,000 people in Yemen have fled their homes since fighting between Iran-backed Houthi rebels and government forces escalated this month, the International Organization for Migration said on Monday. About 200 schools have been converted to shelters in south-western Yemen to absorb an influx of families, the International Rescue Committee said.

More than 2,000 people have reportedly fled across the sea into Djibouti. The Houthi advance puts them just 32km from a US military base in the tiny country on the Horn of Africa, on the other side of the Bab al-Mandab strait.

On Monday, experts warned that the closure of Saudi Arabia’s east-west pipeline – which has been vital for Riyadh to move oil from the strait of Hormuz to the Red Sea export hub of Yanbu – will further pile pressure on its shipments and global oil supplies. Officials have estimated it could take weeks to fully repair it.

“The big question for traders right now is ​the duration of the east-west ‌outage. Any prolonged ​disruption and the associated supply ​loss could easily push prices to the next level higher,” said Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade.

Research company Rystad Energy said on Monday that since late August, an average 2.6m to 4m barrels of oil a day moved through the pipeline and out of the port of Yanbu – a volume it said was now at risk of “disappearing from the market”.

Janiv Shah, vice-president of oil markets for Rystad Energy, noted the recent jump in Brent prices proved the market was already responding to “a significant loss of supply”. Saudi inventories could sustain exports in the coming days, but that could “change quickly,” Shah added.

On Tuesday morning, Brent crude oil rose 1.17% to $106.92 a barrel. The average price of diesel in the US hit $6 per gallon for the first time last week, as the Iran war, combined with Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, squeezed supply.

The Houthi leadership has said it is not seeking to block all commercial shipping in the Red Sea, only Saudi-linked ships. Supplies from Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest exporter of oil, are vital to economies in Africa and Asia, which rely on oil imports from the Middle East and have been hit hardest by the disruption in trade.
Experts say the stock buffers that existed in the system earlier this year, shielding the world from the worst effects of an oil shock by limiting price increases, have now largely disappeared.

Since the war began in February, countries have released some crude stockpiles to the market, ⁠and the US also lifted restrictions on oil stored on ships floating at sea from countries ​under sanctions. Those buffers have now ‌been “played out”, Chevron CEO Mike ⁠Wirth said on Friday.
“It’s harder to envision a scenario ‌where prices soften and quickly,” he said. “I think the risks remain to the upside over the next few months.“

articles.title: NATO jets shoot down drone over Lithuania
articles.summary: Lithuania has reported frequent drone incursions since Moscow launched its war against Ukraine. Lithuanian media reports suggest the drone was coming from Russia ally Belarus.

image.caption: Gitanas Nauseda thanked the NATO military alliance for its 'swift response'Image: Jouni Porsanger/Lehtikuva/REUTERS

blocks.text: A drone entered Lithuania's airspace before NATO fighter jets shot it down, the Baltic country's president said in the early hours of Tuesday.
Gitanas Nauseda thanked the military alliance for its "swift response."
"With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region. Together with our NATO Allies, Lithuania will defend its airspace," Nauseda wrote on X.
What do we know about the latest drone incident?

Lithuanian national radio LRT cited preliminary data from the National Crisis Management Center (NKVC) as saying the drone came from neighboring Belarus, an ally of Russia. It was heading west as it was shot.
The broadcaster reported that the drone fell in a rural area near Lake Kaunas, in the center of Lithuania.
Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys said the NATO response sent "a clear message that NATO stands vigilant, committed, and ready."

Lithuania shares a border with Russia's Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad as well as Belarus. Since Russia's fullscale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, such drone incursions have been common in Lithuania, as well as NATO members Latviaand Estonia.
